sections.title: Money & You
sections.blurb: Where money comes from, what you keep, and how to plan a month.

units.title: Being responsible with money
units.blurb: What it means to be financially responsible, and where your habits come from.

levels.title: Money is limited
learn: Tell a need from a want.
See that spending on one thing means not spending on another.

cards.text: Nobody has unlimited money. Because money is limited, you cannot buy everything you would like. Each time you spend, you are choosing.

image.alt: A small coin purse beside a tall shelf crowded with blank boxes

cards.text: A need is something you must have to live and work, such as food, a place to stay, and a way to get to school or work. A want is something you would like but could live without.

image.alt: Bread and a bus pass on one side of a table, a toy robot and a party hat on the other

cards.text: One thing can hold both. You need food, but a restaurant meal is a want. Ask what the person really needs, then what is extra.

image.alt: A plain sandwich in a lunch box next to a fancy covered restaurant plate

cards.text: When you spend on one thing, you give up what else that money could buy. The best other thing you give up is the opportunity cost. A trade-off is giving up one thing to get another.

image.alt: A balance scale with a ticket shape on one pan and gold coins on the other

cards.text: Dev has $40.00 to spend this week. Each choice leaves a different amount for everything else. A $25.00 ticket leaves $15.00.

questions.label: Pick the need
questions.prompt: Priya is deciding what to buy this week. Which one is a need?

terms.meaning: Something you must have to live and work, such as food or a way to get to work.
Something you would like to have but could live without.

questions.hint: A need is something you must have to live and work.

options.text: A third pair of running shoes
options.why: Shoes can be useful, but a third pair is something she would like, not something she must have.
Yes. Food is something you must have to live, so it is a need.
A game skin is fun, but nobody needs it to live or work.
A concert is a want. She can live well without it.

questions.label: Why choose
questions.prompt: Why does everyone have to make choices about money?
questions.hint: Think about what happens when money runs out.

options.text: Money is limited, so spending on one thing leaves less for others
options.why: Right. Limited money is the reason for every trade-off.

options.text: Stores only sell a few things
options.why: There are plenty of things to buy. The limit is the money, not the products.

options.text: Only people with low pay need to choose
options.why: Everyone has limited money, so everyone trades off, just with different amounts.
Prices do move, but even steady prices mean you cannot buy everything.

questions.label: Opportunity cost
questions.prompt: Mei has $30.00. She could buy a haircut or a book she really wants. She buys the haircut. What is her opportunity cost?

terms.meaning: The best other thing you give up when you choose one thing.

questions.hint: It is the best thing you give up.

options.why: The haircut is what she got. The opportunity cost is what she gave up for it.

options.text: Nothing, since she got what she paid for
options.why: She did give something up. The same $30.00 cannot also buy the book.
She spent all $30.00, and the cost is what she gave up, not what is left.

options.text: The book she did not buy
options.why: Yes. The opportunity cost is the best thing she gave up.

questions.label: Money left
questions.prompt: Dev has $40.00 and buys a $25.00 ticket. How much is left for everything else?
questions.hint: Subtract the price from what Dev had.
questions.why: Money left is what you had minus what you spent.
questions.miss: Take the price of the ticket away from the $40.00.

traps.why: That adds the price to the money. Spending takes money away, so subtract.

questions.label: Two purchases
questions.prompt: Amir has $50.00. He spends $18.00 on food out and $14.00 on a game. How much does he have left?
questions.hint: Find the total spent first.
questions.why: Add what he spent, then take it from what he had.
questions.miss: Add the two purchases first. Then subtract the total from $50.00.

traps.why: That is the total Amir spent. The question asks what is left.

questions.label: Spot the trade-off
questions.prompt: Which sentence describes a trade-off?

terms.meaning: Giving up one thing to get or keep another.

questions.hint: A trade-off gives something up to get something else.

options.why: That is about prices changing. A trade-off is about giving one thing up for another.

options.text: A bank keeps your money safe
options.why: That is what a bank does. It is not a choice between two things.

options.text: Spending $20.00 on a hoodie leaves $20.00 less for other things
options.why: Yes. Getting one thing costs you the chance to use that money on something else.
That is a feeling, not a choice that gives something up.

questions.label: Find the price
questions.prompt: Dev has $40.00. Tap the item that would leave Dev with $28.00.
questions.hint: Take each price away from $40.00 until you reach $28.00.
questions.why: $40.00 - $12.00 = $28.00, so the cards are the bar.
questions.miss: That item does not leave $28.00. Subtract each price from $40.00 and compare.

questions.label: Pick the want
questions.prompt: Lena buys a bus pass to get to work and a $5.00 drink at a cafe. Which one is the want?

terms.meaning: Something you would like to have but could live without.

questions.hint: Which one could she live and work without?

options.why: The pass is how she gets to work, so it is a need.
Yes. She can live and work without it. The pass gets her to work, so it is a need.
A drink is nice, but nobody must have it to live or work.
The pass is a need because she needs it to get to work.

levels.title: When the money shrinks
learn: See what a person cuts first and what they protect.
Work out a cut as dollars and as a percent.

cards.text: Sometimes money shrinks. Shifts get cut, a gift stops, or a bill goes up. Then you cannot keep every spending line the same. Something has to get smaller.

image.alt: A full stack of gold coins beside a shorter stack, a blank calendar behind

cards.text: What a person cuts first, and what they protect, shows what matters most to them. Two people with the same smaller amount can choose differently. That is a difference in what they value.

image.alt: Two open boxes of gold coins, each with a different group of coins under a glass dome

cards.text: Kit spends $200.00 in a month. Then Kit's money shrinks to $130.00. Here is how Kit changed each line.
To compare a cut, work out the cut and the percent cut. Cut = before - after. Percent cut = cut / before x 100. Fun went from $50.00 to $15.00. That is a cut of $35.00, which is 70% of the fun line.

image.alt: A tall stack of gold coins with most coins lifted off by a small crane

cards.text: A share is one part of the whole. Food was $60.00 of $200.00, a 30% share. After the cut it is $55.00 of $130.00, about 42%. A line can shrink in dollars and still take a bigger share.

image.alt: A round pie-shaped coin with one large slice pulled out beside it

questions.label: Biggest cut
questions.prompt: Kit cut every line when money shrank. Which line was cut by the most dollars?
questions.hint: Cut = before - after. Compare the Cut column.

options.why: Yes. Fun fell by $35.00, the biggest cut in dollars.
Food fell by only $5.00.
Saving fell by $15.00. That is large, but fun fell by more.
Gifts fell by $10.00, less than fun.

questions.label: Total cut
questions.prompt: Kit's month shrank from $200.00 to $130.00. How much did the month fall by?
questions.hint: Subtract the new amount from the old one.
questions.why: The fall is what Kit had before minus what Kit has now.
questions.miss: Take the smaller month away from the bigger one.

traps.why: That adds the two months. A fall is the difference, so subtract.

questions.label: Fun percent
questions.prompt: Fun went from $50.00 to $15.00. What percent of the fun line was cut?

terms.meaning: One part of a whole, often shown as a percent.

questions.hint: Cut divided by the starting amount, then x 100.
questions.why: Percent cut is the cut divided by the starting amount.
questions.miss: Find the cut in dollars first. Then divide by the starting $50.00.

traps.why: That is the cut in dollars. Divide it by the $50.00 you started with to get a percent.

questions.label: Saving percent
questions.prompt: Saving went from $30.00 to $15.00. What percent of the saving line was cut?
questions.hint: Divide the cut by $30.00.
questions.why: The cut was half of what saving started as.
questions.miss: Find the cut in dollars, then divide it by the starting $30.00.

traps.why: That is the cut in dollars, not a percent.

questions.label: Food share
questions.prompt: After the cut, food is $55.00 of Kit's $130.00 month. About what percent share is that? (to the nearest whole percent)

terms.meaning: One part of a whole, often shown as a percent.

questions.hint: Divide the food line by the new total.
questions.why: A share is the part divided by the whole.
questions.miss: Divide $55.00 by the new total of $130.00, then x 100.

traps.why: That was the share before the cut ($60.00 of $200.00). Use the new total.

questions.label: Same cut
questions.prompt: Two people each lose $70.00 from a $200.00 month. One cuts mostly fun. The other cuts mostly saving. What does this show?
questions.hint: Think about what each person kept.

options.text: One of them did the arithmetic wrong
options.why: Both cut $70.00. The difference is where the cut fell, not the math.
They each lost $70.00 from $200.00, so their months are the same size.

options.text: One of them cut too much
options.why: Both cut the same total. They simply chose different lines.

options.text: They protected different things, which shows different priorities
options.why: Yes. What a person protects when money shrinks shows what matters to them.

questions.label: Largest percent
questions.prompt: Tap the line that was cut by the largest percent.
questions.hint: Compare the heights of the five bars.
questions.why: Fun was cut by 70%, the largest percent of the five.
questions.miss: That bar is not the tallest. Compare all five heights.

questions.label: Name the idea
questions.prompt: Kit gives up some fun to keep food. What is this called?

terms.meaning: Giving up one thing to get or keep another.

questions.hint: Giving one thing up to keep another.

options.why: A refund is money given back. Kit is making a choice.
A bonus is extra money. Kit has less money.
Yes. Kit gives up one thing to keep another.
A bill is a payment that is owed. Kit is choosing what to cut.

levels.title: Rules you did not choose
learn: See that many money rules were picked up, not chosen.
Spot the rule behind a choice.

cards.text: Most of us heard things about money long before we had any. "Save for a rainy day." "Quality lasts." Short sayings are easy to remember, so they stay with us.

image.alt: A coat on a hook and an open blank notebook with a pencil beside a rainy window

cards.text: A saying you hear often can turn into a rule. You do not decide on it. You just follow it. "Save for a rainy day" can become the rule: always set some money aside.

image.alt: A path of worn stepping stones across a small garden stream

cards.text: Rules come from many places: people around us, school, what we see online, and what happens to us. Most were picked up, not chosen. We often do not notice that we follow them.

image.alt: A ring of blank speech bubbles drifting toward a plain coin purse

cards.text: A rule can help, or it can get in your way. A good question is: do I still agree with this rule? You are allowed to keep a rule, change it, or let it go.

image.alt: A signpost with three blank arrows at a fork in a path

cards.text: Here are some sayings and the rules they can become.

figure.title: A saying and the rule it can become
rows: Pay more for something that lasts

questions.label: Where from
questions.prompt: Where do many of our rules about money come from?
questions.hint: Think about who and what is around you as you grow up.

options.text: A law every adult must follow
options.why: There is no law for most personal money rules. They are habits we pick up.

options.text: What we heard and saw around us over the years
options.why: Yes. Most rules are picked up from the people and places around us.

options.text: A test we take in school
options.why: Tests may check what we know, but our rules mostly come from daily life.

options.text: A plan we wrote at age ten
options.why: Most people did not write them. They were picked up without deciding.

questions.label: Spot the saying
questions.prompt: Noor follows the rule "never pay full price." Which saying could be behind it?
questions.hint: Which saying leads to waiting for a lower price?

options.text: A bargain is worth waiting for
options.why: Yes. Waiting for a lower price fits the rule "never pay full price."
That saying leads toward spending now, the opposite of waiting.
Sharing is about giving. It does not explain the sale rule.

options.text: Always borrow when you need to
options.why: Borrowing is about getting money, not about the price.

questions.label: Rule in action
questions.prompt: Ravi gets $100.00 as a gift. He keeps $80.00 in savings and spends $20.00. Which rule fits what Ravi did?
questions.hint: Look at how much he kept.

options.text: Spend gifts the day you get them
options.why: He kept most of his gift, so this does not fit.
He saved $80.00, so he does not follow this rule.
Nothing in what he did points to friends.

options.text: Keep most of any money that comes in
options.why: Yes. He kept most of the gift, which fits that rule.

questions.label: Ten percent
questions.prompt: Jun follows the rule "put 10% of any money I get aside." Jun gets $60.00 for a birthday. How much does Jun put aside?
questions.hint: 10% is the same as dividing by 10.
questions.why: Ten percent is one tenth.
questions.miss: Ten percent of an amount is one tenth of it.

traps.why: That is what is left after the tenth is set aside. The question asks for the tenth.

questions.label: Ten percent more
questions.prompt: Jun is paid $85.00 for a weekend job. Using the same rule, how much does Jun put aside?
questions.hint: Divide by 10.
questions.why: One tenth of $85.00.
questions.miss: Divide the $85.00 by 10.

traps.why: That is what is left after the tenth is set aside. The question asks for the tenth.

questions.label: Find the amount
questions.prompt: Jun puts 10% of each amount aside. Tap the amount where Jun sets aside $8.00.
questions.hint: Ten percent is one tenth. Which amount, divided by 10, gives $8.00?
questions.why: 10% of $80.00 is $8.00, so the third bar.
questions.miss: That is not it. Take a tenth of each amount and see which gives $8.00.

questions.label: Rules are
questions.prompt: Which statement about money rules is true?
questions.hint: Think about the cards.

options.why: Most rules were picked up from around us, not chosen with care.
People can look at a rule again and change it.

options.text: Many are picked up without us deciding on them
options.why: Yes. We often follow rules we never chose.
Children pick up money rules too, often long before they have money.

questions.label: Good question
questions.prompt: Maya notices she follows the rule "never ask for help with money." What does the unit suggest she ask herself?
questions.hint: The cards give a good question.

options.text: How can I follow it even harder?
options.why: The point is to check the rule, not to push it further.

options.text: Do I still agree with this rule?
options.why: Yes. Looking at a rule again is how you decide whether to keep it.

options.text: Why did nobody ever stop me?
options.why: This puts the blame on others. The useful step is to look at the rule.

options.text: Is it too late to change?
options.why: People can change a rule at any age.

questions.label: Rule and cut
questions.prompt: Ana follows the rule "save first." Her month shrinks from $200.00 to $130.00. Which line will her rule protect most?
questions.hint: Her rule says what comes first.

options.why: Yes. A "save first" rule protects the saving line when money shrinks.
Her rule puts saving first, so fun is more likely to be cut.
Her rule is about saving, not gifts.
A rule shows up as a choice. It will decide what Ana protects.

levels.title: What people value
learn: Name four kinds of values and spot them in spending.
See that no kind is better than another.

cards.text: A value is something that matters a lot to you. What a person spends on, and what they protect when money is short, often shows their values. People value different things.

image.alt: Three small gift boxes with plain ribbons standing in a row on a shelf

cards.text: One way to sort values is into four kinds. Inner values are about who you are: freedom, peace of mind, a sense of purpose. Social values are about people: helping, giving, belonging.

image.alt: A glowing lantern on a table beside two mugs and a blank card

cards.text: Physical values are about the things around you: comfort, quality, a place you like. Financial values are about security: a cushion for surprises, saving, not running short.

image.alt: A sturdy wooden chair and a lamp in a cosy corner beside a small locked coin box

cards.text: There is no best kind. Most people care about all four and lean toward one or two. The lean can change as life changes. Here is one made-up month, sorted by kind.

figure.title: Lee's $200.00 month, by kind of value

cards.text: Spending alone does not tell you everything. A new coat could come from comfort (physical) or from wanting to fit in (social). To read a value, ask why a person spends, not only what.

image.alt: A winter coat on a hook with two blank thought bubbles above it

questions.label: What a value is
questions.prompt: What is a value?

terms.meaning: Something that matters a lot to you.

questions.hint: Think of what matters to you.

options.why: A price is what you pay. A value is about what matters to you.

options.text: An amount in a savings account
options.why: That is a balance. A value is something you care about.

options.text: A rule a store makes you follow
options.why: A store rule is a policy. A value is personal.

options.text: Something that matters a lot to you
options.why: Yes. Values are what matter most to a person.

questions.label: Match: inner
questions.prompt: Tam pays for a pottery class because making things gives Tam a sense of purpose. Which kind of value is this mainly?
questions.hint: Who is it about?

options.why: Social is about other people. Tam's reason is personal.
Physical is about the things around you, such as comfort or quality.
Yes. A sense of purpose is about who you are.
Financial is about security and saving.

questions.label: Match: social
questions.prompt: Ola buys a gift for a friend and chips in for a team fundraiser. Which kind of value is this mainly?
questions.hint: Who is the money for?

options.why: Inner is about who you are and your purpose.
Yes. Giving and belonging are social values.
Physical is about things and comfort.
Financial is about security and saving.

questions.label: Match: financial
questions.prompt: Bea keeps a cushion for surprises and checks her balance before she buys anything. Which kind of value is this mainly?
questions.hint: Read the card on physical and financial values again.

options.why: Yes. A cushion and not running short are about security, a financial value.
Inner is about purpose and freedom.
Social is about other people.
Physical is about things and comfort.

questions.label: Social share
questions.prompt: Read the figure. What percent of Lee's $200.00 goes to social values?

terms.meaning: One part of a whole, often shown as a percent.

questions.hint: Social is $60.00 of $200.00.
questions.why: Share = part / whole.
questions.miss: Divide the social amount by Lee's whole month.

traps.why: That is the amount in dollars. Divide it by the $200.00 whole.

questions.label: Social gap
questions.prompt: Read the figure. How much more does Lee put toward social than toward financial?
questions.hint: Subtract the smaller bar from the larger.
questions.why: The gap is the difference.
questions.miss: Take the financial bar away from the social bar.

questions.label: Find the quarter
questions.prompt: One kind gets 25% of Lee's $200.00. Tap that bar.
questions.hint: What is 25% of $200.00?
questions.why: 25% of $200.00 is $50.00, which is the financial bar.
questions.miss: That bar is not $50.00. Work out 25% of $200.00 first.

questions.label: Which suggests
questions.prompt: When money shrinks, Sky cuts treats for self but still pays for a friend's gift. What does this suggest?
questions.hint: Think about what Sky protected.

options.why: Nothing here says Sky has a problem. It shows what Sky protects.
There is no mistake. Sky made a choice that fits Sky's values.
Everyone values something. Sky protected the gift.

options.text: Social values matter a lot to Sky
options.why: Yes. What a person protects shows what matters to them.

questions.label: No best kind
questions.prompt: Which statement matches the cards?
questions.hint: Look at the card about "no best kind".

options.text: Everyone should value financial things most
options.why: The cards say there is no best kind.

options.text: A person can have only one kind
options.why: Most people care about all four and lean toward one or two.

options.text: No kind of value is better than another
options.why: Yes. People lean differently, and that is fine.
The cards say a person's lean can change as life changes.

levels.title: Habits: plan, save, borrow with care
learn: Say what a habit is and name three money habits.
See how small habits add up.

cards.text: A habit is something you do without deciding each time. Brushing your teeth is a habit. So is checking a price before you pay. Money habits are what you do with money on a normal day.

image.alt: A toothbrush in a glass beside a small notepad and a pencil on a shelf

cards.text: Habits begin like rules: you pick them up. The good news is you can build new ones. A habit forms when you repeat something, like setting money aside the day you are paid.

image.alt: A row of small potted seedlings growing taller from left to right

cards.text: Three money habits come up again and again in this course. Budgeting is planning what money is for before you spend it. Saving and investing is keeping some for later and letting it grow.

image.alt: An open blank notebook beside a small piggy bank and a tiny watering can

cards.text: The third habit is borrowing with care. It means borrowing only what you can pay back, and paying on time. Paying on time builds a record that lenders can see. A lender is a person or business that lends money and expects it back.

image.alt: A small lantern lighting a narrow wooden bridge over a gap, a coin on each side

cards.text: Here are the three habits side by side.

figure.title: Three money habits
rows: Plan what money is for before you spend it
Keep some for later and let it grow
Borrow what you can pay back, and pay on time

cards.text: Small habits add up. If you set aside $20.00 each week, you have $520.00 after 26 weeks and $1,040.00 after a year (20 x 52).

questions.label: What a habit is
questions.prompt: What is a habit?

terms.meaning: Something you do without deciding each time.

questions.hint: Think of brushing your teeth.

options.text: A big purchase you plan once
options.why: A one-time purchase is a decision. A habit repeats.

options.text: Something you do without deciding each time
options.why: Yes. A habit runs on its own once it is built.

options.text: A rule a bank makes you follow
options.why: A bank rule is a policy. A habit is what you do yourself.

options.text: A bill that arrives every month
options.why: A bill is a cost. A habit is what you do.

questions.label: Pick the habit
questions.prompt: Dan writes down what each dollar of his pay is for before he spends any of it. Which money habit is this?

terms.meaning: A plan for what each dollar of a month is for.

questions.hint: It is about planning before you spend.

options.why: Yes. Planning what money is for before you spend it is budgeting.
That is keeping some for later and letting it grow.
That is about borrowing what you can pay back and paying on time.

questions.label: The record
questions.prompt: Which habit is about building the record that lenders look at?

terms.meaning: A person or business that lends money and expects it back.

questions.hint: Read the card about lenders again.

options.why: Budgeting is planning your money, not a record lenders read.
Saving is keeping money for later. It does not build that record.
Yes. Paying back on time builds the record that lenders look at.

questions.label: Bill surprise
questions.prompt: Lia sees that her phone bill is due in 3 days and she did not plan for it. Which habit would have helped her see it coming?
questions.hint: Which habit plans ahead?

options.why: Saving builds money for later but does not show what bills are coming.
Yes. A budget lists what money is for, including bills that are coming.
Nothing here is about borrowing. The problem is not planning ahead.

questions.label: Half a year
questions.prompt: Sam sets aside $20.00 each week. How much is that after 26 weeks?
questions.hint: Weekly amount x number of weeks.
questions.why: Multiply the weekly amount by the number of weeks.
questions.miss: Multiply the $20.00 by 26.

questions.label: A whole year
questions.prompt: Priya sets aside $15.00 each week. How much is that after 52 weeks?
questions.hint: There are 52 weeks in a year.
questions.why: Weekly amount times 52.
questions.miss: Multiply the $15.00 by the 52 weeks in a year.

traps.why: That multiplies by 12 months. The $15.00 is a weekly amount, so use 52.

questions.label: Reach $780
questions.prompt: At $20.00 a week, tap the bar where the total reaches $780.00.
questions.hint: Divide $780.00 by $20.00 to find the weeks.
questions.why: $20.00 x 39 weeks = $780.00, the third bar.
questions.miss: That bar is not $780.00. Read the value on each bar.

questions.label: How it forms
questions.prompt: Ana has a rule: "save first." What turns that rule into a habit?
questions.hint: Think about brushing your teeth.

options.why: Reading is a start, but a habit needs repeating.

options.text: Repeating it until it runs on its own
options.why: Yes. Repeating is what builds a habit.

options.text: Waiting until you feel like it
options.why: A habit runs even when you do not feel like it.
A friend might help, but the habit comes from doing it.

levels.title: What a month costs
learn: List a month by category and put weekly costs on a monthly scale.
Add a month and find its biggest line.

cards.text: Your own month has a cost, even if someone else pays it. To find it, list what you spend by category: phone, food out, bus fares, clothes, subscriptions, fun.

image.alt: A blank ruled notebook and a pencil surrounded by a phone, a bus ticket and a folded shirt

cards.text: Some costs repeat each week and some each month. Before you add them, put them on the same scale. The usual choice is a month.

image.alt: A wall calendar and a desk calendar with blank squares, a ruler between them

cards.text: To turn weekly into monthly, multiply by 52, then divide by 12. A month is not four weeks. $10.00 a week is $10.00 x 52 / 12 = $43.33 a month.

image.alt: Many small coin piles in a long row, divided into twelve neat groups

cards.text: Here is Jonah's month. Every line is on a monthly scale in the last column.
Add the Per month column to get the cost of the month. The biggest line is where a change would matter most.

questions.label: Same scale
questions.prompt: Why do you change weekly costs into monthly costs before you add them?
questions.hint: You can only add things that are measured the same way.

options.text: So every cost covers the same stretch of time
options.why: Yes. You can only add costs that cover the same time.

options.text: Weekly costs are not real costs
options.why: They are real. They just cover a different stretch of time.
A month holds more than a week, so monthly numbers are bigger.
No rule requires it. It is how you compare and add.

questions.label: Food out
questions.prompt: Jonah spends $12.00 a week on food out. How much is that in a month? (x 52 / 12)
questions.hint: Multiply by 52, then divide by 12.
questions.why: Weeks to a year first, then split the year into 12 months.
questions.miss: Multiply by 52 first, then divide by 12. A month is not four weeks.

traps.why: That is $12.00 x 4. A month is a little longer than four weeks.

questions.label: Bus tickets
questions.prompt: Jonah spends $8.00 a week on bus tickets. How much is that in a month? (x 52 / 12)
questions.hint: Multiply by 52, then divide by 12.
questions.why: Same steps: x 52, then / 12.
questions.miss: Multiply by 52 first, then divide by 12.

traps.why: That is $8.00 x 4. Use 52 weeks over 12 months.

questions.label: Fun a month
questions.prompt: Jonah spends $15.00 a week on fun. How much is that in a month?
questions.hint: Multiply by 52, then divide by 12.
questions.why: x 52, then / 12.
questions.miss: Multiply by 52 first, then divide by 12.

traps.why: That is $15.00 x 4. A month is about 4.33 weeks.

cards.text: Being responsible with money does not mean spending as little as possible. It means three things: know your number, decide on purpose, and plan before you spend.

levels.title: Wages and salary
learn: A wage pays you for hours. A salary pays you for the job.
You will turn both into one monthly number you can compare.

cards.text: Money from work comes in two main ways. A wage is a set rate for each hour you work. A salary is a set amount for the whole year, paid in equal parts.

image.alt: A punch time clock on the left and a wall calendar with blank squares on the right, a balance scale between them

cards.text: With a wage, more hours means more pay. With a salary, your pay stays the same in a busy month. That makes it easy to plan. Extra hours do not change it unless overtime rules apply.

image.alt: A steady row of identical blank envelopes on a desk beside a tall uneven stack of blank time cards

cards.text: A year is 52 weeks and 12 months, so a month is not four weeks. To turn weekly pay into monthly pay, multiply by 52 and divide by 12.
An hourly wage times your hours is your gross pay. At $13.00 an hour for 12 hours a week, you earn $156.00 each week. Gross means before anything is taken off.

image.alt: A blank time card sliding into a punch clock, plain gold discs spilling out below

cards.text: Jobs in the game list a wage and the hours you work each month. The Job Centre shows that pay before deductions. That is your gross pay. Next you will see what is taken off it.

image.alt: A small job centre building with a glowing doorway and a blank notice board outside on a winter evening

levels.title: Income tax, federal and Alberta
learn: The first part of your yearly income is tax-free.

cards.text: Income tax pays for schools, roads and hospitals. Two governments tax your pay: Canada (federal) and Alberta. Your employer takes both off each pay and sends them in.

image.alt: A school building, a road bridge and a hospital building in a row at dusk

cards.text: Everyone gets a basic personal amount. It is the first part of your yearly income that has no income tax. In 2026 it is $16,452 for federal tax and $22,769 for Alberta tax.
Tax rates grow in steps called brackets. Each rate applies only to the income inside its bracket. These are the first steps for 2026.
Moving into a higher bracket never cuts your take-home pay. Only the dollars above the line are taxed at the higher rate. The dollars below it are taxed as before.

image.alt: A wide staircase of five steps with plain gold discs resting on each step, the top step glowing

cards.text: The pay stub also applies credits, for example for your CPP and EI, so tax is a little lower than rate x pay. At a part-time student job you earn less than both tax-free amounts, so no income tax is taken. If some was taken anyway, file a return to get it back.

levels.title: Alberta's pay rules
learn: Alberta law sets a minimum wage, overtime rules and vacation pay.

cards.text: Alberta has employment standards. They are rules about pay and work that most employers must follow. A boss cannot ask you to give them up.

image.alt: A sturdy shield standing in front of a work apron and a hard hat

cards.text: The general minimum wage is $15.00 an hour. If you are under 18, the student rate is $13.00 an hour for your first 28 hours in a week while school is in session. Hours past 28 go back to $15.00. Over breaks and summer, $13.00 applies to all regular hours.

image.alt: Two blank price tags, one larger and one smaller, hanging from a shop shelf beside a school backpack

cards.text: Overtime is extra pay, or time off, when you work more than the legal limit. The hours and the rate are set by Alberta law, and some jobs are different. Look up the exact rules on alberta.ca before you rely on them.

image.alt: A wall clock with extra plain gold discs spilling from behind it, a moonlit window beside it

cards.text: Vacation pay is part of what you earn. It is a share of your pay that is set aside for time off, and it may be paid out or taken as time off. The share depends on how long you have worked for the employer.

image.alt: A beach chair and a suitcase beside a small glass jar slowly filling with plain gold discs

cards.text: Your employer must give you a statement of your pay. Check it with the steps you learned. If something looks wrong, ask your employer first. Alberta Employment Standards can help if that does not work.

units.title: Careers and pathways
units.blurb: Pick a career, find what it pays, and see the way there.

levels.title: Five ways money arrives
learn: Name the five ways money reaches a person.
Match a made-up person's money to the right way.

cards.text: Money reaches people in five main ways: wages, salary, self-employment, investment income and government benefits. Most people start with the first. Over a lifetime, many people use more than one.
Wages and salary are pay from an employer. A wage is a rate for each hour. A salary is a fixed amount for the year, paid in parts. You already know how to turn either one into a monthly gross pay.

image.alt: A time clock and a blank calendar, each with a stack of gold discs below

cards.text: Self-employment means you work for yourself. Customers pay you, not an employer. Some months bring more money and some bring less. You pay your own costs, such as supplies, out of what customers pay you.

image.alt: A wheelbarrow and a push mower on a lawn with a jar of gold discs

cards.text: Investment income is money your money earns. Interest on a savings account is one kind. A share of a company's profit is another. You do not work hours for it, but you needed money to start.

image.alt: A seedling with gold discs growing on its branches beside a blank jar

cards.text: Government benefits are payments from a government to people in certain situations. Employment Insurance, which you met in the pay unit, is one: it can pay you for a while after a layoff. A benefit is paid only when its rules are met.

image.alt: A stone bridge over a gap with gold discs along its path

questions.label: Bike repair
questions.prompt: Tomas fixes bikes for neighbours. Each customer pays him directly, and some months he has no customers. Which way does his money arrive?

terms.meaning: Working for yourself. Your customers pay you, and you cover your own costs.

questions.hint: Who pays him: an employer, or his customers?

options.why: A salary is a fixed amount from an employer. Tomas has no employer, and his pay is not fixed.
Yes. Tomas works for himself, and his customers pay him. His pay changes from month to month.
Investment income comes from money you own. Tomas earns his by working.
A benefit comes from a government. Tomas's customers pay him.

questions.label: Savings interest
questions.prompt: Mei's savings account adds interest to her balance each month. What kind of money is that?

terms.meaning: Money a bank pays you for keeping your savings with it.

questions.hint: Her money is earning money.

options.why: Yes. Interest is money that her savings earn. She did no hours of work for it.
A wage is pay for hours worked. Mei does not work any hours for interest.
Self-employment is money from customers you serve. Interest comes from the bank.
A benefit is paid by a government. Interest is paid on her savings.

questions.label: After a layoff
questions.prompt: Jo is laid off and receives Employment Insurance payments. Which way does that money arrive?

terms.meaning: Employment Insurance. It pays you for a while if you lose a job through no fault of your own.

questions.hint: The payment comes from a government program.

options.why: A wage is pay for hours worked. Jo is no longer working those hours.
Investment income comes from money you own. EI comes from the EI program.
A salary comes from an employer. Jo's employer let Jo go.
Yes. EI is paid under government rules to people who lose a job through no fault of their own.

terms.meaning: A set amount for the year, paid in equal parts.
A set rate of pay for each hour you work.

Yes. A salary is a fixed amount for the year, paid in equal parts.
Investment income comes from money you own, not from an employer.

terms.meaning: A set rate of pay for each hour you work.

questions.hint: An employer pays for your work.

Yes. A wage is paid by an employer for each hour worked.
EI is a government benefit, not pay from an employer.
That is self-employment. Customers pay you, not an employer.

levels.title: Read a job posting
learn: Read a job's wage and hours and work out its monthly gross pay.
Compare two jobs by what they pay in a month, not by the wage alone.

cards.text: A job posting tells you four things: the title, the employer, the hourly wage and the hours in a month. In the Job Centre, the Cashier job at Corner Mart pays $15.28 an hour for 118 hours a month.

image.alt: A corkboard with four blank cards, a pencil, a clock and gold discs

cards.text: Here are four of the twelve entry jobs. The wage is for one hour. The hours are for a whole month. The employers are made-up businesses in the game.
Monthly gross pay is the wage times the hours in a month. For the Cashier job: $15.28 x 118 = $1,803.04. This is gross pay, before CPP, EI and tax come off.

image.alt: A balance scale with a clock on one side and gold discs on the other

cards.text: Do not compare wages alone. A higher wage with fewer hours can pay less. Retail associate pays $17.06 an hour for 132 hours: $2,251.92. Daycare assistant pays less per hour, $16.73, for 159 hours: $2,660.07.

image.alt: Two balance scales, one with a thin tall tower of discs, one with a wide pile

cards.text: To change hours a month into hours a week, multiply by 12 and divide by 52. The Cashier job's 118 hours a month is about 27.2 hours a week. The full-time week in class is 40 hours.

image.alt: A calendar with one week highlighted, a small clock and gold discs

The wage is the pay for one hour. It does not say how many hours you work.

terms.meaning: Your pay before anything is taken off.

questions.miss: Multiply the hourly wage by the hours in the month.

questions.miss: Multiply the hourly wage by the hours in the month.

questions.label: Hours a week
questions.prompt: The Cashier job is 118 hours a month. About how many hours is that in a week, to one decimal place? (hours a month x 12 / 52)
questions.hint: Hours in a year first, then split into 52 weeks.
questions.why: A year has 12 months and 52 weeks, so hours a month go up by 12 and then down by 52.

levels.title: Starting, overall and top pay
learn: Say what starting pay and top pay mean for one occupation.
Read three wage numbers and see why one number never tells the whole story.

cards.text: One occupation does not have one wage. ALIS, the Alberta government career website at alis.alberta.ca, is where Albertans look up what an occupation pays. Its wage table gives three averages, not just one.

image.alt: An open blank book with a magnifying glass and three coloured ribbon bookmarks

cards.text: Starting pay is the average for people just beginning in the occupation. Most entry jobs in the Job Centre use a starting number. The Warehouse associate at Keystone Distribution starts at $15.45 an hour.

image.alt: A step stool at the foot of a staircase with one gold disc on the lowest step

cards.text: Overall pay is the average for experienced people in the same occupation. Top pay is the highest of the three averages. Pay rises with experience, and the Job Centre notes say which number each wage comes from.

image.alt: A three-step staircase with taller stacks of gold discs on each higher step

cards.text: Here are all three for one occupation. A Warehouse associate starts at $15.45 an hour, averages $17.93 with experience, and the top average is $21.48.

figure.title: Warehouse associate: three averages an hour

cards.text: One number can mislead you. Read only the top number, and you expect more than you earn at the start. Read only the starting number, and you think the job never pays more. Read all three, then ask how long it takes to get there.

image.alt: Three blank picture frames holding small, medium and large stacks of gold discs

levels.title: Ways in
learn: Compare going straight to work, an apprenticeship, and college or university.
See why an apprentice is paid while learning.

cards.text: There are three common ways into a career. You can go straight to work in an entry job. You can train as an apprentice. Or you can study at a college or university first. Each costs time, and each pays differently at the start.

image.alt: A signpost at a three-way fork leading to a workshop, a college and a shop

cards.text: Straight to work means you earn from your first month. The twelve entry jobs in the Job Centre work this way. You learn on the job, and your pay rises in steps.

image.alt: A shop counter with a register, an apron on a hook and a stack of gold discs

cards.text: An apprenticeship is a paid way to learn a trade. In the game, Spark Line Electric hires a first-period apprentice electrician. ALIS lists $33.58 an hour as the starting wage for electricians (the journeyperson wage). The first period pays half: $16.79.

image.alt: A workbench with a coil of cable, a hard hat, a toolbelt and gold discs

cards.text: Each period pays a bigger share of the journeyperson wage: 50%, 60%, 70% and 80%. An apprentice is paid while still learning, and the pay rises with each period.

College or university means you study first, so you usually start earning later. A diploma or a degree often comes with a student loan, and a loan means a payment each month. A trade with a paid apprenticeship may have a loan line of zero.

image.alt: Textbooks and a graduation cap with a short chain of gold discs attached

cards.text: None of the three is best for everyone. Ask what each costs you in time before your pay catches up. This course gives no price for school, so look up the real cost of a program before you choose it.

image.alt: An open notebook, a pencil, a magnifying glass and a blank sticky note

questions.label: Cashier job

questions.hint: No training program comes first.

Yes. Priya goes into an entry job and learns while she earns.
Priya is not studying first. She is starting work now.

Yes. An apprentice works for an employer and is paid while training.
A loan is borrowed money. It is not pay for work.

levels.title: Steps up
learn: Work out a raise in dollars an hour, dollars a month and percent.
Compare steps up on the Job Centre's paths.

cards.text: Most Job Centre jobs have steps up. A step is a new title with a new wage and new hours. A Cashier at Corner Mart can become a Retail supervisor, and later a Store manager. The Job Centre shows what each step pays.

image.alt: A staircase with three landings, each larger than the last, holding gold discs

cards.text: A step changes the wage and the hours, so compare the monthly gross pay. The Cashier earns $1,803.04. As a Retail supervisor, the same person earns $2,887.12.

figure.title: Cashier path in the Job Centre

cards.text: A raise has three sizes. In dollars an hour: the new wage minus the old wage. In dollars a month: the new monthly gross minus the old one. In percent: the raise divided by the old amount, times 100. Cashier to Retail supervisor: $3.84 an hour, $1,084.08 a month, 25.1% on the wage.

image.alt: Three rulers in gold, coral and royal blue with a pencil and gold discs

cards.text: Where does a new wage come from? A step into a new occupation starts at that occupation's starting average. A step in the same occupation with more experience uses the overall average. Line cook to Cook ($18.62) is more experience. Cook to Chef ($22.06) is a new occupation.

image.alt: A kitchen door and an office door, each with a stack of gold discs at its step

cards.text: In the game, you can apply for the next step after 12 months in your current step. You write a short note about why. Your teacher decides, or the Job Centre promotes you at once, depending on the class. After a no, you wait 3 months to apply again.

image.alt: A blank form on a clipboard, a pen, a blank calendar and a mailbox with a blue flag

levels.title: Does it clear the month?
learn: Use net pay, not gross pay, to test a job against a month's costs.
See how a step up changes what you keep.

cards.text: A month has costs. In class, Mr. Tang's modest Edmonton month on the bus, with no car, costs $2,503.00. To test a job against it, use net pay: the money that lands in your account, not gross pay.

image.alt: A blank calendar, a bus stop sign with a blank panel, and a tray of gold discs

cards.text: The Cashier job grosses $1,803.04 a month. After CPP, EI and income tax, net pay is $1,657.45. That is $845.55 short of $2,503.00.

figure.title: Cashier at Corner Mart: first pay of the year

cards.text: The share you keep is net pay divided by gross pay. Cashier: $1,657.45 / $1,803.04 = 91.9%. Administrative assistant: 82.8%. A bigger gross pay keeps a smaller share, but more dollars.

image.alt: A tall and a short stack of gold discs with a clear jar catching most of them

cards.text: Three of the twelve entry jobs clear $2,503.00 in net pay at the Job Centre's wages and hours: Administrative assistant, Junior bookkeeper and Customer service rep. The other nine fall short.

image.alt: Three glowing doorways in front of nine dim closed ones, all with blank signs

cards.text: A step up changes the answer. As a Retail supervisor, with 151 hours at $19.12, a Cashier's net pay rises from $1,657.45 to $2,456.03. That is only $46.97 short. In the game, a step takes at least 12 months.

image.alt: A staircase with a short and a tall stack of gold discs beside a dashed line

cards.text: Use the Job Centre to try it. Pick a job, look at its steps, and compare each net pay with the month you need. This is the same test your own budget will use.

image.alt: A job centre with a glowing doorway, a blank notice board and a winding path

questions.label: Gross or net
questions.prompt: To test whether a job covers a month's costs, which number should you use?

terms.meaning: What is left after every deduction. It lands in your chequing.
Your pay before anything is taken off.

options.why: Yes. Net pay is what lands in your account. That is the money that pays the bills.
Gross pay is before CPP, EI and tax. You never get to spend it all.
The wage is for one hour. It does not say what you have after deductions.
The top wage is for experienced workers. It does not say what you will take home.

questions.hint: The month, minus net pay.

questions.hint: Net pay divided by gross pay, times 100.

questions.miss: Divide net pay by gross pay, then multiply by 100.

questions.prompt: Tap the one job whose net pay clears $2,503.00.
questions.hint: Compare each bar with the month's cost.

questions.label: Earn more

options.why: Only the extra dollars are taxed more. The dollars below that line keep the old rate.
CPP grows with pay but never faster than the pay itself.

questions.hint: New net pay minus old net pay.

units.title: What Edmonton costs
units.blurb: The real cost of living in Edmonton: where you live and how you get around.

levels.title: Three decisions
learn: Name the three decisions that shape a budget.
See how much of a modest month goes to rent and the bus.

cards.text: Three decisions settle most of a budget before you try any method: where you live, how you get around, and how you get paid. You make them before you ever open a spreadsheet.

image.alt: Three blank signposts on a snowy path pointing different ways

cards.text: In class, Mr. Tang's modest Edmonton month on the bus, with no car, costs $2,503.00. It covers a 1-bedroom, groceries, a bus pass, a phone plan and utilities. With a car in place of the bus, the same month costs $3,313.00.

image.alt: A table with a grocery bag, blank envelopes, a bus pass and a house key

cards.text: Rent and the bus pass are $1,403.00 of the $2,503.00. Everything else in the month, such as groceries, a phone plan and utilities, shares what is left.
The first two decisions have prices you can look up: rent, and the cost of getting around. This unit puts real Edmonton numbers on both, so you can see how far they move a month.

image.alt: A ruler on a blank street map beside a pencil and a transit pass

cards.text: How you get paid is the third decision. It comes at the end of the unit. A budget method comes after all three, in the next unit, because a method can only divide the money you have.

image.alt: An open blank notebook beside a stack of gold discs and a closed laptop

questions.label: Three decisions
questions.prompt: Which of these is one of the three decisions that shape a budget before any budget method?
questions.hint: Think of the biggest costs in a month.

options.why: A method comes after the three decisions. It divides the money you have, but it does not change how much you have.
Yes. Rent, getting around and how you get paid come before a method.
A small want like this barely moves a month. The three decisions are much bigger.

options.text: Which day to do the shopping
options.why: The day you shop does not change what a month costs. The three decisions change it by hundreds of dollars.

questions.label: Why this order
questions.prompt: Why does this unit look at housing and transport before any budget method?
questions.hint: Which costs move the most money?

options.text: They change the month by hundreds of dollars
options.why: Yes. A method cannot fix a month that is too big to start with.
Methods are useful. They just come after the big decisions.

options.text: Housing is the only cost in a budget
options.why: A budget has groceries, a phone and more. Housing is only the largest part.

options.text: They are easier than a method
options.why: Ease is not the reason. Size is: these decisions move the most money.

questions.label: Rent and bus
questions.prompt: In the $2,503.00 month, rent is $1,298.00 and the bus pass is $105.00. How much do the two cost together?
questions.hint: Add the two amounts.
questions.why: Rent and the bus pass together are $1,403.00 a month.
questions.miss: Add the two amounts from the card. Keep the cents.

questions.label: Share of month
questions.prompt: What percent of the $2,503.00 month is rent and the bus pass together ($1,403.00)? Round to the nearest whole percent.
questions.hint: Divide the smaller amount by the whole month.
questions.why: A little over half of the month goes to rent and the bus pass.
questions.miss: Divide $1,403.00 by $2,503.00. Then turn the answer into a percent.

traps.why: That is rent alone. Add the bus pass before you divide.

questions.label: Everything else
questions.prompt: Take rent ($1,298.00) and the bus pass ($105.00) off the $2,503.00 month. How much is left for everything else?
questions.hint: Subtract both amounts from the whole month.
questions.why: Everything else in the month shares $1,100.00.
questions.miss: Subtract rent and the bus pass from the whole month.

questions.label: Car month extra
questions.prompt: The month with a car costs $3,313.00. The month on the bus costs $2,503.00. How much more does the car month cost?
questions.hint: Subtract the smaller month from the larger.
questions.why: The car month costs $810.00 more.
questions.miss: Subtract the bus month from the car month.

questions.label: Largest part
questions.prompt: Tap the bar for the largest part of the modest month.

figure.title: The modest month in three parts

questions.hint: Compare the heights of the bars.
questions.why: Rent is the tallest bar at $1,298.00. It is the biggest single cost.
questions.miss: Read the amount on each bar. The largest part is the tallest bar.

questions.label: What is left
questions.prompt: Sol has already chosen a place to live and a way to get around. Which of the three decisions is left?
questions.hint: Name the three, then cross off the two Sol has made.

options.why: A method is not one of the three decisions. It comes after them.
Sol has already chosen this one.
Sol has already chosen this one.
Yes. Where to live, how to get around and how to get paid are the three.

questions.label: Rent share
questions.prompt: Rent is $1,298.00 of the $2,503.00 month. What percent of the month is rent alone? Round to the nearest whole percent.
questions.hint: Divide rent by the whole month.
questions.why: Rent alone is a little over half of the modest month.
questions.miss: Divide $1,298.00 by $2,503.00, then turn the answer into a percent.

levels.title: Four ways to live
learn: Name four ways to live at 22 and put them in order of cost.
Say what each one pays for.

cards.text: At 22 you have four main ways to live: stay at home, share a place with roommates, rent a place alone, or buy. Each one puts a different amount of your pay into housing.

image.alt: Four different doors in a row: a family door, a double door, a narrow door and a house door

cards.text: Staying at home usually means a contribution to the household instead of rent. With roommates, you share one rental and split the rent. Renting alone means you pay all of it yourself.

image.alt: Two sets of keys on one hook and a single set on another hook

cards.text: Buying means you own the place. You pay a mortgage, which is a loan, and the costs of owning a home. At 22 it is the most expensive of the four.

image.alt: A small house with a blank sale sign in a snowy front yard

cards.text: Mr. Tang's Edmonton averages: a 1-bedroom is $1,298.00 a month and a 2-bedroom is $1,581.00. Share the 2-bedroom with one roommate and each person pays half: $790.50.
Ranked from cheapest to most expensive, the four ways are: stay at home, roommates, rent alone, buy. The order is easy to guess. How big the gaps are is the part people guess badly.

image.alt: Four steps rising in height with a gold disc on each

questions.label: Cheapest way
questions.prompt: Which way to live usually costs the least?
questions.hint: The ranking runs cheapest to most expensive.

options.why: Sharing cuts the rent, but you still pay a share of a rental.
Renting alone means paying all of the rent.
Yes. A household contribution is usually the lowest of the four.
Buying is the most expensive of the four.

questions.label: Dearest way
questions.prompt: Which of the four ways does the lesson rank as the most expensive at 22?
questions.hint: Look at the ranked list on the last card.

options.why: Renting alone is dear, but buying ranks above it.
Yes. Buying adds a mortgage and the costs of owning a home.
Sharing is the second cheapest.
Staying at home is the cheapest of the four.

questions.label: What split means
questions.prompt: Two people share a 2-bedroom and split the rent. What does that mean?

terms.meaning: To share a cost so that each person pays a part of it.
The money you pay each month to live in a place you do not own.

questions.hint: Think about who pays what.

options.text: Two people pay one rent between them
options.why: Yes. The rent is shared, so each person pays a part.

options.text: Each person pays the full rent
options.why: That would double the cost. Splitting means sharing one rent.

options.text: The landlord charges half the rent
options.why: The landlord still charges the full rent. The two tenants share it.
Rent is still due. It is just shared.

questions.label: Split the rent
questions.prompt: A 2-bedroom costs $1,581.00 a month. Two people split the rent equally. How much does each person pay?
questions.hint: Divide by two. Keep the cents.
questions.why: Half of $1,581.00 is $790.50 each.
questions.miss: Divide the whole rent by the number of people sharing it.

traps.why: That is the whole rent. Each person pays only half of it.

questions.label: A year alone
questions.prompt: Renting a 1-bedroom alone costs $1,298.00 a month. What is that for a whole year?
questions.hint: A year has 12 months.
questions.why: Twelve months of $1,298.00 is $15,576.00.
questions.miss: Multiply one month by the number of months in a year.

questions.label: Cheapest rent
questions.prompt: Tap the bar for the cheapest way to rent for one person.

figure.title: Rent for one person, three ways

questions.hint: Compare the heights of the bars.
questions.why: The split 2-bedroom is $790.50, the shortest bar.
questions.miss: The cheapest way is the shortest bar. Read the label under it.

questions.label: Alone or split
questions.prompt: Which costs one person less each month: the 1-bedroom alone at $1,298.00, or half of the 2-bedroom?
questions.hint: Work out half of the 2-bedroom first.

options.why: The 1-bedroom is smaller, but one person pays all of $1,298.00. Half of the 2-bedroom is only $790.50.
Yes. Half of $1,581.00 is $790.50, which is less than $1,298.00.
Work out half of $1,581.00. It is not $1,298.00.

questions.label: A mortgage
questions.prompt: What is a mortgage?

terms.meaning: A loan used to buy a home, paid back over many years.

questions.hint: Which of the four ways uses one?

options.why: Rent is for a place you do not own. A mortgage is for one you buy.
A deposit is returned when you move out. A mortgage is a loan.

options.text: A loan used to buy a home
options.why: Yes. You pay it back over many years, and the home is what the loan is for.
A mortgage is not a tax. It is borrowed money.

questions.label: Rent in a year
questions.prompt: Two people split a $1,581.00 2-bedroom equally. How much rent does each person pay in a year?
questions.hint: Find one person's month first. Then multiply by 12.
questions.why: Each person pays $790.50 a month, so $9,486.00 a year.
questions.miss: Find each person's rent for one month. Then take a whole year of it.

levels.title: The roommate number
learn: Work out the saving from sharing a 2-bedroom.
Turn the yearly saving into hours of work.

cards.text: A 1-bedroom alone is $1,298.00 a month. Half of a $1,581.00 2-bedroom is $790.50. The difference is $507.50 a month.
Over a year the difference is 12 x $507.50 = $6,090.00. That comes from one decision about a lease. It is not a raise, not a promotion and not a budget method.

image.alt: A calendar of twelve blank squares with a stack of gold discs by each

cards.text: Put the saving in hours of work. To earn $6,090.00 at $15.00 an hour before deductions you would need $6,090.00 / $15.00 = 406 hours. That is about 8 hours a week, every week of the year.

image.alt: A wall clock beside a long row of blank time cards and a stack of gold discs

cards.text: These rents are Edmonton averages. A real place can cost more or less. What matters here is how big the gap is. The exact dollar will change from one building to the next.

image.alt: A scale balancing a gold disc against a small model apartment building

questions.label: Monthly saving
questions.prompt: Rent alone is $1,298.00. Half of a 2-bedroom is $790.50. How much less per month is the roommate way?
questions.hint: Subtract the smaller rent from the larger.
questions.why: Sharing saves $507.50 a month.
questions.miss: Subtract the roommate rent from the rent alone. Keep the cents.

questions.label: Saving in a year
questions.prompt: Sharing a 2-bedroom saves $507.50 a month. How much does it save in a year?
questions.hint: A year has 12 months.
questions.why: Twelve months of $507.50 is $6,090.00.
questions.miss: Multiply the monthly saving by 12.

questions.label: Hours of work
questions.prompt: At $15.00 an hour before deductions, how many hours would you work to earn $6,090.00?
questions.hint: Divide the amount by the hourly wage.
questions.why: It takes 406 hours of work at $15.00 an hour.
questions.miss: Divide the amount you need by what one hour pays.

questions.label: Hours a week
questions.prompt: Spread 406 hours over 52 weeks. About how many hours a week is that? Round to the nearest whole hour.
questions.hint: Divide by the number of weeks in a year.
questions.why: About 8 hours of extra work every week, all year.
questions.miss: Divide the hours by 52, then round.

questions.label: What it is
questions.prompt: What is the best way to describe the $6,090.00?
questions.hint: Which two numbers is it the difference between?

options.why: No employer pays it. It is rent you do not spend.

options.text: The yearly saving from one housing decision
options.why: Yes. It is the difference between two ways to live, over 12 months.

options.text: The cost of having a roommate
options.why: It is the saving from having one, not a cost.
A whole 2-bedroom is $1,581.00 a month. The $6,090.00 is a difference.

questions.label: Saves $6,090
questions.prompt: Tap the bar for the way that costs $6,090.00 less in a year than renting a 1-bedroom alone.

figure.title: Rent for a year, one person

questions.hint: Compare each bar with the first one.
questions.why: Alone costs $15,576.00 a year. Split costs $9,486.00. The difference is $6,090.00.
questions.miss: Subtract each bar from the 1-bedroom bar. Look for a difference of $6,090.00.

questions.label: About averages
questions.prompt: The $1,298.00 and $1,581.00 rents are Edmonton averages. What does that tell you about a real place?

terms.meaning: A typical figure: the total of the prices divided by how many there are.

questions.hint: An average sits in the middle of many prices.

options.text: It may cost more or less
options.why: Yes. An average is a typical price, not a promise for every home.
An average is typical, not exact.
Some places cost less than an average. Some cost more.
The average covers many kinds of buildings.

questions.label: Another split
questions.prompt: Mia leaves a 1-bedroom at $1,298.00 and shares a 2-bedroom that costs $1,500.00, split equally. How much less does she pay each month?
questions.hint: Find her half first.
questions.why: Her half is $750.00. She pays $548.00 less than before.
questions.miss: Find her share of the new rent. Then subtract it from the old rent.

questions.label: Yearly roommate rent
questions.prompt: One roommate pays $790.50 a month. What does that come to in a year?
questions.hint: Multiply by 12.
questions.why: Twelve months of $790.50 is $9,486.00.
questions.miss: Multiply one month by the months in a year.

levels.title: What you give up
learn: Say what a saving buys and what it costs you.
Explain why neither choice is the right one.

cards.text: A saving is never free. Sharing a 2-bedroom saves $507.50 a month. In return you give up some quiet, some privacy and some control over your own space, such as a shared kitchen.

image.alt: A shared kitchen counter with two mugs, two cutting boards and a toaster

cards.text: Living alone gives you privacy and space. It costs more, month after month. Neither choice is right for everyone. What matters is that you know the number before you choose.

image.alt: A quiet bedroom with a bed, a reading lamp and a bookshelf

cards.text: People value different things. Needing your own space is a real value, and paying for it is a fair choice. Saving money is a real value too. A choice is sound when it fits what you value and you knew what it cost.

image.alt: A balance scale with a stack of gold discs against an armchair and lamp

cards.text: Here is how a person can weigh it. Wen says her own space is worth $300.00 a month to her. Living alone costs $507.50 more than sharing, so it costs her $207.50 more than she says it is worth.

image.alt: A desk with a calculator, a blank sticky note, a plant and gold discs

cards.text: Look at both sides together: the saving in dollars, and what you give up in space. A choice made with both in front of you is a good one, whichever way it goes.

image.alt: Two open doors leading to a shared room and a small quiet room

questions.label: Sharing costs
questions.prompt: Which of these is something you give up by living with a roommate?
questions.hint: Think about what changes inside the home.

options.why: You still pay rent. It is just a smaller share.
The saving is what you gain, not what you give up.

options.text: Any say in who your friends are
options.why: Sharing a home does not decide who your friends are.

options.text: Some privacy and control of your space
options.why: Yes. The saving comes with a shared home.

questions.label: Living alone costs
questions.prompt: Compared with sharing, what is the cost of living alone in a 1-bedroom?
questions.hint: Look at the first line of the table in level 3.

options.why: Living alone gives more privacy, not less.
Living alone means the kitchen is yours.
Yes. Privacy and space come with a bigger rent.
A 1-bedroom alone has a kitchen that is all yours. The cost is the higher rent.

questions.label: No right answer
questions.prompt: Rae shares a 2-bedroom to save money. Lee pays more to live alone. What does the lesson say about the two choices?
questions.hint: Is the lesson telling you which to pick?

options.text: Rae is right and Lee is wrong
options.why: The lesson does not rank one choice above the other.

options.text: Both can be sound if each knew the cost
options.why: Yes. The test is knowing the number and what you give up.

options.text: Lee is right because space always matters most
options.why: Space matters a lot to some people and less to others.
Both are ordinary choices.

questions.label: Cost over value
questions.prompt: Wen says her own space is worth $300.00 a month to her. Living alone costs $507.50 more than sharing. How much more is the cost than the worth she names?
questions.hint: Subtract the smaller amount from the larger.
questions.why: The extra cost is $207.50 more than Wen says the space is worth.
questions.miss: Subtract what Wen says the space is worth from the extra monthly cost.

questions.label: Extra for a year
questions.prompt: If Wen pays the extra $507.50 a month to live alone, how much extra is that in a year?
questions.hint: A year has 12 months.
questions.why: Twelve months of $507.50 is $6,090.00.

questions.label: A real answer

questions.hint: The lesson asks you to know something before you choose.

options.why: Yes. Either choice is real if you knew what it cost.

Living alone is a real answer too, with its own price.
Staying at home is a real answer as well.

questions.label: Worth more
questions.prompt: Tap the person whose own space is worth more per month than the extra $507.50 cost of living alone.

figure.title: What each person says their space is worth, per month

questions.hint: Compare each bar with $507.50.
questions.why: Zara's $600.00 is more than $507.50. The other two are less.
questions.miss: Read the amount on each bar and compare it with $507.50.

questions.label: Hours for space
questions.prompt: Living alone costs $507.50 more each month. At $15.00 an hour before deductions, about how many hours of work is that? Round to the nearest hour.
questions.hint: Divide the extra cost by the hourly wage.
questions.why: About 34 hours of work each month pays for the extra space.
questions.miss: Divide the monthly extra cost by what one hour pays.

levels.title: Bus pass or car
learn: Compare a bus pass with the all-in cost of a car.
Find the gap in a month and in a year.

cards.text: A monthly bus pass in Edmonton is $105.00. Owning a car costs between $680.00 and $1,150.00 a month, all in.

image.alt: A snowy bus shelter with a bus arriving and a car parked nearby

cards.text: All in means every cost of the car, not just the loan payment: the payment, insurance, fuel, maintenance and registration. Most people think of the payment and stop. At your age, insurance is the biggest single piece.

image.alt: A car with a fuel can, a key, a wrench and a blank form on the hood

cards.text: Take the midpoint of the car range: ($680.00 + $1,150.00) / 2 = $915.00 a month. Against the $105.00 pass, the car costs $810.00 more each month.

image.alt: A ruler marked at its middle with a toy bus at one end and a toy car at the other

cards.text: Over a year that is 12 x $810.00 = $9,720.00. It is also the gap between the modest month on the bus, $2,503.00, and the same month with a car, $3,313.00.

questions.label: All in means
questions.prompt: Which list is what "all in" includes for a car?

terms.meaning: Every cost of owning the car, not just the loan payment.

questions.hint: All in leaves nothing out.

options.text: The monthly payment on the loan alone
options.why: The payment is only one piece. Insurance, fuel and the rest add up too.

options.text: Payment plus fuel, with no insurance
options.why: Insurance is left out here, and it is the biggest piece at your age.

options.text: Insurance and registration, with no fuel
options.why: Fuel and the payment belong in the total too.

options.text: Payment, insurance, fuel, upkeep and registration
options.why: Yes. All in adds every cost of owning the car.

questions.label: Biggest piece
questions.prompt: At your age, which piece of the all-in cost of a car is the biggest single one?

terms.meaning: A plan you pay for so that the plan covers some of the cost if something goes wrong.

questions.hint: The card names one piece.

options.why: Registration is a small yearly cost compared with the others.
Fuel adds up, but insurance is larger at your age.
Yes. Insurance is the biggest single piece for a young driver.
People think of the payment first. At your age insurance is larger.

questions.label: The midpoint
questions.prompt: The car range runs from $680.00 to $1,150.00 a month. What is the midpoint?

terms.meaning: The number halfway between a low figure and a high figure.

questions.hint: Add the two ends. Then divide by two.
questions.why: Halfway between $680.00 and $1,150.00 is $915.00.
questions.miss: Add the low and the high figures, then divide by 2.

questions.label: Monthly gap
questions.prompt: The car costs $915.00 a month at the midpoint. The bus pass costs $105.00. How much more does the car cost each month?
questions.hint: Subtract the pass from the car.
questions.why: The car costs $810.00 more a month.
questions.miss: Subtract the bus pass from the car cost.

questions.label: Gap in a year
questions.prompt: The car costs $810.00 more than the bus pass each month. How much more is that in a year?

levels.title: Cash or on the books
learn: Say what a worker gives up by being paid cash off the books.

cards.text: Ana's manager says: "I can put you on the books at $15.00 an hour, or pay you $17.00 cash." Cash is $2.00 more an hour. Over 52 hours in a month, that is $884.00 in cash against $780.00 gross on the books.

image.alt: A desk with a thin blank envelope and a thick blank envelope and a pen

cards.text: On the books, CPP and EI come off. At 52 hours that is $29.06 of CPP (5.95% of pay above $291.66) and $12.71 of EI (1.63% of pay). Income tax is $0.00, as it is at this income.
Those two lines are not lost. CPP counts toward your pension. EI is what could pay you if you lost the job through no fault of your own. Cash pays nothing toward either one.

image.alt: A piggy bank and a life ring on a wall with gold discs below

cards.text: Cash also leaves no record of income. You cannot show what you earn when you apply for a loan, a lease or a mortgage. With no T4, you also have nothing to file a tax return with. At a part-time student income, any tax withheld would have come back to you anyway.

image.alt: A filing cabinet with an open drawer of blank folders and an empty tray

cards.text: Not reporting income is illegal for the employer and for you. The worker is not automatically the innocent one.

image.alt: A wooden gavel on a blank page beside a pair of scales

cards.text: Here is a plain test for honest dealing in money: would you be comfortable if the other person knew everything you know? A deal that holds up when it is fully visible is usually honest. This is a question for you to ask yourself.

image.alt: A clear glass window with a gold disc visible through it

units.title: Budget methods
units.blurb: Four ways to budget: 50/30/20, zero-based, envelopes and pay yourself first.

levels.title: A rule you decide once
learn: Say why a rule set in advance works better than being careful.
Name the pay number a budget starts from.

cards.text: Many people say, "I will just be careful with money." It works for a few days. Then every purchase is a new argument with yourself, and you lose many of them. That is a design problem, not a problem with you.

image.alt: A blank list on a corkboard beside a half empty jar of gold discs

cards.text: A budget is not just a list of what you spent. It is a rule you decide in advance. You decide once, so you do not have to decide again at every purchase. Example: "No more than $40.00 a week on eating out."

image.alt: A blank signpost at a snowy crossroads with gold discs lining one path

cards.text: A budget starts from take-home pay, which is net pay: gross pay minus deductions. At $2,600.00 gross in a month, the game's pay stub gives net pay of $2,249.05. That is the number you split, not the $2,600.00.

figure.title: Pay stub, one month at $2,600.00 gross

cards.text: A good rule has an amount and a time. "$40.00 a week" is a rule. "Spend less on food" is a wish. A rule also tells you when you have hit the limit, so you know when to stop.

image.alt: A measuring tape and a blank card beside gold discs and a small clock

cards.text: This unit covers four ways to write the rule: 50/30/20, zero-based, envelopes and pay yourself first. Each one is built for a different problem. You will see what each does well and where it is hard, then match them to people.

image.alt: Four plain doors of different colours in a hallway with blank signs

questions.label: Why careful fails
questions.prompt: Why does "I will just be careful" often stop working?
questions.hint: Think about what happens at the next purchase.

options.text: Careful people earn less take-home pay
options.why: Care does not change what you earn. The problem is in how the decisions get made.

options.text: Every purchase turns into a new decision to argue about
options.why: Yes. Without a rule set in advance, you decide again each time, and tired decisions are weaker.

options.text: Being careful is not allowed once you have a job
options.why: Nothing stops you from being careful. It simply does not hold up without a rule.

options.text: It works, but only if you have a high gross pay
options.why: Gross pay is not the cause. A rule helps at any pay.

questions.label: Which is a rule

terms.meaning: A plan for what each dollar of a month is for.

questions.hint: A rule has an amount and a time.

options.text: Move $50.00 to savings on every payday
options.why: Yes. It has an amount and a time, and it is decided before the money is spent.

options.text: Try to spend less this month
options.why: This is a wish. It has no amount and no point where you stop.

options.text: Hope some money is left at the end
options.why: Hoping is not a rule. Nothing is decided in advance.

options.text: Be more careful at the mall
options.why: No amount, no time. You would still decide at each purchase.

An amount and a time. It is a rule.
An amount and a time. It is a rule.

options.why: Yes. There is no amount, so you cannot tell when you have reached it.

The wage is one piece of the pay. A budget needs the month's total after deductions.
Yes. Take-home pay is what lands in your account, so it is what you can plan with.

learn: Split a take-home pay into needs, wants, and savings and debt.
Sort spending into the right bucket.

cards.text: The 50/30/20 rule splits your take-home pay into three buckets. 50% goes to needs, 30% to wants, and 20% to savings and debt payments. It is the budgeting rule most people have heard of.

image.alt: A round pie in three slices of blue, coral and gold on a blank tray

cards.text: Needs are costs you must pay to live and work: rent, groceries, utilities and getting to work. Wants are what you choose beyond that, like eating out or streaming. Savings and debt payments are money you put away or pay back on loans.

image.alt: A key, bread and bus ticket stub on one side of a table, a movie ticket and game controller on the other

cards.text: Here is a take-home of $2,000.00. Needs get $1,000.00, wants get $600.00, and savings and debt get $400.00. The three shares always add back to the whole take-home.

On $2,600.00 gross, full-time at minimum wage, the game's pay stub gives take-home of $2,249.05 a month. The buckets are below, to the nearest dollar. They add to $2,250, a little over the take-home, only because of rounding.

Some purchases sit between buckets. A phone you need for work is a need. A newer model with extras is a want. Ask: could I live and work this month without it? If yes, it is a want. Be honest, because the rule only helps if you sort honestly.

image.alt: A phone with a blank screen on a desk with a notebook and a magnifying glass
