learn: Work out the take-home you need for a given amount of needs.
Read a needs share above 50% as useful information.

cards.text: The rule is also a check. Add up your needs and ask: are they about half of my take-home? If needs are much more than half, the rule has told you something true. The rent and transport choices from the last unit are taking a large share.

image.alt: A balance scale tilting toward a heavy blue block over a lighter stack of gold discs

cards.text: Here are the class figures for the needs of a modest Edmonton month: rent, groceries, utilities and transit. The first is a one-bedroom alone. The second is sharing with a roommate. They leave out the phone plan and some other costs, so they are lower than the $2,503.00 month.

figure.title: Needs in a modest Edmonton month

cards.text: If needs are half of take-home, then take-home must be double the needs. For $2,203 of needs you need $4,406 of take-home. With a roommate, $1,696 of needs calls for $3,392.

figure.title: Take-home needed for needs to be 50%

cards.text: Now set those needs against that take-home of $2,249.05, full-time at minimum wage. $2,203 is 98% of it. $1,696 is 75.4%. Both are above 50%. The rule is not failing. It is showing what that pay can and cannot hold.

image.alt: A tall jar with a coral line halfway up and gold discs filled above it

cards.text: The roommate lowers the take-home you need by $1,014, and that comes from one decision about where to live, not from budgeting harder. If needs are over half, you can lower the needs, raise the take-home, or both.

image.alt: Two keys on a ring above a short stack of gold discs next to a taller one

questions.label: Take-home alone
questions.prompt: Needs are $2,203 a month. For needs to be half of take-home, how much take-home is needed?
questions.hint: Half of take-home is needs. So take-home is how many times the needs?
questions.why: If needs are half, take-home is twice the needs.
questions.miss: Double the needs. Half of take-home is the needs.

questions.label: With a roommate
questions.prompt: With a roommate, needs are $1,696 a month. How much take-home is needed for needs to be 50%?
questions.hint: The same step as for the one-bedroom.
questions.why: Double the needs.
questions.miss: Double the needs.

questions.label: The gap
questions.prompt: Take-home of $4,406 is needed alone and $3,392 with a roommate. How many dollars less take-home does the roommate case need?

figure.title: Take-home needed for needs to be 50%

questions.hint: Find the difference between the two.
questions.why: Subtract the smaller take-home from the larger.
questions.miss: Subtract the roommate figure from the alone figure.

questions.label: Needs share
questions.prompt: Needs of $2,203 on a take-home of $2,249.05. What percent of take-home is that? Round to one decimal place.
questions.hint: Needs divided by take-home.
questions.why: Divide the needs by the take-home, then turn it into a percent.
questions.miss: Divide the needs by the take-home pay, then multiply by 100.

traps.why: That is the limit in the rule, not this person's share.

questions.label: Roommate share
questions.prompt: Needs of $1,696 on a take-home of $2,249.05. What percent of take-home is that? Round to one decimal place.
questions.hint: Needs divided by take-home.
questions.why: Divide the needs by the take-home, then turn it into a percent.
questions.miss: Divide the needs by the take-home pay, then multiply by 100.

questions.label: Over half
questions.prompt: A person's needs are 70% of their take-home. What does the rule tell them?

terms.meaning: Costs you must pay to live and work, such as rent, groceries, utilities and transport.

questions.hint: The rule is a check, not a law.

options.text: The rule does not work and should be dropped
options.why: The rule did its job. It showed that the needs are heavy.

options.text: Needs take more than their share, so rent or transport is worth a look
options.why: Yes. The check showed something true: the needs are heavy, and housing and transport are the usual place to look.

options.text: Their take-home pay was worked out wrongly
options.why: Nothing says the pay is wrong. The needs are simply a large share.
A high needs share leaves less for savings, not more.

questions.label: Furthest over
questions.prompt: The 50% limit on $2,249.05 is about $1,125. Tap the bar that goes furthest over that limit.
questions.hint: Compare each bar with the 50% limit bar.
questions.why: The one-bedroom alone is $2,203, which is $1,078 over the limit.
questions.miss: Look for the tallest bar.

questions.label: What a roommate does
questions.prompt: What does a roommate change in the 50% check?
questions.hint: What happens to the needs figure?

options.text: It lowers the needs, so less take-home is needed
options.why: Yes. The limit is still half of take-home. The needs got smaller.
Pay stays the same. Only the cost of living changes.
The rule is the same. The needs are smaller.

options.text: It has no effect on the check
options.why: It lowers the needs by a large amount, which changes the check.

questions.label: Over the limit
questions.prompt: Taylor's take-home pay is $2,600.00 and needs are $1,540.00. By how many dollars are needs over the 50% limit?
questions.hint: Find the 50% limit first.
questions.why: Find half of take-home, then take that from the needs.
questions.miss: Half of $2,600.00 is the limit. Then subtract it from the needs.

levels.title: Zero-based
learn: Give every dollar of a take-home a job until none is unassigned.
Say what zero-based does well and what it costs.

cards.text: Zero-based budgeting works differently. There are no shares. You give every dollar of take-home a job until none is left over. The rule is: take-home minus all the jobs equals zero.

image.alt: A tray of small blank jars in a grid, each holding a few gold discs

cards.text: A job can be rent, groceries, a phone bill or fun money. Saving is a job too. A dollar with no job is easy to lose in small buys that you did not plan.

image.alt: A gold disc with a blank paper tag beside other tagged discs in a line

cards.text: Tomas has $2,100.00 of take-home. He has given jobs to $1,835.00. That leaves $265.00 with no job yet.

Tomas gives the last $265.00 a job: $100.00 more to savings and $165.00 to a cushion for surprises. Now his take-home minus his jobs equals zero. Zero does not mean an empty account. The saving dollars are still his.

image.alt: A white tray with every gold disc in its own small bowl and a balanced scale behind

cards.text: The strength is that nothing leaks, because every dollar has a place on purpose. The cost is effort. You do it every month, and again when pay or prices change. It works well for a person who will sit down and do it. A person who skips it gets none of the benefit.

image.alt: An open blank ledger with a pencil and calculator on a desk next to an empty calendar page

questions.label: What is zero
questions.prompt: In zero-based budgeting, which amount ends up equal to zero?

terms.meaning: A plan for what each dollar of a month is for.

questions.hint: Think about dollars with no job.

options.text: Your account balance at the end of the month
options.why: Savings are still in your account. Zero is about unassigned dollars, not an empty account.

options.text: The amount you spend on wants
options.why: Wants can be any amount you decide on, including a job for fun money.
Saving is itself a job. It is not set to zero.

options.text: Take-home minus all the jobs you give the dollars
options.why: Yes. Every dollar has a job, so nothing is left without one.

questions.label: No job yet
questions.prompt: Look at the table. Tomas has given jobs to $1,835.00 of his $2,100.00 take-home. How many dollars have no job yet?
questions.hint: Take-home minus the jobs so far.
questions.why: Take the jobs from the take-home.
questions.miss: Subtract the jobs so far from the take-home pay.

questions.label: After a new job
questions.prompt: Tomas gives $100.00 more to savings. How many dollars still have no job? (Start from the $265.00 that had none.)
questions.hint: Take the new job from the free dollars.
questions.why: The new job uses up part of the free dollars.
questions.miss: Subtract $100.00 from the dollars that had no job.

questions.label: Where saving goes
questions.prompt: Where does saving go in a zero-based budget?
questions.hint: Look back at Tomas's table.

options.text: It is whatever is left at the end
options.why: Leftover dollars are the ones with no job. Zero-based gives saving a job first.
Savings are inside the budget. It is a dollar with a purpose.

options.text: It gets its own job, like any other category
options.why: Yes. A dollar for savings is a dollar with a job.
Zero applies to dollars with no job. Savings is a job.

questions.label: The cost
questions.prompt: What does a zero-based budget cost you?
questions.hint: Read the last card about its cost.

options.text: A fee paid to the bank
options.why: A budget has no fee. The cost is the work you put in.
Yes. You place every dollar, and you redo it when things change.
It does not change the pay. It changes what you do with it.

options.text: The right to spend on wants
options.why: You can give wants a job too, such as fun money.

questions.label: Who has none
questions.prompt: Pia has $1,900.00 of take-home. She gave jobs to $750.00 rent, $280.00 food, $60.00 phone, $200.00 savings and $110.00 fun. How many dollars have no job?
questions.hint: Add the five jobs first.
questions.why: Add the jobs, then take them from the take-home.
questions.miss: Total the five jobs, then subtract that from $1,900.00.

questions.label: Biggest job
questions.prompt: Tap the bar for the biggest job in Tomas's budget.
questions.hint: Find the tallest bar.
questions.why: Rent is $800.00, the tallest bar.
questions.miss: Compare the heights. Which bar is the tallest?

questions.label: Who it suits
questions.prompt: Which person is zero-based most likely to work for?
questions.hint: Think about the cost of the method.

options.text: Someone who will sit down each month and place every dollar
options.why: Yes. It rewards the person who does the monthly work.

options.text: Someone who wants a budget that takes no time
options.why: It takes real time each month, so this is the opposite.

options.text: Someone who would rather not look at their money
options.why: Zero-based asks you to look at every dollar.
Cash is the envelope method. Zero-based can be used with any money.

questions.label: Too many jobs
questions.prompt: Quinn has $1,500.00 of take-home. The jobs he gave add up to $1,640.00. By how many dollars are the jobs more than his take-home?
questions.hint: Compare the two amounts.
questions.why: The jobs are more than the money. The difference is how far over he is.
questions.miss: Subtract the take-home from the jobs.

levels.title: Envelopes
learn: Say how the envelope method sets a limit for each category.
Work out what is left in an envelope.

cards.text: The envelope method is the oldest. You take cash and put a set amount in an envelope for each category, like groceries or going out. You spend only from that envelope. When it is empty, that category is finished until next month.

image.alt: Three blank labelled envelopes in a wooden tray, one stuffed with gold discs

cards.text: The limit is something you can see and hold. Many people find that handing over cash is felt more than tapping a card, so spending slows down. That feeling is a big part of why people use the method.

image.alt: A hand holding out gold discs beside a blank bank card on a table

cards.text: Rae fills three envelopes at the start of the month. Each envelope has a fixed amount. She will spend only from the envelope for that category.

On the 12th, Rae has spent $64.50 of her $100.00 going-out envelope. A friend asks her out for $40.00. She has $35.50 left. She can say no, wait for next month, or choose to move money from another envelope. The empty envelope makes her choose.

image.alt: A nearly empty envelope with two gold discs beside a blank invitation card

cards.text: You do not need cash to use the idea. The phone version uses a separate account or card for each category, with a set amount in it. The limit stays, but the feeling of handing over cash is weaker. Envelopes fit spending you pay for as you go, like groceries and going out. Rent paid online does not.

image.alt: Three phones with blank screens, each linked by a line to its own jar of gold discs

questions.label: Empty envelope
questions.prompt: What happens when an envelope is empty?

terms.meaning: A set amount of cash kept for one category. When it is empty, you stop.

questions.hint: Read the first card.

options.text: It is refilled from savings automatically
options.why: Nothing refills it. The empty envelope is the stop sign.

options.text: You pay with a card until payday
options.why: That would remove the limit. The method means you stop.

options.text: The other envelopes are closed too
options.why: Each envelope works on its own.

options.text: That category is finished until next month
options.why: Yes. That is the rule that makes the limit real.

questions.label: Cash feeling
questions.prompt: Why do many people find they spend less from an envelope of cash than from a card?
questions.hint: The second card says why.

options.text: Cash is worth more than card money
options.why: A dollar is a dollar. The difference is how it feels.

options.text: Stores charge less when you pay in cash
options.why: Prices are the same. The difference is in how spending feels.

options.text: Handing over cash is felt more than tapping a card
options.why: Yes. Seeing the money leave your hand makes the cost feel real.

options.text: A card tap costs extra each time
options.why: A tap does not cost extra. It just feels lighter.

questions.label: Going out left
questions.prompt: Look at the cards. Rae put $100.00 in her going-out envelope and has spent $64.50. How much is left?
questions.hint: Cash put in minus cash spent.
questions.why: Take what she spent from what she put in.
questions.miss: Subtract the amount spent from the amount put in.

questions.label: Per shop
questions.prompt: Rae splits her $300.00 groceries envelope equally across 5 planned shopping trips. How much is that for each trip?
questions.hint: Divide the envelope by the number of trips.
questions.why: Share the envelope equally over the trips.
questions.miss: Divide $300.00 by 5.

questions.label: All the cash
questions.prompt: Look at the table of Rae's envelopes. How much cash is in all three envelopes together?
questions.hint: Add the three amounts.
questions.why: Add the three amounts.
questions.miss: Add all three amounts.

questions.label: Least left
questions.prompt: On the 20th, this is how much is left in Rae's envelopes. Tap the envelope with the least money left.

figure.title: Left in Rae's envelopes on the 20th

questions.hint: Find the shortest bar.
questions.why: Going out has $3.50 left, the shortest bar.
questions.miss: Compare the heights. Which is the shortest?

questions.label: Phone version
questions.prompt: Which one is the phone version of the envelope method?
questions.hint: Same idea, no cash.

options.text: One account for all money with no limits
options.why: With no limit per category, there is no envelope.

options.text: A separate account with a set amount for each category
options.why: Yes. Same idea: a fixed amount per category, and stop when it is empty.

options.text: A budget that splits take-home into three shares
options.why: That is 50/30/20, which splits by percent.

options.text: A list of every dollar and its job
options.why: That is zero-based budgeting.

questions.label: Best fit
questions.prompt: Which spending fits an envelope best?
questions.hint: The last card says what fits.

options.text: Going out, paid as you go
options.why: Yes. You pay each time you spend, so you can take it from the envelope.
Online bills do not go through an envelope of cash.

options.text: A bill that comes off your account automatically
options.why: Nothing passes through your hands, so you cannot stop at empty.
It is one large payment, not an everyday purchase.

questions.label: Groceries left
questions.prompt: Rae put $300.00 in her groceries envelope. She has spent $87.30, then $64.15, then $52.80. How much is left?
questions.hint: Add the three trips first.
questions.why: Add the three trips, then take that from the envelope.
questions.miss: Total the three amounts, then subtract from $300.00.

levels.title: Pay yourself first
learn: Say why moving savings first beats saving what is left.
Work out what remains to budget after paying yourself.

cards.text: Pay yourself first changes the order. Most people spend first and plan to save what is left. What is left is often zero. Here, you move your saving out on payday, before you can spend it. Then you budget what remains.

image.alt: A wall slot and pipe leading to a small safe beside a larger pile of gold discs on a table

cards.text: Set it up once and it can run on its own. A bank can move a set amount to a savings account each payday. In the unit on being responsible with money, you saw that setting money aside the day you are paid is a habit. This is that habit, made automatic.

image.alt: A clock beside a pipe carrying gold discs from a counter into a covered safe

cards.text: Compare two people with the same pay. Mia plans to save what is left. Noor moves $150.00 to savings on payday. By the end of the month Mia has $0.00 left to save, and Noor has $150.00 saved.

figure.title: Same pay, different order
rows: At the end, if any is left

cards.text: A small amount adds up. $75.00 a month is $900.00 in a year (75 x 12). Pick an amount you can keep up, because a small amount that continues beats a big amount that stops.

After the saving moves, you budget the rest. On the game's take-home of $2,249.05, moving $225.00 leaves $2,024.05 to budget. In the game, the Net Worth building lets you move money to savings. You move it yourself.

image.alt: A small safe and a large tray of gold discs on a desk with a blank notebook

questions.label: The order
questions.prompt: What is the order in pay yourself first?

terms.meaning: Move your saving out on payday, before you can spend it.

questions.hint: The name says what comes first.

options.text: Spend freely, then save what is left
options.why: That is the order that often leaves zero to save.

options.text: Budget every cost, then save at year end
options.why: Waiting until year end is the opposite of paying yourself first.

options.text: Save only in months with extra money
options.why: That makes saving depend on luck.

options.text: Move savings on payday, then budget what remains
options.why: Yes. Saving comes first, and the rest of the budget works from what is left.

questions.label: Why it fails
questions.prompt: Why does "save what is left" often fail?
questions.hint: Think about what is left after spending.

options.text: Banks do not accept small deposits
options.why: Small amounts are accepted. The money is simply spent before it can be moved.

options.text: Savings accounts close at month end
options.why: Accounts stay open. The problem is the order.

options.text: What is left at the end of the month is often zero
options.why: Yes. Spending expands to fill the money, so nothing is left to move.

options.text: Saving is not allowed before year end
options.why: You can save at any time.

questions.label: What remains
questions.prompt: Lee has $1,900.00 of take-home and moves $190.00 to savings on payday. How much is left to budget?
questions.hint: Take-home minus the saving.
questions.why: Take the saving off first. The rest is what you budget.
questions.miss: Subtract the saving from the take-home.

questions.label: A year
questions.prompt: Eli moves $120.00 to savings every month. How much is that after 12 months?
questions.hint: There are 12 months in a year.
questions.why: Multiply the monthly amount by 12.
questions.miss: Multiply the monthly amount by 12.

questions.label: How much of pay
questions.prompt: Fay has $2,000.00 of take-home and moves $300.00 to savings on payday. What percent of her take-home is that?
questions.hint: Saving divided by take-home.
questions.why: Divide the saving by the take-home, then turn it into a percent.
questions.miss: Divide $300.00 by $2,000.00, then multiply by 100.

questions.label: Most saved
questions.prompt: Mia saves whatever is left at the end of each month. Tap the month she saved the most.
questions.hint: Find the tallest bar.
questions.why: October is $40.00, the tallest bar.
questions.miss: Compare the heights of the six bars.

questions.label: Mia in total
questions.prompt: Look at the bars. How much did Mia save in the six months in total?
questions.hint: Add all six bars.
questions.why: Add the six months.
questions.miss: Add the six bars together.

questions.label: Noor beats Mia
questions.prompt: Noor moves $50.00 each payday for 6 months. How many dollars more is that than the $80.00 Mia saved by leftovers?
questions.hint: Find Noor's six-month total first.
questions.why: Find Noor's total, then compare.
questions.miss: Multiply $50.00 by 6, then subtract $80.00.

questions.label: Combine methods
questions.prompt: Which statement about pay yourself first is true?
questions.hint: It decides only what happens first.

options.text: It cannot be used with another method
options.why: It is often paired with the others.

options.text: It can be used together with any of the other methods
options.why: Yes. It only decides what happens to the first dollars, so the rest can follow any method.

options.text: It replaces the need to know your take-home
options.why: You still need your take-home to know what remains.

options.text: It only works with cash envelopes
options.why: It works with any of the methods.

questions.label: Habit link
questions.prompt: Which earlier idea does pay yourself first make automatic?
questions.hint: Which habit sets money aside?

options.text: Setting money aside the day you are paid
options.why: Yes. The same habit, run by the bank instead of by memory.

options.text: Borrowing only what you can pay back
options.why: That is about borrowing, not saving.

options.text: Checking a price before you pay
options.why: That is a good habit but it is about spending.
The stub shows pay. It does not move any money.

levels.title: Choosing a method
learn: Match a method to the trouble a person has.
Combine pay yourself first with another method.

cards.text: There is no single best method. Each one fixes a different problem. So ask: what do I find hard about money? Then pick the method built for that.

image.alt: A snowy fork in the road with a signpost of four blank arrows in four colours

cards.text: Here are the four methods side by side. Each has a strength and a hard part.

Match the method to the trouble. If you lose track of where money goes, zero-based. If one category empties the month, envelopes. If saving never happens, pay yourself first. If you want something simple, 50/30/20.

image.alt: A ruler, a marker, an envelope box and a safe in a row, each beside a gold disc

cards.text: You can combine them. Pay yourself first goes with any of the others, because it only decides the first dollars. For example: move savings on payday, then use envelopes for groceries and going out.

image.alt: A safe joined by a ribbon to two envelopes in a tray with gold discs between them

cards.text: In the next unit, Build your budget, you will choose a method and use it on the take-home pay of a career you pick. Decide now what you find hardest about money, so you know which method to try first.

image.alt: An open door onto a bright path across snow with a blank binder and pencil on the step

questions.label: Sol saves
questions.prompt: Sol finds that nothing is ever left to save at the end of the month. The rest of his month works fine. Which method fits that trouble?
questions.hint: Match his one trouble to the table of four methods.

options.why: It places every dollar, which is far more work than a problem about saving needs.
They limit categories. Sol's trouble is that saving gets no turn.
It sets a share for savings, but does not move the money out before you can spend it.
Yes. It moves saving to payday and leaves the rest of his month as it is.

questions.label: Ravi eats out
questions.prompt: Ravi knows where his money goes, but going out empties his month by the 20th. Which method fits?
questions.hint: Read the “Does well” column of the table.

options.why: Ravi already knows where his money goes. His trouble is the stop, not the tracking.
It protects saving. Ravi's trouble is one category.
Yes. A fixed amount for going out with a firm stop when it is empty.
It sets a share for wants as a whole. It has no firm stop for going out.

questions.label: Kai simple
questions.prompt: Kai wants a plan he can write down in a minute: three numbers from his take-home. Which method fits?
questions.hint: Use the Does well column in the table.

options.why: It needs a job for every dollar, which is far more than three numbers.
Yes. It is three shares of take-home, with very little work.
It needs one envelope per category and cash or accounts to carry.
It covers only the saving, not the whole month.

questions.label: Mei tracks
questions.prompt: Mei keeps losing track of where her money goes, and she does not mind sitting down once a month to sort it. Which method fits?
questions.hint: Use the Does well column in the table.

options.why: Yes. Every dollar gets a job, and Mei is willing to do the work.
It groups spending into three lumps, so it would not show where each dollar went.
They limit categories, but do not list every dollar.
It protects saving but does not track the rest.

questions.label: Two troubles
questions.prompt: Luca never saves, and he also overspends on going out. He wants his saving moved before he can spend it, and a firm stop on going out. Which choice covers both?

terms.meaning: Move your saving out on payday, before you can spend it.
A set amount of cash kept for one category. When it is empty, you stop.

questions.hint: Two troubles can take two methods.

options.why: They would stop the overspending but do nothing to move saving first.
It plans every dollar, but does not move saving out first or stop a category when it runs out.
It gives shares, but not a firm stop on going out and not saving first.

options.text: Pay yourself first plus a going-out envelope
options.why: Yes. One handles saving, and the other gives going out a firm stop.

questions.label: Combining methods
questions.prompt: Which statement is true?
questions.hint: The fourth card says it.

options.text: Once you choose a method you can never change it
options.why: You can change methods when your trouble changes.

options.text: Only one method may be used in a month
options.why: Methods can be combined.

options.text: Pay yourself first can go with any of the other three methods
options.why: Yes. It only decides the first dollars, so the rest can follow any method.

options.text: Envelopes cannot be used with saving
options.why: You can pay yourself first and also use envelopes.

questions.label: Combined plan
questions.prompt: Nia has $2,400.00 of take-home. She moves $360.00 to savings, puts $150.00 in a going-out envelope and $320.00 in a groceries envelope. How much is left for everything else?
questions.hint: Add the three amounts first.
questions.why: Take each of the three amounts from the take-home.
questions.miss: Total the three amounts, then subtract from $2,400.00.

questions.label: Kai's limit
questions.prompt: Kai uses 50/30/20 on a take-home of $2,600.00. His needs are $1,420.00. By how many dollars are his needs over, or under, the 50% limit? Give the difference as a positive number.
questions.hint: Find the 50% limit first.
questions.why: Find 50% of take-home, then compare with the needs.
questions.miss: Half of $2,600.00 is the limit. Then compare it with $1,420.00.

questions.label: After groceries
questions.prompt: Look at what is left of a $2,000.00 take-home after each step of a combined plan. Tap the bar that is lower than $1,500.00 but higher than $1,350.00.
questions.hint: Check each bar against both amounts.
questions.why: $1,420.00 is the only bar between $1,350.00 and $1,500.00, the third bar.
questions.miss: Rule out the bars that are above $1,500.00 or below $1,350.00.

image.alt: A winter street at dusk with a bank, a market stall and a library in a row

units.title: Build your budget
units.blurb: Build a monthly budget on the net pay of a career you chose.

levels.title: Start from net pay
learn: Start a monthly budget from net pay, never from salary or gross pay.
Turn a wage and hours into the monthly income line.

cards.text: A monthly budget is a plan for one month. It lists the money coming in, then every line the money goes to. It starts from one number: the money that really lands in your account, which is your net pay.

image.alt: A blank calendar page on a corkboard beside a small jar of gold discs

cards.text: The most common mistake is to start from the salary or from gross pay. Gross pay includes CPP, EI and tax that never reach you. A budget built on gross pay runs short every month.

image.alt: A tall pile of gold discs with three sliding into a blank envelope

cards.text: Here is how to find the number. Hana is made up. She started as a Cashier and stepped up to Retail supervisor in the Job Centre: 151 hours at $19.12. Gross pay is $19.12 x 151 = $2,887.12. Net pay is $2,456.03.

A budget is for one month, so every line is a monthly amount. A week is not a quarter of a month. Multiply a weekly cost by 52 and divide by 12. Groceries of $100.00 a week come to $433.33 a month, not $400.00.

image.alt: A blank wall calendar beside a shopping basket of bread, apples and milk

cards.text: Every line has two parts: an amount and a reason. The reason says where the number came from. This is how Hana writes her income line.

figure.title: Hana: the income line
rows: Net pay: Retail supervisor, after CPP, EI, tax

questions.label: Where to start
questions.prompt: Which number does a monthly budget start from?

terms.meaning: What is left of your pay after every deduction. It is the money that lands in your account.

questions.hint: Think about which number reaches your account.

options.text: Your gross pay for the month
options.why: Gross pay includes CPP, EI and tax that never reach you. A budget on gross pay runs short.

options.text: Your net pay for the month
options.why: Yes. Net pay is the money that actually lands in your account, and that is what you can spend.
A year is the wrong size for a monthly budget, and a salary is before deductions too.
A wage is a rate. You still need the hours and then the deductions to find what lands.

questions.label: Pick the line
questions.prompt: Look at Hana's pay stub. Which line goes on the income line of her budget?
questions.hint: Which amount lands in her account?

options.why: Yes. The last line of the stub is net pay, the money that lands.
That is her gross pay, before the deductions. It does not reach her account.
Tax is one of the deductions. It comes off and does not land.
CPP is a deduction, so it is not what Hana has to spend.

questions.label: Hana gross
questions.prompt: Hana works 151 hours a month as a Retail supervisor at $19.12 an hour. What is her gross pay for the month?

terms.meaning: Your pay before anything is taken off.

questions.hint: Wage x hours.
questions.why: Gross pay for an hourly job is the wage times the hours.
questions.miss: Multiply the hourly wage by the hours worked in the month.

questions.label: Total deductions
questions.prompt: Look at Hana's pay stub. How much do the four deductions come to in all?
questions.hint: There are four lines between the earnings and net pay.
questions.why: The four deduction lines are CPP, EI, federal tax and Alberta tax. Added together they are what comes off the gross pay.
questions.miss: Add the four deduction lines: CPP, EI, federal tax and Alberta tax. Do not add the earnings or the net pay.

questions.label: Cashier income
questions.prompt: A Cashier at Corner Mart has gross pay of $1,803.04. The deductions are CPP $89.93, EI $29.39, federal tax $26.27 and Alberta tax $0.00. What goes on the income line?

terms.meaning: What is left of your pay after every deduction. It is the money that lands in your account.

questions.hint: The budget uses the amount that lands, not the gross pay.
questions.why: The income line is net pay: gross pay minus all four deductions.
questions.miss: Take all four deductions off the gross pay. What is left is net pay.

traps.why: That is the gross pay. The income line uses net pay, $1,657.45.

questions.label: Groceries a month
questions.prompt: Hana spends about $95.00 on groceries each week. What is that for a month? Multiply by 52, divide by 12, and round to the nearest cent.
questions.hint: Change weeks to a year first, then split the year into 12 months.
questions.why: A month is 52 / 12 weeks, about 4.33. Weekly costs go on a monthly budget as the weekly cost x 52 / 12.
questions.miss: Do not multiply by 4. Multiply the weekly amount by 52, then divide by 12.

traps.why: That is the weekly amount x 4. A month has about 4.33 weeks, so the line comes out too low.

questions.label: Four weeks
questions.prompt: Omar writes groceries as $100.00 a week x 4 = $400.00 a month. What is wrong with that line?
questions.hint: How many weeks are in a year? How many months?

options.text: It is too high. A month has only 4 weeks
options.why: A month is a little longer than four weeks, so x 4 undercounts.

options.text: Nothing. Four weeks make a month
options.why: A year has 52 weeks and 12 months. That is about 4.33 weeks a month, not 4.

options.text: It is gross pay instead of net pay
options.why: Gross and net are about income. Groceries is a spending line, so this is a different mistake.

options.text: It is too low. A month is about 4.33 weeks, so the line is $433.33
options.why: Yes. Weekly x 52 / 12 is the right way to put a weekly cost on a monthly budget.

questions.label: Pick the bar
questions.prompt: Tap the bar for the amount that goes on Hana's income line.
questions.hint: Look for the amount that lands in her account.
questions.why: Net pay, $2,456.03, is the amount that lands. It is the third bar.
questions.miss: Gross pay and deductions are not what lands. Read the card about the income line again.

questions.label: Good income line
questions.prompt: Which monthly income line has a number and a reason?
questions.hint: A reason says where the number came from.

options.why: This is the gross pay, and "my pay" does not say where it came from.
The number is net pay, but "seems right" is not a reason. It does not say where the number came from.

options.text: Income $2,456.03: net pay after CPP, EI and tax
options.why: Yes. The number is net pay and the reason says where it came from.

options.text: Income $29,472.36: net pay for a year
options.why: A monthly budget needs a monthly income. This line is a year of net pay.

levels.title: Savings first
learn: Put savings in as the first line, before the others.
Work out a savings line as a share of net pay.

cards.text: Pay yourself first means the savings line goes in before rent or food. You decide the amount now. If you wait and write whatever is left at the end, that number is often zero.

image.alt: A small gold jar at the front of a line of larger empty jars

cards.text: One way to pick the amount is a share of net pay. The 50/30/20 rule puts 20% toward savings and debt payments together. Hana has no debt, and her net pay is $2,456.03. Twenty percent of it is $491.21, rounded to the cent.

image.alt: A pie with one thin slice lifted onto a blank plate beside a gold disc

cards.text: Hana tries four shares. The money left for every other line is net pay minus the savings line. A bigger share saves more and leaves less to spend.
Hana picks 15%, which is $368.40 a month. She picks the amount she can keep up. A small amount that continues beats a big amount that stops. In a year it is 12 x $368.40 = $4,420.80.

image.alt: A seedling in a pot with a ruler, gold discs at its roots and a watering can

cards.text: A savings line is a line like any other: it needs an amount and a reason. It also fits the other methods. In zero-based budgeting saving is a job for a dollar, so you save first, then give every other dollar a job.

image.alt: Two jars on a counter, one full of gold discs and one with coloured buttons

questions.label: Which first
questions.prompt: When you pay yourself first, which line goes into the budget first?

terms.meaning: Put your savings in first, on payday, then plan what remains.

questions.hint: The name says who gets paid first.

options.why: Rent is a large line, but pay yourself first puts savings ahead of it.
Yes. The savings amount is decided before the other lines, so it cannot be squeezed out.
Discretionary spending comes last, after the lines you have to plan for.
Food is a need and gets its line, but savings is the line that goes first.

questions.label: Twenty percent
questions.prompt: Hana's net pay is $2,456.03. What is 20% of it? Round to the nearest cent.
questions.hint: Twenty percent is the same as 20 / 100.
questions.why: A share of net pay is the net pay times the percent, divided by 100.
questions.miss: Multiply the net pay by 20, then divide by 100. Round to the nearest cent.

traps.why: That is 20% of the gross pay, $2,887.12. A savings share is taken from net pay.

questions.label: Ten percent
questions.prompt: If Hana saved 10% of her net pay of $2,456.03, how much would the savings line be? Round to the nearest cent.
questions.hint: Ten percent is one tenth.
questions.why: Ten percent is one tenth of the net pay.
questions.miss: Divide the net pay by 10. Round to the nearest cent.

questions.label: Left to budget
questions.prompt: Hana's savings line is $368.40 and her net pay is $2,456.03. How much is left for every other line?
questions.hint: Net pay minus the savings line.
questions.why: After the saving moves out first, the rest of the net pay is what the other lines share.
questions.miss: Subtract the savings line from the net pay.

questions.label: A year of saving
questions.prompt: Hana saves $368.40 every month. How much is that over 12 months?
questions.hint: There are 12 months in a year.
questions.why: A year has 12 months, so a monthly saving is multiplied by 12.
questions.miss: Multiply the monthly saving by the number of months in a year.

questions.label: Left for the rest
questions.prompt: Tap the bar for the money left for the other lines when Hana saves 15% of her net pay.

figure.title: Left for the other lines out of $2,456.03

questions.hint: Find the bar for the 15% share.
questions.why: At 15%, $368.40 is saved and $2,087.63 is left, the third bar.
questions.miss: That bar is not the 15% share. Read the label under each bar.

questions.label: Good reason
questions.prompt: Which savings line is a share of net pay, with a real reason?
questions.hint: A reason names the amount and where it came from.

options.text: Savings $368.40: 15% of net pay, an amount I can keep up
options.why: Yes. It names the share, says what it is a share of, and says why the amount is chosen.
That is the mistake. A leftover is often zero, and this reason does not say where the number came from.

options.text: Savings $500.00: sounds like a good number
options.why: "Sounds good" does not say where $500.00 came from. It could also be far more than the budget can hold.
A savings share is taken from net pay. $433.07 is 15% of the gross pay.

questions.label: Leftover plan
questions.prompt: Selam plans to save whatever is left at the end of the month. Last month nothing was left. What is the problem with the plan?

terms.meaning: Put your savings in first, on payday, then plan what remains.

questions.hint: Think about which lines get the money first.

options.text: Saving is a bad idea when money is short
options.why: Saving is the point of the plan. The problem is where it sits in the order.

options.text: She needs to use gross pay instead
options.why: Gross pay is not what lands. A budget uses net pay.

options.text: She should save more than 20% of net pay
options.why: The size is not the problem. Even a small saving works if it goes in first.

options.text: The savings only get what the other lines do not use
options.why: Yes. Other lines take the money first, so the leftover is often zero. Pay yourself first reverses the order.

levels.title: A place to live and its bills
learn: Fill the lines that come with a home, using the class prices.
Write a reason that says where each number came from.

cards.text: Rent is the biggest line, and it comes from the housing choice in the Edmonton costs unit. Alone in a 1-bedroom: $1,298.00 a month. Sharing a 2-bedroom that averages $1,581.00 with one roommate: $790.50 each. The line says which choice and why.

image.alt: A small model apartment building beside a house key and a blank tag

cards.text: Other lines come with a home. Utilities (power, heat and water) cost $280.00 to $460.00 a month in the class figures. A phone plan costs $40.00 to $80.00. Pick a number inside the range, and the reason says it is your pick.

image.alt: A lamp, a water tap, a radiator and a phone in a row with blank tags

cards.text: Internet is a home line too, but the class gives no price for it. A made-up person can state an assumption. Hana says her share of the house internet is $35.00 a month. The reason says it is an assumption, not a source.

image.alt: A router with small lights beside a mug and an open blank notebook

cards.text: Here are Hana's four home lines, each with its reason. Rent is half of the 2-bedroom average. The others sit inside the class ranges or say they are an assumption.

figure.title: Hana's home lines
rows: Hana's assumption: the class gives no price

cards.text: Utilities is the line people forget. A budget that leaves it out misses at least $280.00 by the class figures. And if every number is round, like $500 or $1,000, it looks guessed. A number with a source, like $790.50, looks researched.

image.alt: A shelf of matching jars of gold discs beside one jar of coins and a blank receipt

questions.label: Roommate rent
questions.prompt: A 2-bedroom averages $1,581.00 a month. Two people split it equally. What does each person pay?
questions.hint: Two people share the whole rent.
questions.why: Splitting a bill between two people means dividing it by 2.
questions.miss: Divide the 2-bedroom rent by the number of people sharing it.

questions.label: Home lines total
questions.prompt: Add up Hana's four home lines: rent, utilities, phone and internet. What do they come to?

figure.title: Hana's home lines
rows: Hana's assumption: the class gives no price

questions.hint: Add the first four rows of the table. Do not add the last row.
questions.why: The four lines are added to find what her home costs each month.
questions.miss: Add the four amounts: rent, utilities, phone and internet. The last row of the table is already a total.

questions.label: Inside the range
questions.prompt: Which amount is inside the class range for utilities, $280.00 to $460.00 a month?
questions.hint: The amount has to be between the two numbers.

options.why: $190.00 is below the bottom of the range, $280.00.
$520.00 is above the top of the range, $460.00.

questions.label: Missing line
questions.prompt: A budget has these home lines: rent $790.50, phone $55.00 and internet $35.00. Which home line is missing?
questions.hint: The lines that come with a home are rent, utilities, phone and internet.

options.why: A student loan has its own section and is not one of the lines that come with a home.
Yes. Power, heat and water come with a home, and the class figures put them at $280.00 to $460.00. It is the line people forget.
A car belongs with getting around, not with the home lines.

questions.label: Rent share, roommate
questions.prompt: Hana's rent is $790.50 and her net pay is $2,456.03. What percent of her net pay is the rent? Round to one decimal place.
questions.hint: Divide the rent by the net pay.
questions.why: The share is the part divided by the whole, times 100.
questions.miss: Divide the rent by the net pay, then multiply by 100. Round to one decimal place.

questions.label: Rent share, alone
questions.prompt: If Hana rented a 1-bedroom alone at $1,298.00, what percent of her net pay of $2,456.03 would the rent be? Round to one decimal place.
questions.hint: The same steps as for the roommate rent.
questions.why: Living alone puts more than half of her net pay into rent.
questions.miss: Divide the rent by the net pay, then multiply by 100. Round to one decimal place.

questions.label: Real reason
questions.prompt: Which reason says where a rent number came from?
questions.hint: Look for the reason that shows its figure.

options.why: Yes. It names the choice and the figure the number came from.
"About what rent costs" does not say where $790.50 came from.
A feeling is not a source. A reason needs a figure or an assumption you can defend.

options.text: $790.50: it is a round enough number
options.why: $790.50 is not round, and being round is no reason for a number to be right.

questions.label: Smallest home line
questions.prompt: Tap the bar for Hana's smallest home line.
questions.hint: Compare the heights of the four bars.
questions.why: Internet, $35.00, is the smallest of the four.
questions.miss: That bar is not the shortest. Look for the smallest amount.

questions.label: All round
questions.prompt: Priya finds that every number in her budget is a multiple of fifty: $800, $300, $50, $400. What does that suggest?
questions.hint: Where do round numbers usually come from?

options.text: The budget must be right, since round numbers are exact
options.why: Round numbers are not more exact. Real prices and sources are rarely all round.

options.text: She should round every number up to be safe
options.why: Rounding up does not give a source. Each line still needs a reason.

options.text: Nothing, because reasons are only for big lines
options.why: Every line needs a reason, big or small.

options.text: The numbers may be guesses, so each needs a source
options.why: Yes. A budget of round numbers looks estimated instead of researched. A source for each line fixes that.

levels.title: Getting around and food
learn: Price how you get around and what you eat, with a reason.
Use the all-in cost of a car and monthly food amounts.

cards.text: Transportation is a choice from the Edmonton costs unit, now with a price. A monthly bus pass is $105.00. Owning a car costs $680.00 to $1,150.00 a month, all in. The reason says why you chose it.

image.alt: A blank bus pass on a toy bus beside a toy car and a tall stack of gold discs

cards.text: All in means every cost of the car, not just the payment. Theo is made up. His shift starts before the first bus, so he needs a car. His car costs $855.00 a month all in, which is inside the class range.
Groceries cost $370.00 to $490.00 a month in the class figures. Hana buys about $95.00 of groceries a week. That is $95.00 x 52 / 12 = $411.67 a month, inside the range.

image.alt: A market basket of carrots, apples, bread and milk in front of a blank calendar

cards.text: Dining out has no class price, so it needs an assumption you can defend: how many times a month, at what cost. Hana eats out 4 times a month at $16.50, which is $66.00. She counts it here, so it does not appear again later.

image.alt: A cafe table with a cup, a plate, a blank menu and a few gold discs

cards.text: Here are Hana's lines for getting around and food, each with its reason.

figure.title: Hana's getting around and food
rows: The class price of a monthly pass
4 times a month at $16.50: her assumption

questions.label: Car all in
questions.prompt: Add up Theo's car costs: payment, insurance, fuel, maintenance and registration. What is the all-in cost for a month?

terms.meaning: Every cost of owning the car, not just the loan payment.

questions.hint: There are five costs in the table.
questions.why: All in means every cost of the car. The all-in line is the sum of all five.
questions.miss: Add all five costs in the table. The payment alone is not the all-in cost.

questions.label: Car or bus
questions.prompt: Theo's car costs $855.00 a month all in. The bus pass is $105.00. How much more is the car each month?
questions.hint: Subtract the smaller from the larger.
questions.why: The gap is the car cost minus the bus pass.
questions.miss: Subtract the bus pass from the all-in car cost.

questions.label: Groceries a month
questions.prompt: Ola spends $105.00 on groceries each week. What is that for a month? Multiply by 52 and divide by 12.
questions.hint: A month is not four weeks.
questions.why: Weekly costs go on a monthly budget as the weekly cost x 52 / 12.
questions.miss: Multiply by 52 first, then divide by 12.

traps.why: That is $105.00 x 4. A month is about 4.33 weeks, so the line is too low.

questions.label: Dining out
questions.prompt: Zara plans to eat out 3 times a month at $18.50 each. What does her dining out line come to?
questions.hint: Times a month x cost each time.
questions.why: The line is the number of times a month x the cost each time. It is Zara's assumption, so the reason says both numbers.
questions.miss: Multiply the number of times by the cost each time.

questions.label: Three lines
questions.prompt: Add up Hana's bus pass, groceries and dining out. What do the three lines come to?

figure.title: Hana's getting around and food
rows: The class price of a monthly pass
4 times a month at $16.50: her assumption

questions.hint: Add the first three rows. The last row is already a total.
questions.why: The three lines make up getting around and food for her month.
questions.miss: Add the three amounts: bus pass, groceries and dining out. Do not add the total row too.

questions.label: Best car line
questions.prompt: Which car line follows what the unit teaches about the all-in cost?

terms.meaning: Every cost of owning the car, not just the loan payment.

questions.hint: All in means every cost of owning the car.

options.why: The payment is only one part of the cost. Insurance, fuel, maintenance and registration are left out.

options.text: $1,150.00: the top of the class range
options.why: The top of the range is not a reason. A made-up person's car has its own costs.

options.text: $855.00: payment, insurance, fuel, maintenance and registration
options.why: Yes. All in means every cost, and the reason lists them.

options.text: $105.00: the price of a bus pass
options.why: That is the bus pass, not a car.

questions.label: Dining source
questions.prompt: Where does the number for a dining out line come from?
questions.hint: Is there a class figure for this line?

options.text: A class price list for dining out
options.why: The class figures give no price for dining out.

options.text: Your own assumption: how often, and the cost each time
options.why: Yes. The class gives no price for it, so you state an assumption and the reason says the count and the cost.
That range is for groceries only. Dining out is a separate line.
Take-home pay is the income. The spending line comes from what you plan to do.

questions.label: Theo's car
questions.prompt: Tap the bar for Theo's all-in car cost.
questions.hint: Look for the bar labelled with his name.
questions.why: Theo's car, $855.00, is the third bar. It sits between the bottom and the top of the class range.
questions.miss: That bar is not labelled Theo's car. Read the label under each bar.

questions.label: Car reason
questions.prompt: Which reason says why the job needs a car?
questions.hint: The reason must connect the car to the job.

options.text: The shift starts before the first bus runs
options.why: Yes. It ties the car to the job. The reason also needs the all-in cost beside it.

options.text: Cars are more fun than buses
options.why: That is a want. A reason for the line must say why the job needs the car.
What a friend has does not make the job need a car.

options.text: The top of the range is a safe number
options.why: That is about the number, not about why the job needs a car.

levels.title: Loans and the rest
learn: Fill the student loans line, even when it is zero.
Plan discretionary spending as money you choose to spend.

cards.text: Student loans is a line to fill in, not to skip. If a career needs a diploma or a degree, most people finish with a loan and a payment each month. That payment belongs in the budget.

image.alt: A graduation cap on a book beside a paper scroll and a jar of gold discs

cards.text: A trade with a paid apprenticeship may have a loan line of zero. A zero is a correct answer when the reason says why. A blank is the mistake. This course gives no price for school, so look up a real payment before you write a number.

image.alt: A toolbox with a hammer and wrench beside an empty tagged jar and a gold disc

cards.text: Discretionary spending is everything not in the other sections: clothes, subscriptions, gifts, the gym. Put each item in one place only. Hana counts dining out under food, so it is not here again. Her values show in what she picks.

image.alt: A scarf, headphones, a wrapped gift and a yoga mat in a neat pile

cards.text: Here are Hana's discretionary lines with their reasons. Her loan line is $0.00, because she went straight to work and has no school loan.

figure.title: Hana's discretionary lines
rows: Work clothes and a winter coat
Social value: giving to people she cares about
Keeps her energy up for shifts

cards.text: Before you plan discretionary lines, find the room. Hana's net pay is $2,456.03. Savings, home, getting around and food, and loans come to $2,166.57. The room left is $2,456.03 - $2,166.57 = $289.46.

image.alt: A tray of small bowls, most holding gold discs and one left empty

questions.label: Trade loan line
questions.prompt: Marcus is an apprentice electrician. He is paid while he learns and owes no school loan. What goes on his loan line?
questions.hint: A line can be zero, but it still needs a reason.

options.text: Nothing, because he has no loan
options.why: A blank looks like a forgotten line. Write $0.00 and say why.

options.text: The line is skipped for trades
options.why: The section stays. A trade may have a loan line of zero, but the line is still there.

options.text: A number copied from a friend
options.why: A number with no source is weak. His real answer is zero, with a reason.

options.text: $0.00, with a reason that says why
options.why: Yes. A zero with a reason is a correct answer. The reason says he was paid while learning and owes nothing.

questions.label: Diploma career
questions.prompt: A career needs a two-year diploma. What does its student loans line probably need?
questions.hint: Think about what most people have when they finish school.

options.why: The loan has to be paid back after school ends. That is when the payments start.

options.text: Nothing, because loans are not budget items
options.why: A loan payment is money out each month, so it is a budget line.

options.text: A monthly payment, with a source for the number
options.why: Yes. Most people finish a diploma or a degree with a loan and a payment, and it belongs in the budget.

options.text: A share of net pay, like savings
options.why: A loan payment is not chosen like a savings share. It comes from the loan.

questions.label: Two subscriptions
questions.prompt: Hana has two subscriptions at $11.99 each. What do they cost together in a month?
questions.hint: Two plans, same price.
questions.why: Two plans at the same price cost twice that price.
questions.miss: Multiply the price of one plan by 2.

questions.label: Discretionary total
questions.prompt: Add up Hana's four discretionary lines. What do they come to?

figure.title: Hana's discretionary lines
rows: Work clothes and a winter coat
Social value: giving to people she cares about
Keeps her energy up for shifts

questions.hint: Add the first four rows. The last row is a total.
questions.why: The four lines added up are the discretionary spending in her month.
questions.miss: Add clothes, subscriptions, gifts and the gym. Do not add the total row too.

questions.label: Room to plan
questions.prompt: Hana's net pay is $2,456.03. Her other sections come to $2,166.57. How much room is left for discretionary lines?
questions.hint: Net pay minus the other sections.
questions.why: The room is net pay minus every other section.
questions.miss: Subtract the other sections from the net pay.

questions.label: Not yet planned
questions.prompt: Hana has $289.46 of room and plans $145.98 of discretionary lines. How much is not planned yet?
questions.hint: The room minus the lines.
questions.why: What is not planned is the room minus the lines already planned. Those dollars still need a job.
questions.miss: Subtract the planned lines from the room.

questions.label: Which value
questions.prompt: Hana puts money toward gifts for people she cares about. In the first unit you met four kinds of values. Which kind fits gifts best?
questions.hint: Who is the gift for?

options.text: Inner, which is about freedom and peace of mind
options.why: Inner values are about who you are. Gifts are about other people.

options.text: Social, which is about people and giving
options.why: Yes. Social values are about people: helping, giving and belonging.

options.text: Physical, which is about comfort and quality
options.why: Physical values are about things around you, like comfort and quality.
Financial values are about a cushion and not running short. Gifts are about giving.

questions.label: Biggest line
questions.prompt: Tap the bar for Hana's biggest discretionary line.
questions.hint: Compare the heights of the four bars.
questions.why: Clothes, $55.00, is the biggest of the four.
questions.miss: That bar is not the tallest. Look for the biggest amount.

questions.label: Which section
questions.prompt: Which of these belongs in the discretionary section?

terms.meaning: Spending on things you choose, such as clothes, subscriptions, gifts and the gym.

questions.hint: Which of these is spending you choose, beyond the other sections?

options.why: Yes. Clothes, subscriptions, gifts and the gym are discretionary.
Groceries have their own line under food.
The bus pass belongs with getting around.
Rent belongs with the home lines.

levels.title: Add it up
learn: Find whether a month is left over, at zero or short.
Fix a short month by lowering a line or raising income.

cards.text: To finish a budget, add every line and take the total from the income. The answer is one of three things: money left over, exactly zero, or short. Each one tells you something.

sections.title: Investing Foundations
sections.blurb: How money grows, what shrinks it, and how to choose what to own.

units.title: Why invest
units.blurb: Saving and investing do different jobs, and time is the biggest tool you have.

levels.title: Saving and investing do different jobs
learn: Say what saving is for and what investing is for.
Match a goal to saving or investing by when you need the money.

cards.text: Saving and investing do different jobs. Saving keeps money safe and ready for something soon. Investing puts money to work so it can grow for something far away. This level is about telling the two jobs apart.
Saving: Priya wants a $480.00 bike in 8 months. She sets aside $60.00 a month. She needs the whole amount by a set date, so she keeps it safe and easy to reach. Saving is for goals that are close.

Investing: Luis is 20 and wants money for when he is 65. That is 45 years away, so he will not need it soon. This kind of money can be put to work and left alone for a long time. Investing is for goals that are far away.

Ask one question first: when will I need this money? Money needed within a year or two is saving money. Money you will not touch for ten years or more is investing money. In between, people weigh it up. This unit uses the clear cases.

Putting money to work can bring losses as well as gains. The Risk and return unit, later in this section, covers that. Many people do both jobs: some money for soon, some for later. Paying yourself first can fill either one.

cards.text: Rae and Sam each have $1,000.00. Rae keeps hers in a jar at home. Sam puts his in an account that pays 6% a year. The 6% is an example. A year later, Rae still has $1,000.00. Sam has $1,060.00.
The account pays interest. Interest is money paid to you for letting the bank hold yours. The amount the account holds is its balance. A rate of 6% means $6 for every $100 in a year.
Here is how the two grew over 30 years, to the nearest dollar. The jar never changes. The account does not rise by $60 every year. It rises by a little more each year. The next unit explains why.

figure.title: $1,000 in a jar and in an account

cards.text: Look at the gap: the account balance minus the jar. At year 10 it is $791. At year 20 it is $2,207. At year 30 it is $4,743. Same $1,000, same 30 years, and the gap keeps growing.

Now see what the account added in each ten years. The first ten years added $791. The next ten added $1,416. The last ten added $2,536. Each ten years adds more than the one before. The next unit explains how.

Two things to keep in mind. The 6% is an example, and the rate a real account pays can change. Also, prices rise over time, which the Inflation unit explains. For now, just compare what the jar and the account hold.

cards.text: Meet two savers. Amara saves $200 a month from age 18 to age 28, then stops and never adds again. Ben waits. He saves $200 a month from age 28 to age 65. Same pay, same $200. Who has more at 65?
Here is what each put in. Ben put in 3.7 times as much as Amara. Amara put in less than a third of what Ben did. Look at the last row too: Amara’s first deposit had 47 years until 65. Ben’s had 37.

Now the balances at 65, with growth at 8% a year as an example. They are worked out month by month and shown to the nearest dollar. Amara has $699,195. Ben has $543,280. Amara is $155,915 ahead although she put in less.

Where did the money come from? Amara put in $24,000 and ends with $699,195, so $675,195 is growth. Ben put in $88,800 and ends with $543,280, so $454,480 is growth. Her money had ten more years to grow.
This chart follows Amara’s balance. She stops adding at 28, yet the line keeps climbing, and it climbs more steeply later. Time did that work, not new deposits.

Time is not the whole story. At 6% in the same example, Ben ends with more. Only the rate changed. So the rate matters as well as the time. The next unit explains how the growth works, so you can see why.

cards.text: Jordan is 22 and takes home $2,000.00 a month. That is net pay, the money left after deductions. On payday, before anything else, Jordan moves 10% to savings. 10% of $2,000.00 is $200.00. That is paying yourself first.

This is the pay yourself first habit, set up once and repeated every payday. Jordan did not save a large amount. It was 10% of pay, for a long time. The 7% is an example and real rates change. The next unit explains how the growth happens.

levels.title: Interest is a price for money
learn: Say what interest is and what a yearly rate means.
Work out one year of interest on any amount.

cards.text: Interest is the price of using money. When you lend money, you earn interest. When you borrow, you pay it. When you keep money in a savings account, the bank uses it, and the bank pays you interest.
The money you start with is the principal. Interest is extra money added on top of it. A rate says how much, as a percent of the principal. A rate of 5% means $5 of interest for every $100.

A rate is a percent for one year. To find a year of interest, change the rate to a decimal and multiply by the principal. 5% is 0.05, and 2% is 0.02. For $400.00 at 5%: $400.00 x 0.05 = $20.00 in one year.
Here is one year of interest at 5% on four different principals. Twice the principal earns twice the interest. The rate is the same in every row.

After one year you hold the principal plus the interest. That total is your balance. $800.00 at 3% earns $24.00 in a year, so the balance is $824.00. Next you will see what happens in the years after the first.

levels.title: Simple growth
learn: Find the total when the same interest is added every year.

cards.text: Simple interest is the easiest kind. Each year the interest is figured on the starting amount only. So it is the same dollars every year. $1,000 at 10% earns $100 a year, for as long as you wait.
Here is $1,000 at 10% simple interest. The interest column never changes. The total goes up by $100 every year.
A short way to find a total: principal plus (yearly interest x years). For $1,000 at 10% after 10 years: $1,000 + ($100 x 10) = $2,000. With simple interest, doubling takes 10 years here.
On a chart, simple growth is a straight line. The total rises by the same step each time. Here the step is $500 for every 5 years.

Notice what simple interest ignores. In year 2 you hold $1,100, but you still earn only $100, the interest on the first $1,000. The $100 you were paid last year earns nothing. That changes in the next level.

levels.title: Compound growth
learn: Say how interest can earn interest.
Grow an amount year by year by multiplying by 1 plus the rate.

cards.text: Compound interest adds each year's interest to the balance. The next year's interest is figured on the bigger balance. So your interest starts earning interest too. It is growth on growth.
To grow a balance for one year, multiply it by 1 plus the rate. At 10% that is 1.10. Each year: new balance = old balance x 1.10. $1,000 becomes $1,100, then $1,210, then $1,331.
Follow $1,000 at 10%. Each year's interest is 10% of that year's start. The start is last year's end. So the interest itself grows from year to year.
The first years look a lot like simple interest. Year 1 is the same, $100. Year 2 is $110 against $100. The bars keep rising. Simple interest would give five bars of the same height.
A common slip is to multiply by the rate alone. $1,000 x 0.10 = $100 is only the interest. The new balance is $1,000 x 1.10 = $1,100. For 6% use 1.06. For 4% use 1.04. For 12% use 1.12.

levels.title: The Rule of 72
learn: Estimate how long money takes to double.
Work backwards from years to the rate.

cards.text: Doubling means $1,000 becomes $2,000. How long it takes depends on the rate. The Rule of 72 is a quick estimate, with no calculator. Divide 72 by the rate, as a plain number. The answer is about how many years money takes to double.

At 6%: 72 / 6 = 12 years. At 8%: 72 / 8 = 9 years. At 9%: 72 / 9 = 8 years. A higher rate means a shorter wait. Also, 72 divides evenly by 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 9 and 12, so those rates are easy to do in your head.
The rule is an estimate, not an exact answer. Here it is beside the exact time, with interest added once a year. They are close at these rates. As the rate gets high, the rule drifts away.

You can run the rule the other way. If money doubled in 9 years, the rate was about 72 / 9 = 8%. If it doubled in 6 years, about 12%. Rate x years is about 72, so divide 72 by the one you know to find the other.
Check it once. Multiply $1,000 by 1.08 nine times and you get about $1,999. The rule said $2,000 for 8% and 9 years. That is why people use it for a quick look.

learn: Double an amount forward to a later age.

cards.text: To see where money ends up, double it forward. Say $10,000 at age 29, and nobody adds another cent. At 6% the rule gives a doubling every 12 years: $20,000 at 41, $40,000 at 53, $80,000 at 65.
Here is the same $10,000 at four rates, from age 29 to 65. That is 36 years. The number of doublings is 36 divided by the doubling time. Count down the Doublings column.

Look at the last column. Same money, same 36 years, nothing added. Only the rate changed. At 12% the end amount is 16 times the amount at 4%. Each extra doubling doubles the total again, so a few percent more adds up to a lot.

The rule is a shortcut, so check it. It is fairly close at 4%, 6% and 8%. At 12% it gives $640,000 but the exact amount is $591,356. It does not predict any real rate either. These rates are examples.

Interest can be added more often than once a year. At 6%, adding it every month means 0.5% a month. Over a year that grows money by about 1.0617, not 1.06. It is a bit more, because interest added early in the year earns interest too.

The Net Worth building has a high-interest savings account. It adds interest every game month, so each month's interest joins the balance and earns more. The rate can change, so check the live rate there. The game starts at 2.75% a year, and the building shows its own Rule of 72 line.

units.title: Inflation
units.blurb: Prices rise a little every year, so a dollar that sits still buys less.

levels.title: Prices rise
learn: Say what inflation is and how a yearly rate is found.
Work out a price rise in percent and in dollars.

cards.text: Inflation is a rise in prices in general, year after year. It is not one price going up. It means most prices drift up, so the same shopping costs more. The yearly inflation rate says by how many percent.
Here is a made-up basket of three things, this year and next year. Bread went up, milk went up a little, and the bus ticket stayed the same. Prices do not all move together.

Inflation looks at the whole basket. It went from $12.00 to $12.30. To find the percent change: take the new price minus the old, divide by the old, and multiply by 100. $0.30 / $12.00 = 0.025, which is 2.5%.

You can go the other way with the same trick you used for compound growth. If prices rise 3% in a year, multiply by 1.03. A $50.00 item costs $50.00 x 1.03 = $51.50 next year. For 4% use 1.04, and for 2% use 1.02.

The rates in this unit, such as 3% or 1.5%, are examples from class. Real rates change. The Bank of Canada aims to keep inflation near 2%, inside a range of 1% to 3%. The game has inflation too, and the last level shows where.

levels.title: The rule backwards
learn: Say how prices compound, year after year.

cards.text: Prices compound the way money does. If prices rise 3% every year, the second rise is 3% of a price that has already risen. So each year you multiply by 1.03. A $100.00 basket costs $103.00 after one year and $106.09 after two.
Here is the $100.00 basket at 3% a year. The rise each year is a little bigger than the year before, because it is 3% of a bigger price.

The Rule of 72 works on prices too. Divide 72 by the yearly inflation rate. The answer is about how many years it takes for prices to double. At 3%: 72 / 3 = 24 years. As with money, it is an estimate.

If prices double, a dollar buys half as much. A basket that cost $100.00 now costs $200.00, so $100.00 buys only half of it. Buying power is how much your money can buy. At 3% it halves in about the same 24 years.
Here is the rule at four example rates, beside the basket after that many years. Run it backwards too: prices that doubled in 9 years rose about 72 / 9 = 8% a year.

levels.title: The savings trap
learn: Say why a growing balance can still buy less.
Estimate the change in buying power: rate minus inflation.

cards.text: Here is the class example. A savings account pays 1.5% a year, and prices rise 3% a year. After a year, $1,000.00 in the account is $1,015.00. The balance on the statement went up. Now look at what it buys.
The shopping that cost $1,000.00 now costs $1,030.00. Your $1,015.00 is $15.00 short of it. The balance rose, but the buying power fell.

A quick estimate: the change in buying power is about the account's rate minus the inflation rate. 1.5% - 3% = -1.5%, so buying power fell about 1.5%. It is only an estimate. The exact fall here is about 1.46%.
Four example accounts, with prices rising 3%. Cash kept at home earns 0%, so it loses the whole 3%. An account that earns exactly the inflation rate keeps its buying power.

The Rule of 72 works on a loss too. Buying power falls about 1.5% a year, so it halves in about 72 / 1.5 = 48 years. The balance on the statement rises the whole time, which is why a loss like this is easy to miss.

levels.title: Inflation in the game
learn: Say how the game's price index moves bills and rent.

cards.text: The game has inflation built in. A price index starts at 1.0000 when the season starts. Once each world year it steps up by the yearly rate, the first time one world year in. The game starts at 2.1% a year. The teacher can change it.
Here is the index if the rate stays at 2.1%. The steps compound, as prices did in the last levels. The game rounds the index to four decimal places at each step.

figure.title: The price index at 2.1% a year

cards.text: The index moves prices. A bill issued after a step costs its base amount times the index. Rent in later months does too. A bill already issued is not repriced. Maya's made-up rent is $900.00 and her bills $400.00. After the first step: $918.90 and $408.40.

Wages do not follow the index by themselves. A new hire starts at the job's base wage times the index. After that, pay changes only by a raise (about a year into a job; the game starts at 3%), a promotion, or a raise the teacher grants. So a raise must beat the index to help.

Maya earns $2,000.00 a month and pays $1,300.00 in rent and bills, leaving $700.00. After a 2.1% step her bills are $1,327.30. A 2.1% raise makes her pay $2,042.00, so $714.70 is left. It buys the same as before.

To see the live numbers, open the Bank of DAA. It shows the yearly rate prices rise and how much higher prices are than at the start of the season. The teacher can change the rate, so what you see may not be 2.1%.

units.title: Risk and return
units.blurb: What you can own, how risky each choice is, and four questions to ask first.

levels.title: Saving, lending, owning
learn: Money can work in three different ways.
You will tell them apart and say what each one can pay and risk.

cards.text: Money can work in three ways. You can keep it safe in an account. You can lend it to someone who pays you for the loan. Or you can use it to own a share of something. Each way pays in its own way and has its own risk.

Saving: Amina puts $500.00 in a savings account. The bank pays her a little interest for keeping it there. Interest is a payment for letting someone else use your money. The amount in her account does not go down.
Lending: Tomas lends $800.00 for a year. The borrower promises to pay it back with 5% interest, which is $40.00. The payment is set in advance. The risk is that the borrower cannot pay.

Owning: Jess puts money into a bakery and gets a 2% share. If the bakery is worth $40,000, her share is worth $800.00. If the bakery does better, her share is worth more. If it struggles, her share is worth less. Nothing is promised.
Here are the three side by side. The more a way can pay, the more it usually has to lose.

levels.title: What you can own
learn: Ten common kinds of investment, each in one plain sentence.
You will match a description to its name.

cards.text: There are many things a person can put money into. Ten common ones are on the next cards. Each one is saving, lending or owning, or sits between them. We will name them in plain words.
Mostly saving and lending. These pay interest, and the rate is set in advance.

figure.title: Savings and loans
rows: Money in a bank. Pays a little interest.
Money locked in for a set time at a rate that is guaranteed.
A loan to the government, paid back with interest.
A loan to a company. More interest, but companies can fail.

cards.text: Mostly owning, or holding something in hope it is worth more later.

figure.title: Things you own
rows: A small piece of a single company.
One purchase: a tiny slice of hundreds of companies.
A manager picks the investments. You pay a fee.
A house or property you rent out or sell later.
A metal people buy when they are nervous about money.
Digital currency. No bank or government stands behind it.

cards.text: A fund is one purchase that holds many things at once. Funds charge a fee, a small percent of what you hold each year. The game's Exchange has funds too: one holds every company in town, one holds bonds, and one mixes the two.

A GIC is a loan to a bank for a set time. A bond is a loan to a government or a company. A stock is a share of a company. Gold and crypto are different: nothing is lent and you own no business. People buy them hoping others will pay more later.

questions.hint: Two clues: a set time, and a guaranteed rate.

Yes. The term is set and so is the rate.
Gold has no rate and no term. You hold a metal.

With property you choose it and own it yourself. No manager picks it for you.

levels.title: Safest to riskiest
learn: Risk is the chance of ending with less and how far the value swings.
You will place investments at the safe and risky ends.

cards.text: Risk has two parts. One is the chance of ending with less than you put in. The other is how far the value swings up and down on the way. More chance of loss and bigger swings mean more risk.
At the safe end sit the savings account and the GIC. What you put in is protected and the rate is guaranteed. Next comes the government bond, because governments almost never fail to pay.
A corporate bond is the same idea as a government bond, but a company can fail. Funds come next. An index fund spreads your money over hundreds of companies, so one going bad barely shows.

One company's stock sits much further along. If that company fails, the stock can go to zero. Gold and crypto sit near the risky end. Their prices swing hard, and nothing holds them up except what the next buyer will pay.
Here is a rough order, safest first. Real estate is left out because it could sit almost anywhere.

The ends are settled and the middle is arguable. A mutual fund can be safer than a bond, depending on what its manager picked. Savings accounts are at the safe end and crypto is at the risky end, and those two are not up for debate.

levels.title: How fast can you get it out?
learn: Liquidity is how fast something turns into cash.
You will tell it apart from risk.

cards.text: Liquidity is how fast you can turn something into cash without losing value. It is a different question from risk. Risk asks how much the value might change. Liquidity asks how fast you can get your money out.

A savings account is very liquid: the money is already cash. A stock or an index fund can be sold quickly while the market is open, and the cash arrives in a day or two. That is the class example, not a promise for every case.
A GIC is safe but locked. You cannot touch the money until the term ends, which may be months or years. A house is fairly steady in price, but selling it takes months.
Crypto is the surprise. It sits at the risky end, yet you can sell it in minutes. Quick does not mean safe: you might sell at a loss. Safe does not mean quick: a GIC is locked.
Here is the same list in a new order, fastest first. It is not the same as the order of risk.

Money you may need soon needs liquidity more than a high return. If a bill could arrive next week, a locked GIC or a house is a poor place for that money, because neither can be turned into cash quickly.
