levels.title: Why buy the risky one?
learn: Higher expected return is the pay for taking risk.
You will work with gains, losses and averages.

cards.text: Nobody takes risk for fun. People take it because they expect to be paid for it. The pay is a higher expected return: the average result across many possible outcomes. It is not a promise.

Here is the class example. A savings account pays about 1.5% a year. A stock might gain 8% in a year, or lose 30%. The savings account is dull but steady. The stock could do better and it could do much worse.

Expected is not promised. A made-up stock has four equally likely years: -30%, +4%, +12%, +34%. Add them and divide by four to get the average, the expected return: 5%. Any single year can be far from 5%.
The bars show $1,000 after one year. The stock's results are spread wide. The savings result is narrow. A wide range is what risk looks like.
To find a gain or loss in dollars, subtract the start from the end. To find a percent change, divide that gain or loss by the starting value. A loss of $300 on $1,000 is a change of -30%.

A big drop is hard to undo. Losing 30% of $1,000 leaves $700. Getting back to $1,000 takes a gain of $300 on $700, which is about 42.9%. The risky choice can pay more on average, and its bad years cost more to climb out of.

terms.meaning: The average result across many possible outcomes. It is not a promise.

questions.miss: Add all four, with the minus on the first one, then divide by four.

questions.label: Dollars lost
questions.prompt: Rae has $2,500 in a stock. It falls 30%. How many dollars does she lose?
questions.hint: Take 30% of the amount.
questions.why: A loss in dollars is the percent times the starting value.
questions.miss: Turn 30% into 0.30 and multiply by $2,500.

questions.label: Percent change
questions.prompt: A stock holding grows from $800 to $864. What is the percent change?
questions.hint: Find the gain, then divide it by the starting value.
questions.why: Percent change is the gain divided by the starting value.
questions.miss: Divide the gain by $800, the starting value, not by $864.

questions.label: Compare two
questions.prompt: Mia puts $2,000 in a stock and Ben puts $2,000 in a savings account paying 1.5%. In the stock's best year it gains 34%. How many more dollars does the stock give than the savings account?
questions.hint: Find each gain in dollars, then subtract.
questions.why: Compare the two gains in dollars. The stock's best year beats the savings account by a lot.
questions.miss: Work out the stock's gain and the savings gain, then take one from the other.

questions.label: Below the start
questions.prompt: The bars show $1,000 after one year. Tap the stock result that ended below the $1,000 it started with.
questions.hint: Compare each stock bar with $1,000.
questions.why: The worst year ended at $700, below the $1,000 start. The other stock bars are above $1,000.
questions.miss: Look for the stock bar that is shorter than $1,000.

questions.label: Wide or narrow
questions.prompt: In the bars, which description fits the savings result?
questions.hint: How many results does savings have?

options.text: A wide range, so high risk
options.why: A wide range is what the stock shows. Savings has one result.
The savings result is above $1,000. It does not lose.
The best bar is the stock in its best year.

options.text: One narrow result, so low risk
options.why: Yes. The savings result is close to $1,015 and does not swing.

questions.label: Five percent
questions.prompt: Dana says, "The stock is expected to earn 5%, so next year it will earn 5%." What is wrong with that?
questions.hint: Remember the four years: -30%, +4%, +12% and +34%.

terms.meaning: The average result across many possible outcomes. It is not a promise.

options.text: Nothing, a 5% expectation is a promise
options.why: An expectation is an average, not a promise.

options.text: Five percent is too low to count
options.why: The size is not the problem. The word "will" is.

options.text: Expected is an average; next year can be far from it
options.why: Yes. Any single year can fall anywhere in the range.
It can. The problem is treating an average as a promise.

questions.label: Climb back
questions.prompt: A holding falls from $1,000 to $700. By what percent must it rise to get back to $1,000? Round to one decimal place.
questions.hint: The rise is measured against $700, what it is worth now.
questions.why: The gain needed is $300, and it is measured against the smaller $700.

traps.why: That divides by $1,000. The gain starts from $700, so divide by $700.

questions.miss: Divide the $300 it must gain by $700, the amount it is worth right now.

levels.title: Four questions before you invest
learn: Four questions point to a choice that fits.
You will match made-up people to what fits their answers.

cards.text: Before you put money into anything, ask four questions. The first: when do I need it back? That is your time horizon, how long the money can stay put. Next year is a short horizon. Forty years is a long one.
Second: how much of it do I need? Money you must have for a bill or a goal needs a safe home. Money you can leave alone for a long time can go somewhere that swings.
Third: how fast can I get it out? That is liquidity from the last level. Ask it about the thing you are buying. A locked GIC fails this test for money you may need next week.

Fourth: how will I feel when it drops? If a drop would make a person panic and sell at the bottom, a risky choice may be wrong for that person, whatever the numbers say. This question is honest. It is not a joke.
The answers point toward a kind of choice. They do not pick one thing for you.

figure.title: How the answers point
rows: I need it in a few years
I can leave it a very long time
I might need it any day
A drop would make me sell

cards.text: A short horizon points to the safe end of the order, such as a savings account or a GIC that ends in time. A long horizon and a calm mind allow the risky end, but they do not force it.

questions.label: Time horizon
questions.prompt: Which question is about your time horizon?
questions.hint: The word to look for is "back".

terms.meaning: How long your money can stay put before you need it.

options.text: How fast can I get it out?
options.why: That is the third question, about liquidity.

options.text: When do I need the money back?
options.why: Yes. The horizon is how long the money can stay put.

options.text: How will I feel when it drops?
options.why: That is the fourth question, about your feelings.

options.text: How much of it do I need?
options.why: That is the second question, about how much.

questions.label: Car in two
questions.prompt: Keiko will need $3,000 for a car in two years. A drop would upset her. Which choice fits her answers?
questions.hint: Short horizon, needed cash, dislikes drops.

options.why: Yes. Short horizon, a need for the cash, and she dislikes drops.
A stock can fall hard, and two years is a short horizon.
Crypto swings hard. It does not fit a two-year need.
Gold's price swings, so it does not fit a short horizon.

questions.label: Who can risk
questions.prompt: Two people each have $1,000. Lina needs hers in 8 months. Tomas will not touch his for 30 years and stays calm when prices fall. Who can better afford a risky choice?
questions.hint: Compare the horizons first.

terms.meaning: How long your money can stay put before you need it.

options.why: Lina needs the money soon. A drop could leave her short.
Their horizons are very different, so they are not the same.
A long horizon allows more risk, so Tomas can afford it better.
Yes. A long horizon and a calm mind allow more risk.

questions.label: Any day
questions.prompt: Priya may need her money with one day's notice. Which choice fits that?
questions.hint: Which choice is quickest to reach?

options.why: A GIC is locked until the term ends.
Yes. It is already cash.
A house takes months to sell.

questions.label: Which question
questions.prompt: Sam bought a risky fund. It dropped 20% and he panicked and sold at the bottom. Which of the four questions would have helped him most?
questions.hint: What went wrong was a feeling.

options.text: When do I need it back?
options.why: The horizon matters, but Sam's trouble was how he felt about the drop.

options.text: How will I feel when it drops?
options.why: Yes. If a drop makes you sell, a risky choice may be wrong for you.

options.text: How much of it do I need?
options.why: That is about size. Sam's trouble was his reaction to the drop.

options.text: How fast can I get it out?
options.why: Sam could sell easily. That was not his trouble.

questions.label: Short of goal
questions.prompt: Noor needs $4,000 in 3 years. She will save $100 a month in a savings account for 36 months. Ignore interest. How many dollars short of her goal will she be?
questions.hint: Find the total she saves first.
questions.why: Her savings reach 36 payments of $100, which is less than the goal.
questions.miss: Multiply $100 by 36 months, then subtract from the goal.

questions.label: Safe share
questions.prompt: Mia has $5,000. She needs $1,500 of it within a year. What percent of her money must be somewhere safe and quick to reach?
questions.hint: Divide the part she needs by the whole.
questions.why: The part she needs within a year needs a safe home.
questions.miss: Divide $1,500 by $5,000 and write it as a percent.

questions.label: Most room
questions.prompt: The bars show the share of each person's money that is not needed for at least five years. All four stay calm in a drop. Tap the person with the most room to take risk.

figure.title: Share of money not needed for 5+ years

terms.meaning: How long your money can stay put before you need it.

questions.hint: More money that can stay put means more room for risk.
questions.why: Dee does not need any of it for five years, so Dee has the most room to take risk.
questions.miss: Look for the tallest bar.

questions.label: Won't sell
questions.prompt: Dev will not need his money for 10 years, but a 25% fall would make him sell. Which choice fits that answer?
questions.hint: Which of these does not fall?

options.why: Yes. If a fall would make him sell, he needs something that does not fall.
Crypto swings far more than 25%, which is the thing he cannot stand.
A single stock can fall hard. That would make him sell.
Gold's price swings hard. A fall of 25% is possible, and that is what he cannot stand.

levels.title: A rule beats a mood
learn: A rule made in advance beats a decision made in the moment.
You will compare one company with a fund of many.

cards.text: A drop can feel scary and a rise can feel exciting. A rule decided in advance, before the money is at stake, lets you act the same way in a good month and a bad one.

A common mistake is buying after a rise and selling after a drop. Priya buys 10 units of a fund at $120 after a rise. It falls to $90 and she sells. She paid $1,200 and got $900. She locked in a loss of $300.
Ben follows a rule: $100 into the same fund every month, whatever the price. When the price drops, the same $100 buys more units. He never sells.
A rule has no feelings. It does not promise a good result: any one year can go badly. A good rule only improves your odds over many years. Following it when you feel like quitting is the hard part.

Now one company against a fund of many. If a fund holds 100 companies in equal parts and one falls 35%, the fund falls 0.35%. If you own that one company, you feel the whole 35%. The game can stage a company scandal that takes 35% off one stock.
The Exchange shows "Ups and downs" on the card of most funds and companies. These are the starting figures. You can look at them without buying anything.

figure.title: Ups and downs in the Exchange

questions.label: Why a rule
questions.prompt: Why decide on a rule in advance?
questions.hint: A rule does not feel scared or excited.

options.why: No rule guarantees a profit. It only improves your odds.

options.text: It lets you skip the four questions
options.why: The rule comes from the four questions. It does not replace them.
Prices do what they do. A rule changes how you react.

options.text: You act the same in a good month and a bad one
options.why: Yes. The rule does not change with your mood.

questions.label: Priya's loss
questions.prompt: Priya bought 10 units at $120 each and sold them at $90 each. How many dollars did she lose?
questions.hint: Find what she paid and what she got.
questions.why: She bought after a rise and sold after a drop.
questions.miss: Work out the total paid and the total received, then subtract.

questions.label: Priya's percent
questions.prompt: Priya paid $1,200 and sold for $900. What percent of what she paid did she lose?
questions.hint: Divide the loss by what she paid.
questions.why: Percent loss is the loss divided by the starting amount.
questions.miss: Divide the dollars lost by $1,200, the amount she paid.

questions.label: Ben's end value
questions.prompt: Ben put $100 a month into a fund for 4 months, at prices of $100, $80, $50, $100. He bought 5.25 units in all. The price is $100 at the end. What are his units worth?
questions.hint: Units times the final price.
questions.why: Falling prices bought him more units, so he ends up ahead of the money he put in.
questions.miss: Multiply his total units by the price at the end.

questions.label: Falling price
questions.prompt: Ben puts $100 in every month. What does his rule do when the price drops?
questions.hint: Look at the table: price $50.

options.why: Ben never sells. His rule is to keep buying.
His rule is the same every month, whatever the price.
Yes. A lower price means more units for the same money.
A lower price buys more units, not fewer.

questions.label: Fund of many
questions.prompt: A fund holds 100 companies in equal parts. One company falls 35%. By what percent does the fund fall? Give two decimal places.
questions.hint: The one company is a small part of the fund.
questions.why: One company is 1 part in 100 of the fund, so its drop is spread thin.
questions.miss: Divide the company's fall by the number of companies in the fund.

questions.label: Crash cost
questions.prompt: The game can stage a market crash that takes 25% off the total market fund and 5% off the bond fund. Rae holds $2,000 in each fund. How many dollars does such a crash take in all?
questions.hint: Work out each fund's loss, then add.
questions.why: The crash hits each fund by its own percent.
questions.miss: Take 25% of $2,000, then 5% of $2,000, and add the two.

questions.label: Biggest ups
questions.prompt: The bars show the Exchange's "ups and downs" a year for four securities. Tap the one that swings the most.
questions.hint: The tallest bar swings the most.
questions.why: Callpoint Support swings about 45% a year, the most of the four.
questions.miss: Look for the tallest bar.

questions.label: Spread thin
questions.prompt: Why does a total market fund swing less than one company's stock?
questions.hint: Think of 1 company out of 100.

options.why: It moves, only less than one company's stock does.

options.text: One company going bad barely shows among many
options.why: Yes. The fund spreads the money over many companies.

options.text: A manager promises it will not fall
options.why: Nobody promises that. The fund simply spreads the risk.
This fund holds companies. A bond fund is a different fund.

questions.label: The mistake
questions.prompt: Which action is the common mistake?
questions.hint: Think about which price you buy at and which you sell at.

options.text: Buying after a rise and selling after a drop
options.why: Yes. It buys high and sells low.

options.text: Putting in the same amount every month
options.why: That is Ben's rule, not a mistake.

options.text: Holding a fund that has hundreds of companies
options.why: Spreading the money out is the opposite of the mistake.

options.text: Deciding your rule before you start
options.why: Deciding in advance is the rule idea itself. It is not a mistake.

units.title: Stocks, funds and strategy
units.blurb: Read a stock, read a chart, set a goal and stick to a rule.

levels.title: A share and a ticker
learn: A stock is a share of a company, and a ticker is its short name.
You will tell what you can buy from what you cannot.

cards.text: A company can be cut into equal parts called shares. A stock is a share of a company. If a company has 1,000 shares and you own 10 of them, you own 1% of the company. The more shares you own, the bigger your piece.
Say a company is worth $50,000 in all and has 1,000 equal shares. Each share is worth $50,000 / 1,000 = $50. This is a simple picture. On an exchange, a share costs what buyers and sellers agree on.
A public company sells its shares to anyone on a stock exchange. A private company does not. You cannot buy shares of a private company on an exchange, however well known its name is.

Every company on an exchange has a ticker: a short code of a few letters. Two companies can have similar names, but each ticker belongs to one company. You use the ticker to be sure you have the right one.

A brand name is not always a company. A shop or a product can belong to a bigger company with a different name. To own a piece, you buy shares of the company that owns the brand. These three are made up.

figure.title: Brands and their owners (made up)
rows: Redwood Cycles Ltd, a public company
Yes, shares of Redwood Cycles Ltd

cards.text: The game's Exchange lists eight companies of the town. Each is named after an employer in the Job Centre and has its own ticker. They are made up, so they are the only companies you can buy there. It also lists three funds, each with a ticker. Some people call such a fund an ETF.

questions.label: What a share is
questions.prompt: What is a share of a company?
questions.hint: Picture a pie cut into equal slices. What is one slice of the company?

terms.meaning: One equal part of a company. A stock is a share.

options.text: A loan you make to the company
options.why: A loan is lending, like a bond. A share is owning a part of the company.

options.text: One equal part of the company
options.why: Yes. Owning shares means owning a part of the company.

options.text: A promise that the price never falls
options.why: Nothing about a share is promised. Its price can rise or fall.

options.text: A savings account at the company
options.why: A savings account is a deposit. A share is a part of the company itself.

questions.label: Public or private
questions.prompt: Which of these can you buy shares of on a stock exchange?
questions.hint: Which kind of company sells shares to anyone?

options.text: A private company owned by one family
options.why: A private company does not sell shares on an exchange.
Yes. A public company sells its shares to anyone on an exchange.

options.text: A brand name, apart from its owner
options.why: A brand is not a company. You buy shares of the company that owns it.

questions.label: What a ticker is
questions.prompt: What is a ticker?
questions.hint: Think of a short name, not a number.

terms.meaning: A short code, a few letters, that names one company or fund on an exchange.

options.why: The price changes. The ticker is the fixed short name.

options.text: The company's profit for the year
options.why: Profit is a result. A ticker is only a name.

options.text: The number of shares a company has
options.why: The count of shares is a different fact. A ticker is a code of letters.

options.text: A short code that names one company
options.why: Yes. The ticker tells you exactly which company you are looking at.

questions.label: Which to buy
questions.prompt: Sunny Cones is a brand owned by Northfield Foods, a public company. Mei wants to own a piece of the company that owns Sunny Cones. What does she buy?
questions.hint: Look at the table: who owns the brand?

options.why: Sunny Cones is a brand. It has no shares of its own here.

options.text: Nothing, because brands cannot be owned
options.why: A brand is owned by a company. You can own a piece of that company.
Yes. Shares are of the company that owns the brand.
Only the owner's shares are a piece of the owner.

questions.label: Percent owned
questions.prompt: A company has 2,000 shares. Omar owns 50 of them. What percent of the company does he own?
questions.hint: Divide the shares he owns by all the shares.

terms.meaning: One equal part of a company. A stock is a share.

questions.why: The part you own is your shares divided by all the shares.

traps.why: 50 / 2,000 is 0.025. As a percent that is 2.5%, not 25%.

questions.miss: Divide 50 by 2,000, then change the result to a percent.

questions.label: One share worth
questions.prompt: A company is worth $90,000 in all and has 3,000 equal shares. In this simple picture, what is one share worth?
questions.hint: Split the whole value into equal parts, one for each share.
questions.why: One share is the company's value divided by the number of shares.
questions.miss: One share is one equal part. Which operation splits a total into equal parts?

questions.label: Value of a stake
questions.prompt: A company is worth $50,000 in all and has 1,000 equal shares. Lena owns 20 of them. What are her shares worth in all?
questions.hint: Find the worth of one share first, then multiply by her 20.
questions.why: Her stake is the number of shares times the worth of one share.

traps.why: That is the worth of one share. Lena owns 20 of them.

questions.miss: One share is $50.00 here. How many of them does Lena own?

questions.label: Find the ticker
questions.prompt: Rin works at Corner Mart, one of the Job Centre employers. She wants to look at its shares in the Exchange. Which ticker does she look for?
questions.hint: Find the company name in the table, then read its ticker.

options.why: CALL is Callpoint Support, a different company. Match the name to the ticker in the table.
Yes. CORN is Corner Mart, in the Convenience retail sector.
KEYS is Keystone Distribution. Check the Company column.
AGRA is Agora Coffee Co. Check the Company column.

questions.label: Share or fund
questions.prompt: How is one share of a company different from one unit of a fund such as DAAX?
questions.hint: Think of what a fund holds, from the last unit.

options.text: A share is a slice of one company, a fund unit a slice of many
options.why: Yes. A fund holds many companies at once, which is why it has its own ticker.

options.text: A share is a loan and a fund unit is ownership
options.why: A share is ownership. A fund unit is a slice of what the fund holds.

options.text: A fund has no ticker, but a share does
options.why: Both have a ticker. The Exchange lists three funds with their tickers.

options.text: They are the same thing with two names
options.why: A share is one company. A fund unit holds many companies.

levels.title: Read a quote
learn: A card in the Exchange is a quote: facts about a stock at one moment.
You will read the lines and work with them.

cards.text: A quote is a set of facts about a stock at one moment. In the Exchange, each company has a card. At the top are its ticker, its name and its price in dollars. Prices move once a world month. Most numbers in this level are made up; open the Exchange for live ones.

Next to the price is an arrow and a percent: ▲ for up, ▼ for down. It compares the price with the month before. To find a percent change, divide the change by the old price. A price that goes from $50.00 to $52.00 changed by $2.00, and $2.00 / $50.00 is 4%.
Here is a company card with made-up numbers, in the order the Exchange shows them. The real card also has a spread line, a small chart of the last 12 months and a line about the company.

Buy at (ask) is the price you pay when you buy. Sell at (bid) is the price you get when you sell. The ask sits a little above the price and the bid a little below. The gap between them is the spread, and it is a cost. A later level shows how much.

A dividend is cash a company pays its owners. The card shows the dividend yield: the dividend for a year as a percent of the price, paid in four parts. A $50.00 share with a yield of 4% pays $2.00 a year, which is $0.50 each quarter. Some cards say none.

A fund's card has a Fund fee line where a company has Dividend yield. Ups and downs, from the last unit, sits on most cards. A card tells you what a stock is doing and what it costs. It does not tell you what it will do next.

questions.label: Price you pay
questions.prompt: Which line on a card shows the price you pay when you buy?
questions.hint: Read the names of the two price lines on the card.

terms.meaning: The price you pay when you buy. The card calls it Buy at (ask).

options.why: The bid is the price you get when you sell.
The yield is a yearly payment as a percent of the price, not a price you pay.
That shows how the price changed from the month before.
Yes. The ask is the price at which you buy.

questions.label: Reading the arrow
questions.prompt: A card shows ▼ 2.0% next to the price. What does that mean?
questions.hint: The arrow looks back. Back to when?

options.why: A dividend is shown on its own line, as the yield.

options.text: The price will fall 2.0% next month
options.why: The arrow looks back. It says nothing sure about the future.

options.text: The price is 2.0% lower than the month before
options.why: Yes. The arrow compares the price with the month before.

options.text: You have lost 2.0% of your money
options.why: The arrow is about the stock's price, not about what you own.

questions.label: Yield says none
questions.prompt: A company's card shows Dividend yield: none. What does that tell you?
questions.hint: Look at the card lines and what a dividend is.

terms.meaning: Cash a company pays to its owners.
The dividend for a year, as a percent of the price.

options.why: A card cannot tell you that. Some companies keep their cash to grow.
Yes. Its owners get no cash payments. Any gain would come from the price.

options.text: Its price is about to fall
options.why: No dividend says nothing about where the price goes.
Any company on the Exchange can be bought, with or without a dividend.

questions.label: Percent rise
questions.prompt: A price goes from $60.00 to $63.00. What is the percent change?
questions.hint: Find the change in dollars, then divide by the old price.
questions.why: A percent change is the change divided by the old price.

traps.why: $3.00 is the change in dollars. Divide it by the old price, $60.00, to get a percent.

questions.miss: Subtract first, then divide by the old price, not the new one.

questions.label: Percent fall
questions.prompt: A price goes from $25.00 down to $24.00. By what percent did it fall? Type a positive number.
questions.hint: The old price is the one you divide by.
questions.why: The fall is $1.00, and $1.00 is 4% of the old price, $25.00.

traps.why: That divides by the new price, $24.00. A percent change always divides by the old price.

questions.miss: Divide the $1.00 fall by the price it started from.

questions.label: Cost of shares
questions.prompt: Priya buys 6 shares at the ask of $20.50 each. What does she pay in all?
questions.hint: Shares times the price for one share.

terms.meaning: The price you pay when you buy. The card calls it Buy at (ask).

questions.why: The cost is the number of shares times the ask.

traps.why: $20.50 is the cost of one share. Priya buys 6.

questions.miss: Multiply the number of shares by the price of one share.

questions.label: Dividend a year
questions.prompt: A share costs $80.00 and its dividend yield is 3% a year. How much dividend does one share pay in a year?
questions.hint: The yield is a percent of the price.

terms.meaning: The dividend for a year, as a percent of the price.

questions.why: The yearly dividend is the yield times the price.

traps.why: That is one quarter of it, $0.60. The question asks for the whole year.

questions.miss: Change 3% to 0.03, then multiply by the price.

questions.label: One payment
questions.prompt: Dana owns 30 shares of a company priced at $60.00 with a dividend yield of 2% a year. How much does she get in one quarterly payment?
questions.hint: Yearly dividend per share first, then a quarter of it, then 30 shares.

terms.meaning: The dividend for a year, as a percent of the price.

questions.why: A quarter of the yearly dividend is paid each time, on every share she owns.

traps.why: That is a whole year of dividends, $36.00. One payment is a quarter of it.

questions.miss: The payment comes four times a year. Work out one quarter per share, then multiply.

questions.label: Card owner
questions.prompt: The top of a card shows the ticker SPRK and a price. Which company's card is it?
questions.hint: Match the ticker to a company in the table.

terms.meaning: A short code, a few letters, that names one company or fund on an exchange.

options.why: That company is CALL.
Yes. SPRK is Spark Line Electric, as the table from level 1 shows.
That company is KEYS.

questions.label: Highest yield
questions.prompt: Tap the company with the highest dividend yield.

figure.title: Dividend yield on the card (the Exchange's starting figures)

terms.meaning: The dividend for a year, as a percent of the price.

questions.hint: Compare the bar heights.
questions.why: Corner Mart (CORN) has the highest yield of these five.
questions.miss: Look for the tallest bar.

levels.title: Read a chart
learn: A price chart is a line, and the window you pick changes the story.
You will read a line and work out a percent change.

cards.text: A price chart is a line. The left end is the oldest price and the right end is the newest. When the line rises, the price rose. When it falls, the price fell. The small chart on each Exchange card shows the last 12 months, one point for each world month.
This made-up stock is plotted over eight months. Read it from left to right. It climbs from $20.00 to a peak of $33.00 in Month 5, then slips back to $27.00.
Now look at only the last four months of the same line. These are the same prices as Months 5 to 8. Seen on their own, they look like a steady fall.

figure.title: The same stock, last four months

cards.text: Same stock, two stories. The eight-month chart shows a stock that is up. The four-month chart shows a stock that is down. Neither chart is lying: each shows a different slice. Before you judge a stock, look at more than one window.

To compare two points, find the percent change: (new price - old price) / old price. From Month 2 ($23.00) to Month 5 ($33.00) is a gain of $10.00, and $10.00 / $23.00 is about 43.5%. From Month 6 ($31.00) to Month 8 ($27.00) is a drop of $4.00, and $4.00 / $31.00 is about 12.9%.

The small chart on an Exchange card has no numbers beside it. It is stretched so the lowest point sits at the bottom and the highest at the top. A small move can look like a big one. Read the price and the percent change as well.

levels.title: Cheap or expensive?
learn: A low share price is not a bargain by itself.
You will look at the whole company behind a ticker.

cards.text: A low share price is not a bargain by itself. The price is what one share costs, not what the company is worth. A company is worth its price times its shares. Here the $5.00 share belongs to the bigger company.
Compare moves in percent, not dollars. A $1.00 gain on a $5.00 share is 20%. A $1.00 gain on a $50.00 share is 2%. The dollar gain is the same, but the first share grew ten times as fast.

Where does a price sit in its own year? Find the lowest and highest price of the past 12 months, the range. Position = (price - low) / (high - low). With a low of $20.00, a high of $30.00 and a price of $28.00, the position is 8 / 10 = 80%: near the top of its own year. That does not say if the company is good.
The price is not the whole story. Three questions about the company behind a ticker help. The Exchange's cards do not show these answers, so the next cards use made-up companies.

figure.title: Three questions
rows: Is the price high for what it earns?

cards.text: Sales are what customers pay. Profit is what is left after everything is paid for. Zip Scooters sells more and its price rose more, but it lost money. A price and a business are two different things.

Growing means sales are higher than before. P/E is the price divided by the profit per share: the dollars you pay for each $1.00 of yearly profit. A $60.00 share with $4.00 of profit per share has a P/E of 15. A high P/E means buyers expect a lot. A company with a loss has no P/E.

levels.title: Buying and selling
learn: An order is either a market order or a limit order, and each has a cost.
You will work out what a trade and a fund cost.

cards.text: Every security has two prices: you buy at the ask and sell at the bid. The ask is a little above the price and the bid a little below. The spread is the gap: 1% for a company and 0.2% for a fund. Example: a $40.00 company has an ask of $40.20 and a bid of $39.80.

A market order fills now: at the ask if you buy, at the bid if you sell. A company is bought in whole shares. A fund can be bought by dollars too. The trade ticket shows what an order would cost before you place it.

A limit order lets you name a price. A buy limit means "buy at this price or lower". A sell limit means "sell at this price or higher". It waits until the market reaches your price, for up to 3 world months. Cash for a buy limit is held, not spent, and returns if the order is cancelled or expires.

The spread costs you even when the price does not move. Buy 10 shares at the ask of $40.20 and you pay $402.00. Sell them straight back at the bid of $39.80 and you get $398.00. The round trip cost $4.00.

A fund also charges a yearly fund fee, the MER: a percent of what you hold, taken out of the fund a little each month. If a fund charges 0.5% a year, $1,000 in it costs about $5.00 a year. Company cards show a dividend yield and no fund fee.

Dividends are paid four times a year, in months 3, 6, 9 and 12 of each world year. You can take the cash, or tick DRIP on the Portfolio tab to reinvest it. A reinvested dividend buys more of the same stock at the ask, even a part of a share.

An order with a price you name. It waits until the market reaches that price.

Yes. A market order fills now at the ask or the bid.

Yes. It waits until the market reaches $38.00 or lower.

questions.hint: Think about what "held" means compared with "spent".

questions.hint: Take 0.2% of the amount.

levels.title: A goal has three parts
learn: A goal has an objective, a time limit and strategies. A wish is missing some.
You will tell the two apart and find the missing part.

cards.text: A wish says what you want in a loose way: "I want to be rich someday." A goal has three parts: an objective, a time limit and strategies. With all three, you can check whether you are on track.
The objective is what you want, with an amount: "Have $1,200 for a laptop." A number lets you check your progress. "Some money for a laptop" is a wish, because you cannot tell when you have it.

The time limit is when you need it: "in 12 months". It decides how much risk fits. Money needed in six months belongs near the safe end from the last unit. Money that can wait many years can sit further out.

Strategies are the rules for how you will get there: how much you add each month, what you will buy and what you will not do. "Add $100 a month to a fund" is one. "Never put more than a quarter of the money in one company" is another. Choose two things you will do and one you will not.
Here are two made-up goals split into their parts. Each has an objective, a time limit and a strategy.

figure.title: Two goals, three parts each (made up)
rows: $100 a month into a savings account
$100 a month into company shares; none over 25%

cards.text: Check any goal with three questions. Is there an amount? Is there a time limit? Is there a rule for how? If one is missing, it is still partly a wish. A goal can change when life changes. Change it on purpose, not because of one bad month.

questions.label: Goal or wish
questions.prompt: Which one is a goal with all three parts?
questions.hint: Look for an amount, a time limit and a rule in the same sentence.

terms.meaning: What you want, with an amount.
A rule for how you will reach the goal, or what you will not do.

options.text: Have a lot of money for my future
options.why: This is a wish. It has no amount, no time limit and no rule.
It has an amount and a time limit, but no strategy for how.

options.text: Put $100 a month into a fund
options.why: It has a strategy, but no amount to reach and no time limit.

options.text: Have $1,200 in 12 months by saving $100 a month
options.why: Yes. It has an amount, a time limit and a rule for how.

questions.label: Reading the date
questions.prompt: Mo says: "I want $3,000 by June 2029." Which part of a goal is "by June 2029"?
questions.hint: It says when.

options.why: The objective is the amount, $3,000.
Yes. It says when the goal must be reached.
A strategy says how, such as an amount added each month.

questions.label: Reading the rule
questions.prompt: Which part of a goal is "put $100 a month into a fund"?
questions.hint: It says how.

terms.meaning: A rule for how you will reach the goal, or what you will not do.

options.why: The time limit says when, not how.
Yes. It is a rule for how to reach the goal.
The objective is what you want, with an amount.

questions.label: Missing part
questions.prompt: Zoe says: "I will put $50 a month into a fund until I have $1,000." Which part of a goal is missing?
questions.hint: Check each of the three parts in her sentence.

options.why: The objective is there: $1,000.
Yes. "Until I have $1,000" gives no date or length of time.
The strategy is there: $50 a month into a fund.

questions.prompt: Jin wants $2,700 in 18 months by saving the same amount each month. Ignore any growth. How much must Jin save each month?
questions.hint: Split the objective across the months.

terms.meaning: What you want, with an amount.

questions.why: Equal amounts over the time limit have to add up to the objective.

traps.why: That splits the total across 12 months. Jin saves for 18.

questions.miss: How many equal parts is the $2,700 split into?

questions.label: Short of goal
questions.prompt: Ana wants $3,000 in 3 years. She adds $75 a month for all 36 months. Ignore any growth. How much short of her objective is she?
questions.hint: Find how much she adds in total, then compare with $3,000.
questions.why: What she adds is the monthly amount times the months.

traps.why: $2,700.00 is what she saves. The question asks how far that is from $3,000.

questions.label: Time and risk
questions.prompt: Dev needs $800 in six months for a trip. From the last unit, which kind of choice fits that time limit better?
questions.hint: Short time means little room to wait out a drop.

options.text: One company's stock, in case it rises fast
options.why: One company can fall, and six months is too short to wait for it to recover.

options.text: One near the safe end, such as a savings account
options.why: Yes. A short time limit points to the safe end of the order.

options.text: A choice at the risky end, because it pays more

questions.prompt: Sam writes: "Buy company shares with $80 a month. I will not put more than a quarter of it in one company." Which part is the last sentence?
questions.hint: Is it about what you want, when, or how?

terms.meaning: A rule for how you will reach the goal, or what you will not do.

options.why: It has no amount to reach.

options.text: A strategy, a rule about what not to do
options.why: Yes. A strategy can say what you will not do.
It has no date or length of time.

questions.hint: Divide what she has by the objective.

traps.why: That divides by $3,600. The objective is $2,400.

questions.miss: Divide the $1,200 saved by the full objective.

questions.prompt: Zara saves $100 a month. Tap the first month her total reaches $400.
questions.hint: Read the total for each month.
questions.why: $100 x 4 = $400, so her total reaches $400 in Month 4.
questions.miss: Find the first point at $400.00.

levels.title: Strategy or ranking
learn: Playing for a rank and following a strategy are different choices.
You will treat two plans as an experiment and see why one good week proves little.

cards.text: A game that ranks players by their final result rewards big risks. Only the top places win, so a long shot can be worth trying. Real money works the other way: a long shot that fails costs you. Decide on purpose whether you play for a rank or follow a strategy you could defend.

A short time makes the pull to gamble stronger. Kai started with $10,000 and hoped to reach $12,000. Now he has $10,500 and one week is left. He needs a gain of $1,500 on $10,500, about 14.3% in one week. When you are behind, big bets feel tempting.

A rule decided in advance guards against that pull. It has to be specific: a number or an event. "Sell if the price falls 20% below what I paid" can be followed. "Sell if it goes down" cannot, because you must decide what down means while you are nervous.
Treat two plans as an experiment. Write down the start value. Change one thing between the plans. Run them for the same time. Then compare the percent change: (end - start) / start.

One good week proves little. A result over a short time can be luck, and a plan that wins one week can lose the next. More weeks give more evidence. Trust a result that repeats over a longer time, not one that shows up once.

Trading often has a price. In the Exchange, a quick buy and sell of a company costs about 1% of the money, because of the spread. Five quick round trips of $1,000 cost about $50 before any price has moved. A plan that trades less pays less of it.

questions.label: Why risk
questions.prompt: Why can a ranking push a player to take big risks?
questions.hint: Think about who wins in a ranking.

options.why: They do not. A long shot usually fails, and the player is behind.

options.text: Only the top places win, so a long shot can be worth trying
options.why: Yes. A ranking pays for the best result, not for a steady one.

options.text: A ranking pays everyone the same
options.why: A ranking separates players. The top places win.

options.text: Real money rewards risk the same way
options.why: Real money works the other way: a long shot that fails costs you.

questions.label: Specific rule
questions.prompt: Which rule is specific enough to follow?
questions.hint: Which one has a number you can check?

options.text: Sell if the price falls 20% below what I paid
options.why: Yes. It names a number you can check.
Down by how much, and for how long? It cannot be checked.
A feeling is not a rule. It is the mood the rule is meant to guard against.

options.text: Sell when I think it is time
options.why: This depends on a guess in the moment, not on a number or an event.

questions.label: Needed gain
questions.prompt: Lee has $10,300 and hopes to reach $11,000 in one week. What percent gain does she need? Round to one decimal place.
questions.hint: Find the gain she needs in dollars, then divide by what she has now.
questions.why: She needs $700, and her money now is $10,300.

traps.why: That divides by the goal, $11,000. Divide by what she has now, $10,300.

questions.miss: Subtract first, then divide by the money she has now.

questions.label: Fair test
questions.prompt: Which is a fair experiment between two plans?
questions.hint: A fair test changes one thing.

options.text: One plan starts in January and the other in July, and the number of companies differs
options.why: Two things differ, so you cannot tell which caused the result.

options.text: Both start with $5,000 on the same day; only the number of companies differs
options.why: Yes. Only one thing changes, so a difference in the result points to it.

options.text: The plans hold different companies, trade at different times and start with different amounts
options.why: With so many differences, no result points to one cause.

questions.label: Write first
questions.prompt: What should you write down before an experiment begins?
questions.hint: Percent change compares the end with what?

options.why: A guess is not a record. The experiment is meant to find out.
The end value alone cannot show a change. You need the start too.

options.text: The start value of each plan
options.why: Yes. Without the start you cannot find the percent change at the end.

options.text: The best week of each plan
options.why: You will not know it until the experiment is over.

questions.label: Plan C result
questions.prompt: Plan C starts with $4,000 and ends with $4,160. What is the percent change?
questions.hint: End minus start, divided by the start.
questions.why: The gain is $160.00 on a start of $4,000.

traps.why: That divides by the end value. Divide by the start value, $4,000.

questions.miss: Work out the gain in dollars first, then divide by the start.

questions.label: One week
questions.prompt: Plan A beat Plan B by 3 points in one week. What does that show?
questions.hint: How many weeks is the result based on?

options.text: A is the better plan for good
options.why: One week cannot show that. It could reverse next week.

options.text: Little yet; one short week could be luck
options.why: Yes. A longer record that repeats says more.
B may do better in other weeks. One week proves little.
Results matter, but one week is thin evidence.

questions.label: Four round trips

levels.title: Borrowing to invest, and a watchlist
learn: A loan makes gains and losses bigger, and the interest is owed either way.
You will also write a watchlist: a few names with a reason beside each.

cards.text: Some people borrow money to invest more. A loan has a cost: interest, owed whatever happens to the shares. Mia has $1,000.00. She borrows $1,000.00 more at 8% a year and buys $2,000.00 of shares. The interest for one year is $80.00.

Same 10% move, with and without the loan (the spread is left out to keep the sums short). A rise gives Mia $120.00 instead of $100.00. A fall costs her $280.00 instead of $100.00. The $80.00 of interest is owed either way.
The loan must be paid back whatever the shares do. If they fall 10%, Mia's $2,000.00 becomes $1,800.00. She repays $1,000.00 and $80.00 of interest, so $720.00 of her own $1,000.00 is left.

The borrowed part has to earn its interest before it helps you. Mia's $1,000.00 of borrowed money must gain $80.00, which is 8% of it, just to break even. Borrowing makes gains and losses bigger, and the interest is owed either way.

A watchlist is a short list of companies you follow, with a reason beside each. It is not an order to buy. The Exchange lets you read every card without buying. This one is made up by a person named Jun.

figure.title: Jun's watchlist (made up)
columns: I would change my mind if
rows: Pays a 3.5% yield and moves less
Pays 2.5% and grows with the town
Its price falls 20% in a month

cards.text: A good watchlist has few names from different sectors, so one bad month in one sector does not hit them all. Each reason is a fact, not "it is up today". Each name has a line saying what would change your mind, with a number or an event.

sections.title: Credit & Borrowing
sections.blurb: How borrowing works, what it really costs, and what you own once the debts are counted.

units.title: What lenders look for
units.blurb: Think like the lender: who gets a loan, and what a credit history shows.

levels.title: Credit is trust with a price
learn: Say what a lender and a borrower are, and what interest is.
Work out what a one-year loan costs.

cards.text: Credit means getting money now and paying it back later. The one who lends is the lender. The one who borrows is the borrower. A lender is trusting that the money will come back.
A lender does not lend for free. The borrower pays back the principal, which is the amount borrowed, plus interest. Interest is the price of using someone else's money.
For a loan of one year, interest is the principal times the rate. A $2,000 loan at 10% costs $200 in interest. The borrower pays back $2,200 in all.
Lenders make money from interest. They lose money when a borrower does not pay back. So a lender asks questions before it lends. The big one is: will this person pay me back?

There are a few ways to get money you do not have yet. You can save up first, or you can borrow with a loan or a credit card. Borrowing gets you the money sooner, and it adds interest. Saving first adds no interest, but you wait.

questions.label: Who is the lender
questions.prompt: Mina borrows $800 from a credit union to buy a laptop. Who is the lender?

terms.meaning: A person or business that lends money and expects it back.
A person who gets money now and agrees to pay it back.

questions.hint: The lender is the one who hands over money.

options.why: Mina is the borrower. She is the one who gets the money and pays it back.
Yes. The lender is the one who lends the money. Mina is the one who borrows it.
The store sold her the laptop. The money she borrowed came from the credit union.
The laptop is what she buys. It is not a person or business that lends.

questions.label: What interest is
questions.prompt: What is interest?

terms.meaning: The price of using someone else's money.
The amount you borrow, before interest.

questions.hint: It is a price for a loan.

options.text: The price of using someone else's money
options.why: Yes. The borrower pays it to the lender on top of the amount borrowed.
That is the principal. Interest is extra, on top of the principal.

options.text: The part of a loan already paid back
options.why: Paying back reduces what you owe. Interest is a cost added to the loan.
A lender earns interest. It is a price the borrower pays, not a gift.

questions.label: Interest for a year
questions.prompt: Ines borrows $1,500 for one year at 8%. Interest for one year is the principal times the rate. How much interest does she pay?

terms.meaning: The amount you borrow, before interest.

questions.hint: Principal x rate. Turn 8% into 0.08 first.
questions.why: For one year, interest is the principal times the rate.

traps.why: That moves the decimal point one place too far. 8% is 0.08 of the principal, not 0.008.

questions.miss: Take 8% of the principal. The rate is for the year.

questions.prompt: Why does a lender ask questions before it lends?

options.why: A lender cares about repayment. Being friendly does not pay a loan back.

options.why: Lenders earn money from interest. Their questions are about repayment.

options.text: Because the law bans loans without them
options.why: The cards do not say that. The reason is risk: a lender wants its money back.

options.text: To judge whether the money will come back
options.why: Yes. Lenders lose money when a borrower does not pay back, so they check first.

questions.label: Most interest

questions.hint: Principal x rate for each person.

options.why: Ravi has the biggest principal, but only a 4% rate. His interest is $160.00.

questions.label: When lenders lose
questions.prompt: When does a lender lose money on a loan?

terms.meaning: A person or business that lends money and expects it back.

options.text: When the borrower pays on time
options.why: Paying on time is what the lender hopes for.

options.text: When the borrower does not pay back
options.why: Yes. A loan that is not repaid is the lender's loss.
Interest is how the lender earns money.
Small loans can be repaid in full. Size alone is not a loss.

questions.label: Find the rate
questions.prompt: Leo borrows $1,000 for one year and pays back $1,100 in all. What yearly rate did he pay?
questions.hint: Find the interest first. Then compare it with the principal.
questions.why: The interest is the amount above the principal. Divide it by the principal.
questions.miss: Subtract the principal from the total to find the interest. Then divide that by the principal.

terms.meaning: The price of using someone else's money.

levels.title: Think like the lender
learn: Compare what a person earns with what they ask for.
Work out a payment as a share of income.

cards.text: Picture yourself as a lender. Five people ask for a loan. At first you know only a few things: the job, the income, the amount they ask for and what it is for. Income is the money that comes in each month.
Here are the five. Look at income next to the amount asked for. A big loan on a small income is harder to pay back than the same loan on a big income.

figure.title: Five people asking for a loan

cards.text: A simple check is the share of income. If a loan payment is $200 a month and income is $2,000 a month, the payment takes 10% of income. Payment / income x 100 gives the share. A smaller share leaves more room for rent, food and everything else.
Steady pay is easier to judge. When pay swings from month to month, some months have much less to pay with. When there is no pay, the lender has nothing to go on from income alone.
These facts are only a first look. They show what a person could pay. They do not show what the person has done with money before. That comes next.

questions.label: Same ask
questions.prompt: Hana and Owen both ask for $2,400 for a used car. On the facts in the table alone, who looks safer to lend to?

figure.title: Five people asking for a loan

options.why: Owen's income is $900. The same $2,400 is a much bigger loan for him.
Yes. Her $3,600 income is much bigger, so $2,400 takes a smaller share of it.
The ask and the purpose match, but the incomes do not. Income changes how big the loan is for each person.

questions.why: The payment is one twentieth of her income.

traps.why: That is income divided by payment. Divide the payment by the income.

questions.label: Owen's share

terms.meaning: The money that comes in to you each month.

questions.hint: Payment / income x 100.
questions.why: The payment is one fifth of his income.

traps.why: That is the share left after the payment. The question asks for the share the payment takes.

questions.miss: Divide the payment by the income, not the other way round.

terms.meaning: A person or business that lends money and expects it back.

questions.hint: Principal x rate, as in the last level.
questions.why: For one year, interest is the principal times the rate.

questions.label: Two facts
questions.prompt: Which two facts can a lender compare to see whether payments might fit?

terms.meaning: The money that comes in to you each month.

questions.hint: You need a pay figure and a loan figure.

options.text: Income and the amount asked for
options.why: Yes. A loan that is big next to income is harder to pay back.
A name tells the lender nothing about paying. The purpose does not show the size of the payment next to income.
These say what a person does and wants. They do not show how big the loan is next to the pay.
Income helps, but the purpose does not show the size of the loan. You need the amount asked for.

levels.title: The history changes the picture
learn: Say what a credit history and a credit report are.
Explain why a record of paying counts for more than a high income.

cards.text: Income and the amount asked for are a first look. A lender also wants to know how a person has paid before. That record is the person's credit history. It lists the credit they have had and whether they paid it back on time.
Companies called credit bureaus keep these records. A person's record is their credit report. If you have never had credit, you may have no file at all. Your own credit report is free to ask for.
Here are the same five people again, now with their records. A lender can now see what each person did with money before, not only what they could pay.

figure.title: The same five, with their records
rows: One card for two years, always paid on time
No credit history. Never had a card or a loan
9 years of credit, one late payment 4 years ago
Two cards, always on time. 4 card applications this month
Three cards near their limits. Missed 3 payments last year

cards.text: Income says what a person could pay. History says what a person did pay. Missed payments are a clear warning that a loan may not come back. That is why a high income does not settle the question by itself.

A lender can answer in different ways. It might offer a low rate to someone it trusts, a higher rate to someone it is less sure about, or say no. A higher rate is the lender's price for more risk. In one class example the choices were 6%, 12% and 20%.

questions.prompt: What is a credit report?

options.text: A summary of your income and job

options.text: A note from your bank about your savings
options.why: It covers credit, not savings.

options.text: A record of the credit you have had and how you paid it
options.why: Yes. Lenders use it to see how a person has paid before.

terms.meaning: A record of the credit you have had and how you paid it back.

questions.hint: No credit, no file.

rows: One card for two years, always paid on time

questions.label: Higher rate costs
questions.prompt: Suppose a lender lends $2,000 for one year at 6% to Hana and at 20% to Greta. How much more interest does Greta pay?

terms.meaning: The price of using someone else's money.

terms.meaning: A person or business that lends money and expects it back.

questions.hint: The second card has it.

options.why: You can see your own report as well.

options.why: Checking your own report does not count against you. A lender checking when you apply can.

levels.title: Name the factor
learn: Name the five things a credit score is built from.
Match a fact about a person to its factor.

cards.text: A credit score sums up a credit report in one number. It is built from five things. Paying on time is the biggest of the five. The table names them all.

figure.title: Five things a credit score is built from
rows: Do you pay when a payment is due?
How much of your limit you use
How big is your balance next to your limit?
How long you have had credit
Applying for lots of new credit
Have you asked for a lot of credit lately?
Do you handle more than one kind?

cards.text: In Canada a credit score runs from 300 to 900. A higher number is better for the borrower. Your income, your job and your age are not in the score. A high-paid person can have a low score, and the other way round.
A limit is the most a lender lets you owe on a card. Using a small share of your limit looks safer than using most of it. To find the share, divide what you owe by the limit and multiply by 100.

Length is how long your record is. A longer record gives a lender more to read. New credit is about applications: asking for a lot of credit in a short time can look like a need for money fast. Different types means more than one kind, such as a card and a car loan.

Some of the five you can change soon, and some you cannot. A balance can be paid down in a month. Time passes on its own, so a record only grows longer as the years pass. A missed payment from the past cannot be undone.

questions.label: One of the five
questions.prompt: Which of these is one of the five things a credit score is built from?
questions.hint: Check the table of five.

options.why: Yes. It is the biggest of the five.
Income is not in the score.
Your job is not in the score.
Your age is not in the score.

questions.label: Left out
questions.prompt: Which of these is left out of a credit score?
questions.hint: Look at the second card.

options.why: This is in the score. It is the biggest part.

options.text: How long you have had credit
options.why: Length of credit history is one of the five.

options.text: How much of your limit you use
options.why: This is one of the five.
Yes. Income, job and age are not in the score.

questions.label: Never misses
questions.prompt: Hana never misses a payment. Which of the five does that fact belong to?
questions.hint: Match the fact to the question the factor asks.

options.text: How much of your limit you use
options.why: That is about the balance next to the limit. Hana's fact is about paying when due.

options.text: How long you have had credit

levels.title: Your score in the game
learn: Say what raises and lowers the game's credit score.
Work out what the score changes for you in the game.

cards.text: The game gives you a credit score too. It is the game's own simplified version, not the real thing. Like the real score, it runs from 300 to 900. You have no score until you have a file. Your file opens when you get your first credit product, such as the card.
The game splits 600 points among five factors, the same five you just met. Length counts months: full points come at 36 months of history. New credit counts your applications in the last 12 months.

figure.title: The game's score: points a factor can add

cards.text: Paying on time is the biggest part. A new file starts with 70% of the payment points and gains 10% for each month with an on-time payment. A late payment adds a late mark. Each mark takes 25% of the payment points off, and fades slowly over 24 game months.
Card balance is next. The game checks what share of your limit you owe. The more you owe, the fewer of the 180 points you keep. In between the rows, the game slides smoothly from one row to the next.

figure.title: Card balance: how many of the 180 points you keep

cards.text: When you apply for the card, the game's lender checks three things. Your pay over the last 3 months must average at least $1,000 a month before deductions. Your score, if you have one, must be at least 560. And you must have fewer than 4 applications in the last 12 months.

If you are approved, your limit is your average monthly pay times a share that depends on your score, rounded down to the nearest $100. With no file yet, the share is 50%. It is never less than $500 or more than $2,500. The Credit Bureau shows your own score and why.

units.title: Where your money lives
units.blurb: Accounts, what keeps a deposit safe, saving with help from the government, and what is worth insuring.

levels.title: Where money can live
learn: Say what chequing, savings and registered accounts are each for.
Match a person's need to one of four kinds of place to bank.

cards.text: Money can sit in different accounts, and each account has a job. A chequing account is for spending: your pay lands there and your bills leave from it. A savings account is for money you will need soon and want to keep safe.

Some accounts have a purpose and rules set by the government. These are called registered accounts. Examples are an account for school after high school and one for retirement. A third, the TFSA, can be used for any goal.
The account is one choice. The place that holds it is another. The class sorts places to bank into four kinds. Read what each kind is known for in the table.
These are the class's descriptions. A person picks by what matters to them. There is rarely one right place, and each kind has trade-offs.

rows: Owned by its members, puts money back into the community

levels.title: Is it safe there?
learn: Say who protects a deposit if a bank goes under.
Work out how much of a made-up deposit is protected.

cards.text: A deposit is money you put into an account. If a bank goes under, it may not be able to give deposits back. Some places have a protection for that. Who protects the money, and how much, depends on where it sits.
Read the table. It is the class example. A big bank and an online bank are protected the same way. An Alberta credit union and Alberta's own bank are protected by the province.

figure.title: If it goes under, deposits are protected by

cards.text: CDIC protects up to $100,000 per category. A category is a kind of account, such as chequing, a TFSA or an RRSP. Each category gets its own $100,000. Money above $100,000 in one category is over the limit.

An Alberta credit union's deposits are guaranteed 100%, with no limit. The guarantee comes from the Credit Union Deposit Guarantee Corporation, backed by the Government of Alberta. At Alberta's own bank, the Government of Alberta guarantees 100%.

For most people at 16, $100,000 is far more than they hold, so the limit may never matter. Protection matters more for a family's savings or a business. Where you keep money comes with trade-offs. The point is not to pick a winner.
The game has no bank that fails and no deposit protection to work out. Deposit protection is something to know about real banks, and about where you would keep your own money one day.

levels.title: Help from the government
learn: Say how the RESP, the RRSP and the TFSA each get help from the government.

cards.text: Governments want people to save, so some accounts come with a reward. The class calls it free money. It comes in three forms: money added on top, a tax refund when you put money in, and growth that is tax-free.

An RESP is a Registered Education Savings Plan. It holds money for school after high school. The government adds 20% of the first $2,500 put in each year. That is $500 a year, free. $500 on $2,500 is 20% on day one.

The grant stops at $7,200 per child in total. In the class example, money put in above $2,500 in a year gets no extra grant that year. If a family puts in $1,000, the grant is 20% of $1,000, which is $200.
Here is the grant for different yearly amounts. Past $2,500, the grant stays at $500.
Some families cannot put money in. Lower-income families can get the Canada Learning Bond. It is up to $2,000, and no contribution is needed.

An RRSP is for retirement, and you get a tax refund when you put money in. A TFSA can be used for any goal, and its growth is tax-free. The game's Exchange has a TFSA tab and an RRSP tab. It has no RESP.

figure.title: Three accounts, class example
rows: Grant: 20% on the first $2,500 a year
Retirement. Tax refund when you put money in
18% of last year's income, up to $33,810
Anything. Growth is tax-free. Open it at 18

cards.text: For an RRSP, the limit for the year is 18% of last year's income, up to $33,810. Someone who earned $30,000 last year works out 18% of $30,000, which is $5,400. If 18% comes to more than $33,810, the limit is $33,810.
A TFSA can be for anything. The class example says to open it at 18. The yearly limit is $7,000. If $1,000 goes in, $6,000 of that year's limit is left. Money can come out of a TFSA without tax.

Pick by the goal. School after high school points to an RESP. Retirement, and paying less tax this year, points to an RRSP. Any other goal points to a TFSA. Each account has its own reward, but the purpose comes first.

In the game, the Exchange has a TFSA tab and an RRSP tab. The game starts the TFSA and RRSP limits at the figures in the table. In the first world year there is no RRSP room, because room comes from last year's pay. The game has no RESP.

The game's TFSA has no age check, and room you do not use carries forward. The Retirement building opens when your game character reaches 50. There you choose which accounts pay your retirement income and see how long your savings last.

levels.title: Insure it or risk it?
learn: Say what a premium, a deductible and a claim are.
Compare a year of premiums with the cost of one loss.

cards.text: Insurance swaps a small cost you know for protection from a big cost you cannot predict. You pay a small amount again and again. If something bad happens, the insurer pays a large part of the loss.
Three words to know. The premium is what you pay, here every month. The deductible is what you pay yourself before the insurance pays. A claim is your request for the insurer to pay after a loss.
A phone costs $1,200 to replace. The plan has a $100 deductible. After a loss, the insurer pays the loss minus the deductible. You pay the deductible, and you also paid the premiums before.
The class sorted four cases. The answer depends on the loss and on the law.

figure.title: Insure it or risk it?
rows: Your call: compare the cost of insurance to replacing it
Not optional: car insurance is required to drive in Alberta
Tenant insurance: cheap, and landlord cover is not yours
Already covered by Alberta Health Care

cards.text: To compare, add up a year of premiums and set it next to one loss. A plan at $15 a month costs $180 a year. A $1,200 loss is more than six years of those premiums. But the loss may never happen, and then the premiums bought protection only.

Insurance is for losses you could not afford to cover yourself. A phone is the one case where taking the risk can be reasonable. Alberta Health Care usually does not cover prescriptions, dental and eye care, which is why jobs offer benefits.

units.title: Credit cards and the minimum payment
units.blurb: How card interest builds, and what paying only the minimum really costs.

levels.title: How a card works
learn: Say what a credit limit, a statement and a grace period are.
Tell when a card costs interest and when it does not.

cards.text: A credit card is a loan you can use again and again. A bank or other lender sets a credit limit, the most you can owe on the card. Each purchase uses up some of the limit. Paying the card back gives that room back.

Once a month the card sends a statement. It lists what you bought and the balance, the total you owe. It also shows the minimum payment, the smallest amount you must pay, and a due date. Miss the minimum and the card can charge a fee.
Here is a made-up statement. The balance is what you owe. The room left is the limit minus the balance. This card paid in full last month, so no interest was charged.

The time between the statement and the due date is the grace period. Pay the whole balance by the due date and you pay no interest on those purchases. Canadian rules set a minimum grace period. The class source says at least 21 days. Paid in full every month, a card costs nothing in interest.

Pay less than the whole balance and the grace period is lost. You carry a balance, and the lender charges interest on it. Many cards charge about 20% a year. Some cards also charge a yearly fee. Interest is the next level.

options.text: The interest the card charges in a month

options.text: The amount you owe right now

levels.title: Interest on what you carry
learn: Work out one month of card interest from the balance and the yearly rate.
See why a balance you do not pay down grows.

cards.text: A card quotes its interest rate for a year. That rate is called the APR, the annual percentage rate. The card charges it month by month. One month of interest is the balance x the yearly rate / 12.
Example: a $1,200.00 balance at 24% a year. 24% / 12 = 2% a month. 2% of $1,200.00 is $24.00. The $24.00 is added to what you owe. Interest is rounded down to the cent.

In this unit, interest is figured on the whole statement balance, before your payment comes off. The game's card does it this way. Real cards count interest from each purchase date, so real numbers differ a little.
Suppose nothing is paid on $1,000.00 at 20.99%. Month 1 adds $17.49. Month 2 is figured on the bigger balance, so it adds $17.79. Interest on top of interest is compounding, working against you.
A bigger balance means more interest each month. The same rate on four times the balance costs four times as much. This is why a high balance is so expensive to leave alone.

cards.text: The minimum payment is the smallest amount the card lets you pay each month. Pay at least this much by the due date and the card is not late. It is a small part of the balance, so it feels easy to pay.

The rule used in this unit, the same one the game uses: the minimum is 3% of the balance, but never less than $10.00. It is rounded up to the cent. If the balance is under $10.00, the minimum is the whole balance.

A minimum payment does not stop interest. Interest is figured on the whole balance, then your payment comes off. On $1,000.00 at 20.99%, the minimum is $30.00 and the interest is $17.49. Only $12.51 of the $30.00 pays down what you owe.

The minimum gets smaller as the balance gets smaller, so the balance falls slowly. After six minimum payments of about $28 to $30, the card still owes $927.22. The minimum keeps you on time. It does not pay the card off quickly.

cards.text: Some cards give a reward: a small percent of what you spend comes back. A card with 2% cash back returns $2.00 for every $100.00 you spend. The reward is paid on spending, whether or not you carry a balance.

Spend $500.00 a month and 2% cash back returns $10.00 a month, $120.00 a year. Now the cost of interest: a $3,000.00 balance carried for a year at 20.99% costs about $3,000.00 x 20.99% = $629.70. We use this simple yearly figure to compare cards.

Three made-up cards. Card A has a low rate and no reward. Card B has a high rate and 2% cash back. Card C has a middle rate, 1.5% cash back and a yearly fee. Each person below spends $500.00 a month, $6,000.00 a year.

levels.title: Your card in the game
learn: Say how the game's card charges interest and what a late payment does.

cards.text: The Credit Bureau offers a starter card. The game starts its rate at 20.99% a year, and that rate does not follow the policy rate. A teacher can change it, so read the rate on your own card screen.

Each month the card makes a statement for what you owe. The minimum is 3% of it, never under $10.00. Pay the whole statement and the game charges no interest. Pay less, even $1 less, and it charges interest on the whole statement: on $1,000.00 that is $17.49.

Miss the minimum and the game adds a $29.00 late fee and a late mark. A late mark takes 25% off the payment-history part of your score, then fades over 24 months. Interest and fees are added to the card, so they show up on the next statement.

Autopay can pay the minimum or the full statement each month, if your chequing has enough. The game is simpler than a real card: it charges interest once a month on the statement, not from each purchase date. Interest rules on a real card can differ.

The Credit Bureau has a payoff calculator. Type a balance and a rate, and it shows how long paying only the minimum takes and what it costs. For $1,000.00 at 20.99% it shows 139 months and $1,101.28 in interest.

Rule of 72: divide 72 by the yearly rate to estimate the years a balance takes to double with interest alone. At 21%, 72 / 21 is about 3.4 years. It is an estimate. Late fees only make an ignored card grow faster.

units.title: Quick cash, real cost
units.blurb: Fast ways to borrow, ranked by what they cost.

levels.title: Fast money has a price
learn: Name five ways to get $300 fast and say what each one is.
Explain why a lender that asks few questions charges more.

cards.text: Priya's laptop needs a $300 repair for school. Her pay arrives in 14 days, and she needs the money now. Money that you can get fast when you are short is called quick cash.

Earlier you saw that a higher rate is the lender's price for more risk. A lender that hands out cash in minutes and asks few questions cannot check who will pay it back. It takes more risk, so it can ask for a higher price. That price can be a fee.

Ask a parent or friend: you borrow from someone you know, and there is usually no fee. It can cost something else, like the friendship. Credit card paid in full: it costs nothing only if the shop takes cards and you can pay the whole amount by the due date.

A line of credit is a limit a bank gives you. You borrow what you need and pay interest on what you use. A cash advance is cash you take out of a bank machine with your credit card. It is a loan from the card, and the class example adds a fee to the interest.
A payday loan is a store loan that you repay on your next payday. The store charges a fee for every $100 you borrow. Here are all five ways side by side.

levels.title: A fee is a rate in disguise
learn: Work out a payday loan's fee and what it costs in all.
Turn a fee into a simple yearly rate and compare it with a card.

cards.text: A payday loan is a short loan that you repay on your next payday. Its price is a fee for every $100 you borrow, not a yearly rate. Class notes put Alberta's cap at $15 for every $100. That is the most a lender may charge.

Priya borrows $300 for 14 days. $300 is three lots of $100, so the fee is 3 x $15 = $45. She pays back $300 + $45 = $345. As a share of the loan, the fee is $45 / $300 = 15%. That is 15% for two weeks.

To compare, turn the fee into a yearly rate. A year has 52 weeks, so it holds 26 two-week periods. Repeat the loan all year: 15% x 26 = 390%. This is a simple yearly rate, the fee repeated. It is not compounded.

Compare by rate, not by dollars. A card at about 21% a year charges $63 in a full year on $300 ($300 x 21%). The payday fee is $45, but for only 14 days. The lengths differ, so compare the yearly rates: about 21% for the card and 390% for the payday loan.

The 390% is not what one loan costs. One loan lasts 14 days and costs 15%. The 390% only turns that into a yearly number so you can compare loans of different lengths. The cap is a rule, and rules change, so check the current one.

options.why: The fee is charged once per loan. The 26 counts how often the loan repeats in a year.

levels.title: Rank it
learn: Put the quick ways to borrow in order from cheapest to costliest.
Say what a missed payment can cost and why repeat loans add up.

cards.text: Here is $300 for 14 days five ways, in the class example. Asking a friend and a card paid in full cost nothing. A line of credit costs about $1, a cash advance about $8 and a payday loan $45. The rates for the middle two are examples, not quotes.

How the middle two were worked. Interest for part of a year is principal x yearly rate x days / 365. Line of credit at 10%: $300 x 10% x 14 / 365 = $1.15. Cash advance at 23%: $300 x 23% x 14 / 365 = $2.65, plus a $5 fee = $7.65.

So the order from cheapest to costliest is: nothing (a friend, or a card paid in full), then the line of credit, the cash advance and the payday loan. A young borrower with a small part-time job may not be offered a line of credit at all. It shows what that product costs.

Paying in instalments is a loan with a friendly name. A $120 hoodie in four payments of $30 (4 x $30 = $120) has no interest, but you have the hoodie now and pay later. Two checks help: would I buy it if I had to pay all of it today, and can I cover every payment?

A missed payment can cost more than the payment. There can be a late fee, and each provider sets its own, so no figure is given here. Your bank can charge you when a payment bounces. If it goes to collections, it can hurt your credit score. Returning the item does not cancel the loan on its own.

Fees add up when the loan repeats. Borrow $500 at $15 for every $100: the fee is 5 x $15 = $75, and you pay back $575. Do it every payday for six months, 13 times, and the fees alone are 13 x $75 = $975. That is almost double the $500 you borrowed.
