levels.title: Short of cash in the game
learn: Say when the game lends you money, how much, and how it is paid back.
Compare the loan with another way to cover a shortfall in the game.

cards.text: The game has its own emergency loan. It is the game's, not a payday loan or a cash advance. You see it on your Stress card. Stress runs from 0 (calm) to 100 (crisis). Late bills, no job and missed housing payments push it up. Calm months bring it down.

You can ask for the loan when your stress is 50 or more, one loan at a time. If your stress crosses 80 and you have no loan, the bank lends it to you automatically. The size is the larger of $1,000 and your last net pay, to the whole dollar. The $1,000 is at the game's starting prices.

The game starts the rate at 19.99% a year, paid over 12 months, and it can be set differently. The payments come from your chequing, starting the month after. The game finds each month's interest the way it does for a mortgage, so rate / 12 ($16.66) will not match.

If your chequing is short on payment day, the payment is missed. That month's interest and a $25 fee are added to what you owe. Your stress goes up 10 points, the payment is marked late (it counts once you have a credit history), and the loan runs one month longer. Taking the loan does not lower your stress.

Jo is short $300 for a bill and has $900 in savings. In the Net Worth building, Jo can move money from savings to chequing at once. That gives up only the small interest the savings would have earned. The game starts savings at 2.75% a year and the loan at 19.99%. Paying bills on time also keeps stress down.

questions.hint: Go back to the fourth card.

units.title: Loans: payment and total cost
units.blurb: A longer loan means a smaller payment and a bigger total.

levels.title: A loan with a fixed payment
learn: Read a loan by its principal, rate, term and payment.
Work out the total paid and the total interest.

cards.text: A loan with a fixed payment works like this. You borrow the money once. Then you pay the same amount every month until the loan is gone. The lender and the borrower agree on the plan before the money moves.

Four words describe the loan. The principal is the amount borrowed. The rate is the interest for a year. The term is how long the loan lasts. The payment is what you pay each month. Noor borrows $2,400 at 12% for 12 months.

The payment is worked out so the loan ends exactly on time, and the card tells it to you. A loan paid monthly has one payment for each month of the term, so 12 months means 12 payments. Total paid is the payment times the number of payments.

Noor pays $213.24 twelve times. $213.24 x 12 is $2,558.88, about $2,559. The last payment can be a few cents different, so these loans round to the nearest dollar. Total interest is the total paid minus the principal: $2,559 - $2,400 = $159.

Why is it not 12% of $2,400, which is $288? Each payment pays back part of the principal, so Noor owes less as the months go by. Interest is charged on what is still owed. The next level shows how each payment splits.

questions.label: Fixed payment
questions.prompt: What is a loan with a fixed payment?
questions.hint: Look at the card about how the plan works.

options.text: You pay the whole loan and the interest on the last day
options.why: That is one lump payment at the end. A fixed payment is paid every month.

options.text: You borrow once, then pay the same amount each month
options.why: Yes. The amount stays the same each month until the loan is gone.

options.text: You pay only the interest each month
options.why: Then the principal would never go down. A fixed payment also pays the loan back.

options.text: The payment gets smaller by the same amount each month
options.why: A fixed payment stays the same each month.

The principal is the amount borrowed, not the time.

That is half of 36. The loan lasts 3 years, which is 36 months.

questions.hint: Find the number of payments first.

questions.miss: Work out the total paid first. Then take away the principal.

levels.title: Where each payment goes
learn: Split a payment into interest and principal.
See why the first payments carry the most interest.

cards.text: Each month the lender charges interest on the balance, the part you still owe. Interest for one month is the balance x the rate / 12. Take a $20,000 loan at 8% for 60 months. The payment is $405.53. Month 1 interest: $20,000 x 8% / 12 = $133.33.

The rest of the payment lowers the balance. That part is the principal. In month 1: $405.53 - $133.33 = $272.20 goes to principal. The balance falls to $19,727.80. Interest for each month is rounded to the cent.

Month 2 starts with a smaller balance, so its interest is smaller. The payment stays the same, so more of it goes to principal. The last payment is a few cents different so the balance ends at exactly $0.00.
The interest part of the payment shrinks every month, while the payment stays the same. This is why a loan seems to go down slowly at first and faster later.
In month 1, about 33% of this payment is interest. In month 60 it is under 1%. The first payments carry the most interest and the last carry the least.

questions.label: Month 1 share

levels.title: Shorter or longer
learn: Compare the same loan over different terms.
See what a longer loan costs and what it saves.

cards.text: Take one loan: $20,000 at 8% a year. Only the term changes: 3 years, 5 years or 7 years. Three years is 36 months, 5 years is 60 months and 7 years is 84 months. Each month has one payment.
Here are the three loans side by side. Total paid and total interest are rounded to the dollar. Each total adds up every payment, including the last one, which differs by a few cents.

Read down the table. A longer term means a smaller payment but a bigger total. The 7-year payment is about half the 3-year one, yet it costs over twice the interest. In month 1, interest is 21% of the 3-year payment and 43% of the 7-year one.

Why? Interest is charged on what you owe, for as long as you owe it. A longer loan keeps the balance up for more months, so there are more months of interest. A smaller payment feels easier. It also pays the balance down more slowly.

Interest also has a start time. On a car loan like this one, interest starts on day 1. In the class example of an Alberta student loan, there is no interest while the borrower studies full-time and for 12 months after. Ask when the interest starts.

levels.title: What changes the cost
learn: Name the three things that change what a loan costs.

cards.text: Three things set what a loan costs: how much you borrow, the rate, and the term. Sol borrows $12,000 at 9% for 48 months. The table shows Sol's loan and three changes, one at a time. Each payment is given.

Borrow less, and the payment and the total interest both fall. A lower rate does the same. A shorter term is different: the payment goes up, but the total interest goes down. A longer term does the opposite. Only the term trades one for the other.

You can also pay more than the payment. In this example the extra goes straight to principal. The balance falls faster, so each later month charges interest on less. The loan ends sooner and costs less.

Two people can want different things from the same loan. One wants the lowest payment each month. Another wants the lowest total cost. With only the term changing, no loan has both. Here are three loans for the same $12,000 at 9%.
So when you compare loans, look at the payment and the total interest together. The payment says what each month will feel like. The total interest says what the loan costs.

units.title: Mortgages
units.blurb: The biggest loan most people take: the words, the payment, and what you pay back.

levels.title: The price tag is not the cost
learn: Tell the price of a home from the amount borrowed and the amount paid back.
Work out a down payment as a percent and the total cost of a mortgage.

cards.text: A home costs far more than most people have saved, so most buyers borrow. A loan used to buy a home is a mortgage. The bank is the lender and the buyer is the borrower. The buyer pays interest, the price of using the bank's money.

Take a class example: a home with a price of $400,000. The buyer pays $80,000 up front, from their own money. That is the down payment. The bank lends the rest: $400,000 - $80,000 = $320,000. The down payment is 20% of the price. This is an example price, not an Edmonton average.

Here is the example in one table. The rate is 5% a year and it is fixed, which means it stays the same while the contract lasts. The loan is paid off over 25 years, with one payment a month: 12 x 25 = 300 payments.

The monthly payment on $320,000 at 5% over 25 years is $1,861.14. Total paid is the payment times the number of payments: $1,861.14 x 300 = $558,342.00. Total interest is the total paid minus the amount borrowed: $558,342.00 - $320,000.00 = $238,342.00.

Set the numbers side by side. The home costs $400,000, and the bank is repaid $558,342.00. Add the $80,000 down payment and the buyer has put in $638,342.00. The price tag is not the whole cost: the interest comes on top.

levels.title: Six words
learn: Use the six mortgage words correctly.
Tell the term from the amortization.

cards.text: Six words run through every mortgage. The down payment is the part of the price you pay yourself, up front. The principal is the amount you borrowed and still owe. The interest rate is the yearly price of borrowing, as a percent.

Amortization is how long until the whole loan is paid off. It is often 25 years. The term is how long this rate and this contract last. It is often 5 years. These two are not the same, and they are easy to mix up. Here, term means the contract, not the life of the loan.

Renewal is signing a new term, at whatever the rate is then. Say the amortization is 25 years and the term is 5. The rate is only promised for the first 5 years. When the term ends, you renew, and the rate can be different.
Here are the six words on the class example. The principal starts at $320,000 and goes down as you pay. The 5% rate and the 5-year term go together. After the term, the renewal sets the next rate.

A way to remember: the amortization is the length of the whole loan. The term is the length of one contract inside it. A 25-year loan with 5-year terms has up to five contracts. The first starts when you buy, and each one after starts with a renewal.

questions.hint: Read the card that tells amortization and term apart.

options.text: The rate at the time she renews

levels.title: Your first payment
learn: See how the first mortgage payment is split between interest and the loan.
Read how the split changes over the years.

cards.text: Call the class example mortgage A. Its payment is $1,861.14 every month. The payment is the same each time, but what it pays is not. Part of it is interest. The rest lowers the balance, the amount you still owe.

Interest is charged on what you still owe. In a Canadian fixed-rate mortgage, interest is compounded twice a year, so the monthly rate is about 0.4124%, not 5% / 12 = 0.4167%. The loans unit’s balance x rate / 12 does not apply. The game follows this rule, and so do the numbers here.

Payment 1. You owe all $320,000. Interest is $1,319.65, rounded to the cent. The rest of the payment is $1,861.14 - $1,319.65 = $541.49, and it lowers the balance. You now owe $319,458.51. That is only about 29 cents of each dollar of the payment.
The table shows some payments of mortgage A. The payment is the same each month. Look at the interest column, then the column that lowers the balance, as the years go by.

You owe the most at the start, so the interest is biggest then. Each payment lowers the balance a little, so next month's interest is a bit smaller and more of the same payment goes to the loan. In payment 133, in the twelfth year, the loan share is bigger than the interest share for the first time.

This is why early years feel slow. Most of the first payments go to interest, and the balance falls slowly. Later the same payment pays down the loan faster. The rate is fixed, so the split changes only because the balance gets smaller.

questions.hint: Divide the part by the whole payment.
questions.why: Divide the part that lowers the balance by the whole payment.
questions.miss: Divide the part that lowers the balance by the whole payment. Then turn it into a percent.

questions.label: Why mostly interest

options.why: Yes. The balance is biggest in the first month, so the interest is too.

options.why: There is no such rule. Interest is charged each month on the balance you still owe.

options.text: The rate is higher in the first years
options.why: The rate is fixed for the term. The interest is bigger only because the balance is bigger.

questions.hint: Find the row for payment 240 and the right column.

questions.hint: What does the interest depend on?

options.why: The interest is charged on the balance, and the balance keeps falling.
Yes. The balance falls, so the interest charged on it falls too.
The balance falls with each payment, so the interest gets smaller, not bigger.

options.why: The balance falls in payment 1 too, but interest is still the bigger share for years.

levels.title: Three mortgages
learn: Compare three versions of the same loan.
Say what a longer amortization and a higher rate each do.

cards.text: Take the same $320,000 loan three ways. A is 5% over 25 years. B is 5% over 30 years. C is 6% over 25 years. Each differs from A in one thing only, so you can see what that one thing does.
Here are the three. The payment is monthly. Total interest is the payment times the number of payments, minus the amount borrowed. The 30-year loan has 360 payments. The others have 300.

B against A: the same rate, but 30 years instead of 25. The payment is $153.33 smaller each month. But the total interest is $56,469.60 more. A longer amortization means a smaller payment and a bigger total.

C against A: the same 25 years, but a rate that is one point higher. The payment is $186.24 bigger each month, and the total interest is $55,872.00 more. One extra point of rate adds about as much interest as five more years do.

A buyer can choose the amortization when signing, within what the lender allows. The market sets the rate. So the years are the part a buyer decides, and the rate is the part a buyer has to live with. Next level: the rate can change when the term ends.

levels.title: Year five: renewal
learn: Say what a buyer still owes when the term ends.

cards.text: A mortgage runs on two clocks. The amortization is the whole loan, often 25 years. The term, often 5 years, is how long the rate is promised. When the term ends, you renew: you sign a new term, at whatever the rate is then.

After five years of mortgage A, 60 payments have been made: 60 x $1,861.14 = $111,668.40. But the balance fell by only $320,000.00 - $283,223.76 = $36,776.24. You still owe $283,223.76, and 20 years are left.

figure.title: Money after five years of mortgage A

cards.text: Say the rate is 6% when the term ends. The new payment is worked out on the $283,223.76 still owed, over the 20 years left. It comes to $2,017.09 a month, which is $155.95 more than before. The balance is smaller, but the rate is higher.

What if the rate had gone down instead? Here is the same balance and the same 20 years at two example rates. A lower rate gives a smaller payment and a higher rate gives a bigger one. The 4% and 6% are examples, not a forecast.

figure.title: Renewal on the balance, 20 years left

cards.text: This is the risk a buyer carries. The rate is only promised for the term, so the payment can change at renewal. Ways to make a bigger payment fit: stretch the amortization again (a smaller payment, more interest in all), pay a lump sum on the loan, or spend less somewhere else.

levels.title: A mortgage in the game
learn: Read how the game's Housing building sets up a mortgage.
Work one student's purchase with the game's own maths.

cards.text: In the Housing building a student can buy one of two condos. The game starts with an average Edmonton condo at $202,000 and an older 1-bedroom at $150,000. A teacher can change these, so check the building for what you see.

The game asks for a minimum down payment. For prices like these it is 5% of the price, so $7,500.00 on the $150,000 condo. With less than 20% down, the game adds mortgage default insurance to the loan.

The student picks 25 or 30 years. The game offers 30 years to a first-time buyer (no home yet this season), or to anyone who puts 20% down. The term is 5 years. The game also checks that the student's income can carry the payment, so a student may be told no.

The game's 5-year fixed rate is the policy rate plus 1.95 points. The game starts with a policy rate of 2.25%, so the mortgage rate starts at 4.20%. The policy rate can change, and the mortgage rate moves with it. A mortgage already signed keeps its rate until renewal.

Jordan, a made-up student, buys the $150,000 condo with $15,000.00 down (10%). That is under 20%, so insurance applies: the game's premium is 3.10% of the $135,000.00 borrowed, which is $4,185.00, and it is added to the loan. Jordan picks 25 years at 4.20%.

After 5 years Jordan owes $121,584.59. Say the policy rate has gone up one point, so the 5-year fixed is 5.20%. The game recalculates the payment on that balance over the 20 years left: $812.14, up from $747.31. Next unit: Rent or buy.

units.title: Rent or buy
units.blurb: Two ways to pay for a home, the hidden costs, and what you keep.

levels.title: Two doors
learn: Say what a rent payment and a mortgage payment each buy.
Name what a renter and an owner can and cannot change.

cards.text: Renting and owning are two ways to pay for the same roof. Both give you a place to live. They differ in what each payment buys, who looks after the building and what you can change.

When you rent, you pay a landlord each month. The payment buys the right to live in the home for that month. The landlord owns the home. Your lease sets the rent and how long you can stay. A made-up house like the Mortgages house rents for $2,500.00.

When you own, you pay a mortgage. The Mortgages house costs $400,000. With $80,000 down you borrow $320,000, and the payment is $1,861.14 a month. The home is yours, and the part of each payment that repays the loan adds to what you own.

A furnace breaks in winter. A renter calls the landlord, who owns the furnace and usually sorts it out. An owner calls a repair company and pays the bill. Owning gives you the control and also the costs.

A renter can move when the lease ends, but must ask before big changes such as taking down a wall. An owner can paint or renovate freely, but to move must sell the home, which takes time and costs money.

levels.title: The hidden costs
learn: List what an owner pays besides the mortgage payment.
Add up the true monthly cost of a made-up home.

cards.text: The mortgage payment on the Mortgages house is $1,861.14 a month. That pays the interest and repays the loan. It is not the whole cost of owning the home. An owner pays other costs that the payment does not include.

Property tax is a yearly tax on owning a home. A listing often shows it. Divide the yearly bill by 12 for a monthly cost. The made-up listing for the Mortgages house says $3,900.00 a year. That is $325.00 a month.
A condo or townhouse often has a condo fee. It is a monthly fee for the shared parts of the building, and the listing shows it if there is one. The Mortgages house has none in this example.
Repairs: roofs wear out and furnaces break. The class assumes 1% of the price each year. On $400,000 that is $4,000.00 a year, or $333.33 a month. This is a rule of thumb, not a rule.
Owners also pay for home insurance. The class leaves it out, so the class total comes out a little low. Buying and selling a home bring one-time costs too, such as a lawyer, a realtor and moving.
Add up the Mortgages house: $1,861.14 + $325.00 + $333.33 = $2,519.47 a month, not $1,861.14. Insurance is left out, so the real cost is a little higher.

levels.title: Money gone, money kept
learn: Say which part of a payment is gone and which is kept.
Compare rent with the money gone when you own.

cards.text: Rent is money gone. You get a place to live for the month, and none of the payment comes back to you as something you own. That is not a bad thing: you got the use of a home for the money.

You saw in the Mortgages unit that every mortgage payment has two parts. Interest is the price of the loan, and that money is gone, like rent. The other part lowers the balance, so you owe less. It is called the principal part, and it is kept.

Equity is the part of a home that is yours: its value minus what you still owe. With a $400,000 home and a $320,000 loan, your equity is the $80,000 down payment. Each principal payment adds to it if the value holds.
The first payment on the Mortgages house is $1,861.14. $1,319.65 is interest, so it is gone. $541.49 is principal, so it is kept. These figures come from the game's payment schedule.
After 60 payments you have paid $111,668.40. The balance has fallen from $320,000 to $283,223.76. So $36,776.24 went to the loan and was kept. The other $74,892.16 was interest, and it is gone.

To compare fairly, set rent against the money gone when you own: interest, property tax, condo fee and repairs. Here is year 1 of the Mortgages house. The rent is a made-up listing. One-time costs are left out here and counted in the next level.

Yes. Principal repays the loan, so you owe less and your equity grows.
Property tax is a separate bill, and it is gone.

options.why: Yes. Interest is paid to the lender and does not reduce what you owe.

The down payment becomes part of your equity, so it is kept.
The home is something you own, not money gone.

questions.label: Kept in 5 years
questions.prompt: The Mortgages house started with a $320,000 loan. After 5 years the balance is $283,223.76. How much of the loan has been repaid? Give dollars and cents.

cards.text: Take the Mortgages house two ways. One person buys it. Another person rents a similar house and saves. At the end of each year, we count what each of them has. Every number is a made-up example.

These are the assumptions. They are for this example only, not forecasts or rules. The price is held steady so that you can see the effect of time alone. Renewal after year 5 is ignored: a different rate then would change the answer.

The renter pays $2,500.00. Owning costs $2,519.47 a month, so the renter has $19.47 a month to spare. The renter saves the $80,000 down payment and that difference. Each month the savings earn one twelfth of 3%, and then the difference is added.

cards.text: Take the same home and two people. Person A is moving to Edmonton for a job that might last 2 years. Person B plans to stay 10 years or more, and the down payment is already saved. Is the answer the same for both?

A has little time. Buying costs a lot up front: a down payment (20% of the price in the class example) and the costs of buying and selling. They pay off only if you stay long enough to build equity. Saving $80,000 at $500 a month takes 160 months, about 13 years.

units.title: Net worth
units.blurb: What you own minus what you owe, and the moves that raise it.

levels.title: Who is richer?
learn: Tell what a person earns apart from what a person is worth.
Work out net worth: what you own minus what you owe.

cards.text: Earning a lot and being rich are not the same. Income is money that comes in, such as pay. Wealth is what you hold once debts are counted. Two people can be in one order for pay and the opposite order for wealth.

Colby earns $4,000 a month and drives a new truck. Leah earns $2,800 a month and drives an older car. Who is richer? Pay alone cannot tell you. You need two lists: what each person owns and what each person owes.

What you own is an asset: money in an account, a car, a home. What you owe is a debt, also called a liability: a loan or a card balance. Net worth is your assets minus your debts. It is one number for where you stand today.
Colby's truck could sell for $45,000, but he owes $50,000 on it. He owns $47,000 and owes $50,000, so his net worth is −$3,000. Leah owns $10,000 and owes nothing, so hers is $10,000.

A net worth below zero is negative: the person owes more than they own. It is one day's page, not a grade. Pay is not on the page until it sits in an account. Leah's next pay is income today, and becomes an asset when it lands.

cards.text: To build a page, ask one question about each thing: do I own it, or do I owe it? Chequing, savings, investments and a car are owned. A card balance, a car loan and a student loan are owed.
Assets count at what they could sell for today, not at what was paid. Jordan, a made-up 24-year-old, paid $16,000 for a car. It could sell for $9,000 today, so the page shows $9,000.
Debts count at what is still owed, not at the amount first borrowed. Jordan took a loan to buy the car and still owes $11,000 on it. The page shows $11,000.
Here is Jordan's whole page, with no totals yet. Add the owned lines for the assets. Add the owed lines for the debts. The difference is net worth.

cards.text: A home goes on the owned side at what it could sell for. Its mortgage, the loan, goes on the owed side at what is still owed. Equity is what is left for the owner: the home's value minus what is still owed.

The class example: a $400,000 home. The buyer puts $80,000 down and borrows $320,000 at 5% for 25 years. On day one the equity is the down payment, $80,000. This example leaves out the costs of buying.

The game's mortgage calculation gives a payment of $1,861.14 a month for this loan. After 60 payments, five years, $283,224 is still owed. The balance falls slowly at first. Here the home's value is held at $400,000 so you can watch the mortgage alone.

Why so slowly? Interest is charged on what you still owe, and early on that is a lot. In the first payment of $1,861.14, about $1,320 is interest and about $541 reduces the mortgage. Each later payment shifts a little more toward the loan.

Equity also moves with the home's price, even if every payment is made. If prices fall 10%, the home is worth $360,000 while the mortgage balance is unchanged. If the mortgage were bigger than the value, equity would be negative.

cards.text: Net worth changes only when the owned side and the owed side change by different amounts. A move can change one side or both. The change in net worth is the change in what you own minus the change in what you owe.
Four moves on Jordan's page. A pays down debt. C saves more, or spends less. D invests savings. B is not a strategy: the car just lost value.

cards.text: Move A does not change net worth today. Savings fall $1,800 and the card falls $1,800. The gain comes later. A card at 20% a year charges $1,800 x 20% / 12 = $30.00 a month. Savings at 3% earn $1,800 x 3% / 12 = $4.50 a month (example rates).

Saving $200 a month for a year is $2,400 more owned. Spending $200 less does the same, if the money stays in an account. Investing moves money from one owned line to another. Net worth then changes only by what the investment gains or loses. It can fall as well as rise.

Borrowing to buy something that loses value can leave you owing more than it is worth. Jordan's car could sell for $9,000, and $11,000 is still owed. That pair of lines is −$2,000. Paying the loan down narrows the gap.

cards.text: The Net Worth building shows your page in the game. This is the game's version, so it follows the game's own rules. The big number at the top is net worth: every account balance, plus the value of a home, plus Exchange holdings. Debts are negative balances.

Owned in the game: chequing, high-interest savings, GICs, cash in investing accounts and a rental's damage deposit. A home counts at its value. Exchange holdings count at the bid, the price you would get if you sold. An RRSP counts at face value, before tax.

Owed in the game: a mortgage, a credit card balance, an emergency loan and bills not yet paid. Each is a negative balance, so the game just adds everything. The table in the building lists some of the lines. The number at the top counts every account, including ones the table does not list.

The game leaves things out. It has no line for a car, a phone or other belongings, and no student loan or car loan. A home counts at its full value, with no cost of selling taken off. Jordan's page had more kinds of lines than the game does.

sections.title: Money Systems & Crypto
sections.blurb: What money is, who manages it, how it crosses borders, and what a blockchain changes.

units.title: What money is
units.blurb: Why money exists, who creates it, and where higher prices come from.

levels.title: Why money exists
learn: Say why trading without money is hard.
Name the three jobs money does.

cards.text: Imagine there is no money. Ana has a hoodie and wants pizza. The pizza maker does not want a hoodie. The pizza maker wants a haircut. Trading without money, thing for thing, is called barter.
The barber wants a hoodie. So Ana needs a loop of three: the hoodie goes to the barber, the barber cuts the pizza maker's hair, and the pizza maker gives Ana pizza. Nobody can trade straight across.
Barter needs someone who has what you want and wants what you have. Money fixes that. Everyone takes it. Ana can sell the hoodie to anyone for money, then spend the money on pizza.
Money does three jobs. You buy things with it. You save it for later. You measure prices with it, because everything has a price in dollars.

Is it money? Ask if it does all three jobs. A $20 bill does. So does the balance in a bank account. A gift card for one café fails the first job, because only that café takes it. Points in one video game fail the same way.

levels.title: Money by promise
learn: Say why a $20 bill is worth something.
Say what a central bank does and where new money comes from.

cards.text: A $20 bill is a piece of plastic that costs very little to make. Yet a restaurant will give you a meal for it. The plastic is not why. Something else makes it work.

A gold coin is worth something by itself. That is commodity money. The Canadian dollar is not backed by gold. It is fiat money. Fiat means "by order". It works because of an order, not because of what it is made of.
Fiat money works for three reasons. The law says it can pay a debt. The government takes it for taxes. And you trust that the next person will take it too.

A central bank is the bank for a whole country. In Canada it is the Bank of Canada. It makes the bank notes. The Royal Canadian Mint makes the coins. The central bank also sets a key interest rate. You will see why in level 4.

Most money is not cash. It is numbers in bank accounts. When a bank makes a loan, it does not take cash from a vault. It types new money into the borrower's account. That is where most new money comes from.

levels.title: Where higher prices come from
learn: Show how more money chasing the same goods pushes a price up.
Find what a made-up amount buys years later.

cards.text: Inflation means prices in general go up, so each dollar buys less. One big cause is more money chasing the same goods. Try it on a made-up pizza island. It is a simple model, not a real formula.

On the island, all the money is spent on pizza in the year. So one pizza costs the money divided by the pizzas. In the class example, $1,000 chasing 100 pizzas makes each pizza $10. Print more money and watch the price.

Double the money and keep 100 pizzas, and the price doubles to $20. Double the money and the pizzas, and the price stays $10. More money is fine when there is more to buy. Too much new money chasing the same goods pushes prices up.
Two more causes, simplified. Things get harder or costlier to make: after the storm, $1,000 chases 80 pizzas and each costs $12.50. And people expect prices to rise, so they ask for more.

Here is a $5 snack, with prices rising 1%, 2% and 6% a year for 10 years. This is the class example. The Inflation unit showed how each figure is found. At 2%, a $100 bill buys what $82.03 buys today.

Rising prices hurt most the person with cash in a drawer: it buys less every year. Someone who owes money repays with dollars that buy less. For real prices, the Bank of Canada has an inflation calculator on its website.

levels.title: The central bank's lever
learn: Say what the policy rate is and how it slows prices.
Tell who gains and who loses when it moves.

cards.text: A central bank has a lever: the policy rate. It is the key interest rate the Bank of Canada sets. To slow rising prices, the Bank raises it. Loans cost more, so people borrow and spend less.

figure.title: The money loop
rows: If stores cannot make more, prices rise

cards.text: Look at the loop. A higher rate slows step 1: fewer loans mean less new money in accounts. People spend less, so prices rise more slowly. A lower rate does the opposite: borrowing is cheaper, so people borrow and spend more.

Who feels a rise? Dana's loan costs more: interest for a year is the amount times the rate. Noor's savings earn more. Both rates follow the policy rate in this example. Dana pays $120 more a year. Noor earns $80 more.

figure.title: Same amounts at a higher rate

cards.text: So a higher rate helps savers, who earn more, and hurts borrowers, who pay more. A lower rate does the reverse. Someone who keeps cash in a drawer earns 0%, so a rate change does not change what the drawer earns.

The Bank of Canada aims to keep inflation near 2%, inside a range of 1% to 3%. It does not aim for 0%. If prices fall, people may wait to buy, because things will be cheaper later. That can stall the economy.

levels.title: The Bank of DAA
learn: Say how the game's policy rate reaches your savings and a mortgage.
Work out a rate or an interest amount from the policy rate.

cards.text: The game has its own central bank, the Bank of DAA. It sets one policy rate for the whole town. The game starts at 2.25%, and your teacher can change it. This is the game's small version of what a real central bank does.

A new policy rate starts the next world month. The screen shows when. It also shows the next scheduled announcement month. The game lists 8 a year: months 1, 3, 4, 6, 7, 9, 10 and 12. Your teacher can still set a rate in any month.

The other rates follow the policy rate by fixed gaps. The game starts with the gaps in the table. The line of credit follows prime. The game starts the credit card at 20.99%, and it does not follow the policy rate.

figure.title: Rates that follow the policy rate

cards.text: Savings: each world month the game adds balance x yearly rate / 12, and drops any part of a cent. Mika has $4,000.00. At 2.25% policy her savings rate is 2.75%, and she earns $9.16 the first month. After a rise to 2.75% policy she earns $10.83 the first month.

A new mortgage is priced at the 5-year fixed rate lenders are offering that month. One already running keeps its rate until its term ends, then renews at the new rate and the payment is recalculated. Here is the game's payment for Rafa, with 20 years left, at two policy rates.

figure.title: Rafa renews: $240,000 left, 20 years to go

cards.text: Open the Bank of DAA to see the live numbers. It shows the policy rate, a chart of past rates, and a table of your rates with how each changed since the last move. The teacher can change the rate, so you may not see 2.25%.

units.title: Exchange rates
units.blurb: What a Canadian dollar is worth in another money, and why that changes.

levels.title: Reading a rate
learn: Read an exchange rate and say which money it prices.
Change an amount from one money to the other.

cards.text: Each country has its own money, called its currency. Canada uses Canadian dollars, written C$. The United States uses US dollars, written US$. An exchange rate is the price of one currency in another currency.

In class we use a made-up rate: US$1 = C$1.40. It reads: one US dollar costs C$1.40. From the other side, one Canadian dollar buys about US$0.71 (1 / 1.40, rounded). Real rates change; this one is only an example.
To change US dollars into Canadian dollars, multiply by the rate. A US$60 game costs 60 x 1.40 = C$84.00. The table shows more amounts at the same example rate.

figure.title: US dollars to Canadian dollars at US$1 = C$1.40

cards.text: To go the other way, divide by the rate. C$140.00 / 1.40 = US$100.00. A check: at this rate one US dollar is worth more than one Canadian dollar. So going to Canadian dollars gives a bigger number, and coming back gives a smaller one.

The game has a building called the Exchange. It is a stock exchange: funds and stocks of the town's companies are bought and sold there. It does not swap one money for another, and the game has no foreign money. The rates in this unit are class examples.

Yes. The rate prices one US dollar in Canadian dollars.

options.why: The rate is a price for each dollar, so it multiplies. It is not taken off.

levels.title: Why rates move
learn: Tell a floating rate from a pegged rate.
Say what a higher or lower rate does to a traveller and a buyer.

cards.text: Canada's dollar floats. Its price is set by buyers and sellers of the money, like any price, and it can change every minute. If more people want Canadian dollars, its price rises. If fewer do, it falls.

People need Canadian dollars to buy what Canada sells, such as oil. They also need them to buy Canadian stocks or to earn the interest paid here. More of that means more demand for Canadian dollars. Less means less demand.

Some governments peg their money instead. The government fixes the rate and holds it there. For example, it promises that US$1 is always 10 pesos. That looks steady, but the government can reset the peg later. The next level shows what that does.
Floating and pegged side by side. Canada's dollar floats. The peso is a made-up example of a peg.

figure.title: Floating or pegged
rows: Buyers and sellers of the money
All the time, as demand shifts
Stays put until it is reset

cards.text: Say the rate moves from US$1 = C$1.40 to US$1 = C$1.50. The Canadian dollar is worth less: it takes more of them to buy US$1. A US trip, a US game and a US bill all cost more. Someone holding US dollars gets more Canadian dollars.

levels.title: Devaluation
learn: Say what a devaluation is and what it does to prices and savings.
Use percent change and finish with three conversions.

cards.text: Take a made-up country with a made-up money, the peso. Its government pegs the peso: US$1 = 10 pesos. A US$100 phone costs 100 x 10 = 1,000 pesos there. And 1,200 pesos buys 1,200 / 10 = US$120.00 abroad.

Now the government resets the peg to US$1 = 12 pesos. It has lowered the value of its own money on purpose. That is a devaluation. The same phone costs 100 x 12 = 1,200 pesos, and 1,200 pesos now buys US$100.00.

figure.title: The peso peg, before and after

cards.text: Percent change is (new - old) / old. The phone went from 1,000 to 1,200 pesos: 200 / 1,000 = 20% dearer. What 1,200 pesos buys went from US$120 to US$100: -20 / 120 is about -16.7%. The percents differ because the old amounts differ.
So a devaluation raises the price of imports in the country, and it cuts what savings buy abroad. A floating money can drift the same way, but slowly. A devaluation does it overnight.

Why would a government do it? Its goods get cheaper for buyers abroad. A hat that costs 1,200 pesos costs US$120.00 to a US buyer at 10 pesos per US dollar, and US$100.00 at 12. A cheaper money makes a country's goods cheaper abroad. The trade unit picks that up.

The opposite move, when a government raises the value of its pegged money, is a revaluation. To finish, you will convert at the class rate, US$1 = C$1.40. Multiply to go to Canadian dollars. Divide to come back.

Floating means the market sets the rate. Here a government changed a fixed peg.
Yes. The peso now buys fewer US dollars, so it is worth less on purpose.
The money is the same peso. Only its peg changed.

Yes. 100 x 12 = 1,200 pesos.

options.why: The US price is the same, but the peso price follows the peg. It changes.

units.title: Global trade
units.blurb: Why countries trade, what a tariff does, and who wins and loses.

levels.title: Why countries trade
learn: You will say what an import and an export are.
You will see why two countries can both end up with more by trading.

cards.text: Many things in a Canadian store were made in another country. A good Canada buys from another country is an import. A good Canada sells to another country is an export. Canada sells things like oil, wheat, canola and lumber.

Picture two islands with ten workers each. A Maple Island worker makes 6 hoodies or 2 crates of fruit in a day. A Sun Island worker makes 2 hoodies or 6 crates. A worker on hoodies is not making fruit: that is what the island gives up.

cards.text: Say each island puts 5 workers on hoodies and 5 on fruit, and they do not trade. Maple makes 30 hoodies and 10 crates. Sun makes 10 hoodies and 30 crates. Together the two islands have 40 hoodies and 40 crates.

figure.title: No trade: 5 workers on each good

cards.text: Now each island does only what it does best. Maple puts all 10 workers on hoodies. Sun puts all 10 on fruit. Together they make 60 hoodies and 60 crates. That is 20 more of each, but each island has only one of the two goods.

figure.title: Each island does what it does best

cards.text: So they trade. Maple sends 25 hoodies to Sun, and Sun sends 25 crates to Maple. Maple ends with 35 hoodies and 25 crates. Sun ends with 25 hoodies and 35 crates. Both have more of both than with no trade.

figure.title: After Maple swaps 25 hoodies for 25 crates

levels.title: A tariff is a tax at the border
learn: You will say what a tariff is and who collects it.
You will work out the price of an import after a tariff.

cards.text: A tariff is a tax on goods that come in from another country. The Government of Canada collects it at the border. Countries use tariffs to help the people who make things at home.
Here is a made-up example. A bike made in another country costs $400. The same kind of bike made in Canada costs $460. With no tariff, the imported bike is the cheaper one.

figure.title: Bike prices in Canada, no tariff

cards.text: Say Canada adds a 25% tariff. 25% of $400 is $100. The imported bike now costs $400 + $100 = $500. A 10% tariff adds $40, so $440. Tariff = price before tariff x rate.

figure.title: A tariff on the bike made abroad

cards.text: Who pays? In this example, the store passes the whole tariff on to the buyer. So the government collects the money, and the buyer pays it. In real life, the importer, the store and the buyer share the cost in different ways.
At some tariff rate, the two bikes cost the same. The gap is $460 - $400 = $60. Divide it by the $400 price before tariff: $60 / $400 = 15%. Above 15%, the Canadian bike is cheaper.

levels.title: Dumping and the rules
learn: You will say what dumping is and how a country answers it.
You will match six trade deals to who is in them.

cards.text: Dumping is selling in another country for less than the price at home. It is about price. It has nothing to do with throwing out rubbish. Sometimes the price is even less than it costs to make the good.
Made-up example: a tonne of steel sells for $800 at home and $600 in Canada. That is dumping. A Canadian mill spends $700 to make a tonne. To match $600, it would lose $100 on every tonne.

Canada can answer with an anti-dumping duty: an extra charge that brings the price back up. In this example the duty is the whole gap, $800 - $600 = $200. The steel then sells for $600 + $200 = $800. The law is the Special Import Measures Act. Real cases also look at cost and harm.
A trade deal is when countries agree to cut tariffs between them. Here are six that matter to Canada, with who is in each and the year it started.

cards.text: CUSMA is the deal among Canada, the US and Mexico today. It replaced NAFTA in 2020. The US calls it USMCA. The big one for Alberta is CUSMA, because the US is Canada's biggest customer by far. CETA is with the European Union. CPTPP is with Pacific Rim countries.

levels.title: Who wins, who loses
learn: You will say who gains and who loses when a tariff is added.
You will see how a tariff and an exchange rate both change a price.

cards.text: A tariff helps some people and costs others. Take the bike example. Canada puts a 25% tariff on imported bikes. The imported bike goes from $400 to $500. The Canadian bike still costs $460.

The Canadian bike maker gains, because its $460 bike is now cheaper than the import. The foreign bike maker loses sales in Canada. The government collects $100 on each imported bike. A buyer pays more, either $500 for the import or $460 for the Canadian bike.

Now the other country answers with a tariff on Canadian canola. A farmer who sells canola there finds that buyers must pay more, so they may buy less. When one country protects its makers and the other hits back, it is called a tariff war. Exporters get hurt.

In 1930 the US raised tariffs on thousands of goods. Other countries hit back, and world trade shrank during the Depression. Protecting home makers with tariffs is called protectionism. Each case has people who gain and people who lose.

Tariffs and exchange rates work together. At last unit's class rate, US$1 = C$1.40, a US$50 hoodie is C$70.00. A 20% tariff adds C$14.00. A weaker Canadian dollar makes things bought abroad cost more in Canadian dollars.

units.title: Payments technology
units.blurb: How money moves when you tap, send or pay later, and when it really leaves.

levels.title: When does the money leave?
learn: Sort ways to pay by when the money leaves your account.
Say why paying later can feel free and what it costs.

cards.text: A phone does not hold your money. It holds a card, and the card inside decides how you pay. A phone with a debit card inside works like a debit card. A phone with a credit card inside works like a credit card.
Some ways to pay take the money from your account right away. A debit card does. So does a transfer sent from your bank's app. The money leaves now, and you are spending money you already have.

A credit card works the other way. The bank pays the store now, and you pay the bank later, when you pay the card's bill. You met the statement and the due date in the credit unit. Until you pay that bill, you are borrowing.

A plan that splits a purchase into four payments is a third way. The money leaves bit by bit, on dates the plan sets. You get the item first and pay for it afterwards, so this is borrowing too. Level 3 looks at it closely.
Here are six ways to pay, sorted by when the money leaves your account. Cash and a prepaid card are already gone before you shop, because you loaded them first. That is why they are not borrowing.

cards.text: Paying later can feel free. On the day you tap a credit card, your chequing balance has not changed. The bill comes later. Pay the whole balance by the due date and you pay no interest. Pay less and the lender charges interest.

terms.meaning: A card that lets you borrow now and pay the bill later.

questions.hint: Ask which card is inside the phone.

options.text: Right away, because she used a phone
options.why: The phone does not decide. The card inside does, and a credit card is paid later.
A phone is not a source of money. Someone pays the card's bill, and that is Lena.

options.text: Bit by bit, on a schedule
options.why: That is a plan that splits a purchase into payments. A credit card has one bill.

options.text: Later, when she pays the card's bill
options.why: Right. The phone only carries the card. The credit card adds to Lena's bill, and her chequing is charged when she pays it.

questions.label: Two phones
questions.prompt: Noor and Kai tap their phones at the same shop. Noor's phone has a debit card inside. Kai's has a credit card inside. Whose money leaves their chequing right away?
questions.hint: Look at the card inside each phone.

options.why: Yes. Noor's debit card takes money from her account now. Kai's credit card adds to his bill, which he pays later.
It is the other way round. A credit card is paid later, when the bill comes.
Same tap, different money. The card inside decides when the money leaves.

questions.label: Four payments
questions.prompt: Priya buys shoes with a plan that splits the price into four payments. When does her money leave?
questions.hint: Count how many payments there are.

options.why: That would be a debit tap. This plan takes four smaller payments.

options.text: Bit by bit, on a schedule
options.why: Right. Each payment leaves on a date the plan sets, and Priya has the shoes before she has paid for them all.
One bill later is a credit card. This plan takes four separate payments.

options.text: It never leaves, because the plan is free
options.why: The money still leaves in four pieces. A plan with no interest is not a plan with no payments.

questions.label: Which borrows
questions.prompt: Which one of these is borrowing?
questions.hint: Ask whether you pay someone back later.

options.why: A debit card spends money in your account now, so you are not borrowing.

options.text: Sending a transfer from your bank's app
options.why: A transfer leaves your account right away, so you are not borrowing.
Yes. The bank pays now and you pay the bank later, so you are borrowing until you pay the bill.

options.text: Paying with cash from last week
options.why: The cash was yours before you shopped, so you are not borrowing.

Later, when you pay the bill
Bit by bit, on a schedule

questions.label: Chequing after lunch
questions.prompt: Mia has $240.00 in chequing. She taps her debit card for an $18.50 lunch. Then she puts a $32.00 purchase on her credit card. How much is in her chequing right after both?
questions.hint: Only one of the two purchases has left her chequing so far.
questions.why: The debit purchase left right away. The credit card purchase has not left chequing yet, because it waits on the card's bill.
questions.working: $240.00 - $18.50 = $221.50. The $32.00 is on the card and is paid later.
questions.miss: Take off only the purchase that leaves chequing now. The other one is paid later.

traps.why: $240.00 - $18.50 - $32.00 takes off the credit card purchase too. It has not left chequing yet.

questions.label: Feels free
questions.prompt: Why can paying with a credit card feel free on the day you buy?
questions.hint: What does your chequing balance show on the day?

options.text: Your chequing balance has not changed yet
options.why: Yes. The money leaves later, when the bill is paid, so nothing seems different on the day. It is still borrowing.

options.text: The store gives you a discount
options.why: A discount is a lower price. A credit card does not change the price.

options.text: The bank pays the bill for you
options.why: The bank pays the store. You still owe the bank the full bill.

options.text: Credit card bills have no interest
options.why: Only a bill paid in full by the due date has none. Pay less and the lender charges interest.

questions.label: Statement to pay
questions.prompt: Mia's card statement lists three purchases: $32.00, $45.50 and $12.25. She wants to pay no interest. How much must she pay by the due date?

terms.meaning: The total you owe on the card.

questions.hint: No interest means paying the whole balance.
questions.why: Paying the whole balance by the due date means no interest on those purchases. The balance is the three purchases added together.
questions.miss: Add all three purchases. To pay no interest, the whole balance has to be paid.

traps.why: $32.00 is only the first purchase. The balance is all three.

levels.title: Send and tap
learn: Say how a transfer and a tap work, and what cannot be undone.
Spot the red flags in a message about money.

cards.text: To send money from your bank's app, you pick a person and enter an amount. The money moves from your bank to theirs. It is fast. That is helpful with a friend and risky with a scammer.
With autodeposit turned on, the money lands straight in the other person's account. They click no link. Once it is deposited, you usually cannot get it back. Treat a transfer like handing over cash.

Tapping a card or a phone at a store is fast too. The card inside decides whose money it is: a debit card takes it from your account now, and a credit card adds to your bill. Your bank sets how much a tap can spend, and it can differ by bank and store. Check your bank's app.

Scam messages share red flags. Someone asks for your password: your bank never asks for it by text or email. Someone wants money before you get anything. Someone sends a picture of a payment instead of real money. And you never pay a fee to collect a prize.

A screenshot is not money. Only your own bank app shows what is in your account. An alert in your app for a tap you just made is normal. So when a message says money has arrived or a payment was made, check your own app.

questions.label: After deposit
questions.prompt: Jo sends a transfer by mistake, and it is deposited in the other person's account. What is usually true now?
questions.hint: Read the first card of this level again.

options.text: Jo usually cannot get it back
options.why: Yes. Once a transfer is deposited, you usually cannot pull it back. It is like cash handed over.

options.text: Jo can cancel it any time
options.why: After the money is deposited, you usually cannot cancel it.

options.text: The money returns by itself in a day
options.why: Nothing sends it back on its own. That is why a transfer is treated like cash.

questions.label: Autodeposit step
questions.prompt: Mia has autodeposit on. A friend sends her money. What does Mia have to do to receive it?
questions.hint: The card says what the receiver clicks.

options.text: Nothing, it lands in her account
options.why: Right. With autodeposit the money lands in the account with no link to click.

options.text: Click a link in an email
options.why: Autodeposit has no link to click. The money lands on its own.
With autodeposit nobody answers a question. The money lands on its own.

questions.label: Tap with debit
questions.prompt: Sam taps his phone, which has a debit card inside, to pay $9 at a snack bar. Whose money is it, and when does it leave?
questions.hint: Ask which card is inside.

options.text: His own, from his account right away
options.why: Right. The debit card inside decides it. The money leaves Sam's account now.

options.text: The bank's, later when a bill comes
options.why: A bill later is a credit card. Sam's phone holds a debit card.
The phone only carries the card. It is not a source of money.

questions.label: Tap limit
questions.prompt: Ana wants to know the most one tap can spend. According to this level, who sets it?
questions.hint: The card says where to check.

options.text: It is the same at every bank and store
options.why: The limit can differ by bank and store, so there is no single number.

options.text: This course lists one number for everyone
options.why: This course gives no figure, because the limit is set by your bank.

options.text: Her bank, so she checks her bank's app
options.why: Right. Your bank sets it, and it can differ by bank and store. This course gives no number.

questions.label: Real money
questions.prompt: Mia got three things today. Which line shows money that is really in her account?

figure.title: What Mia received today
rows: From "your bank": reply with your password
A picture showing $200 sent to her

questions.hint: Where does your own account show its money?

options.why: A text can say anything, and it does not show what is in her account.

options.why: Yes. Only your own bank app shows what is in your account. A text or a picture is not money.

questions.label: Password text
questions.prompt: A text says it is from your bank. It says your account is locked and asks you to reply with your password. What is it?
questions.hint: What does your bank never ask for by text?

options.text: Safe, because it names your bank
options.why: Anyone can put a bank's name in a text. A real bank does not ask for a password this way.

options.text: A red flag, because banks never ask that
options.why: Yes. A bank never asks for your password by text or email, so this is a scam.
Speed does not make it safe. A password request by text is the red flag.

questions.label: Deposit first
questions.prompt: A seller of a used guitar says you must send a $120 deposit by transfer before you can see the guitar. Which red flag is this?
questions.hint: What do you have in your hands before you pay?

options.text: Money first, with nothing in hand yet
options.why: Yes. They want money before you get anything. A transfer is like cash, so it is hard to take back.
No screenshot was sent. The flag is paying first.
Nobody asked for a password. The flag is the deposit before you see the guitar.

questions.label: Money lost
questions.prompt: A buyer says they will pay $60 for Ana's lamp. The buyer emails a picture saying $200 was sent by mistake and asks Ana to send $140 back. Ana's bank app shows nothing arrived. If she sends the $140 anyway, how much money does she lose?
questions.hint: What did she actually receive?
questions.why: A picture is not money, and her app shows nothing arrived. The $140 she sends is real money that leaves her account, and a deposited transfer is usually not coming back.
questions.working: She received $0.00. She sent $140.00. She is down $140.00.
questions.miss: Count what she received, then what she sent. Her app is the only proof of money.

traps.why: $60 is the price of the lamp. What Ana loses is the money she sends, and nothing arrived to set against it.

questions.label: Safe message
questions.prompt: Dev's friend sends him $15 for pizza. Dev has autodeposit on, and the $15 shows in his bank app. What is this?
questions.hint: Is the money in his own app?

options.text: A scam, because it was a transfer
options.why: Transfers are normal between friends. The red flags are a password request, money first, a picture of a payment, or a fee to claim a prize.

options.text: A scam, because it was unexpected
options.why: Nothing in the message is a red flag, and the money is in his own app. That is the test.

options.text: Safe, it is in his own app
options.why: Yes. The money is in his account and he clicked nothing. Checking your own app is the test.

questions.label: Pizza split
questions.prompt: Ana paid $48.00 for pizza. Three friends each send her $12.00 by transfer, and Ana has autodeposit on. How much has landed in Ana's account from her friends?
questions.hint: Three friends, each sending the same amount.
questions.why: With autodeposit each transfer lands on its own. Three equal amounts add up.
questions.miss: Multiply the amount each friend sends by the number of friends who send it.

traps.why: $48.00 is what Ana paid for the pizza. The friends send $12.00 each.

levels.title: Is paying in four free?
learn: Work out the payments of a plan that splits a purchase into four.
Show when stacked plans leave you short and what a missed payment costs.

cards.text: A plan that splits a purchase into four payments lets you buy now. In the class example, $400 sneakers become four payments of $100, two weeks apart, in weeks 0, 2, 4 and 6. $400 / 4 = $100. There is no interest if every payment is on time.

So what is the catch? Miss a payment and there can be a late fee. In the class example it is $10 for one missed payment. That is an example, not a real price, and each plan sets its own. One plan on its own looks easy. The catch shows up when plans overlap.
Now stack three plans. Each takes four payments, two weeks apart. The prices add up: $400 + $240 + $160 = $800 in all.
Add what is due each payday and compare it with the $150 you have for payments. The example puts every payment on a payday, every 2 weeks. Real plans pick their own dates.

figure.title: Payday bills and what you have

cards.text: Three paydays are short: week 2 by $10, and weeks 4 and 6 by $50 each. That is $110 in all. Miss one payment on each of those paydays and the late fees are 3 x $10 = $30. To never be short you would need $200 each payday, the biggest bill in the table.

So is paying in four free? Only if every payment is on time. It does not feel like borrowing, and that is the risk: each plan looks small, and the bills add up when plans overlap. Adding a new plan's payments to the ones already due shows the real bill.

questions.label: What it is
questions.prompt: Which sentence describes a plan that splits a purchase into four payments?
questions.hint: Count the payments in the example.

options.text: You pay all of it at checkout
options.why: That is paying now. A split plan spreads the price over four payments.

options.text: You pay in four parts, spread over some weeks
options.why: Yes. The price is split into four payments, and in the class example they are two weeks apart.

options.text: You pay one big bill next month
options.why: One bill later is a credit card. A split plan has four payments.

options.text: You pay four times the price
options.why: The four payments add up to the price. In the example, 4 x $100 = $400.

questions.label: Each payment
questions.prompt: Sam buys a $280 jacket with a plan of four equal payments and no interest. How much is each payment?
questions.hint: Split the price into four equal parts.
questions.why: Four equal payments with no interest add up to the price, so divide the price by four.
questions.miss: Divide the price by the number of payments.

traps.why: $280.00 is the whole price, not one of four payments.

questions.label: When it is free
questions.prompt: In the class example, when is a plan of four payments free?
questions.hint: The example says what must happen on every payment.

options.text: Always, because it has no interest
options.why: No interest only holds when every payment is on time. A missed one can cost a late fee.

options.text: Never, because there is always interest
options.why: In the class example there is no interest when every payment is on time.

options.text: Only when every payment is on time
options.why: Right. There is no interest on time, but a missed payment can bring a late fee.

options.text: Only when the item is cheap
options.why: The price of the item does not decide it. Every payment being on time does.

questions.label: First short payday
questions.prompt: Tap the first payday where the bill is more than the $150 you have.
questions.hint: Compare each bar with $150.
questions.why: Week 0 is $100 and fits in $150. Week 2 is $160, which is $10 more than $150, so the first short payday is week 2.
questions.miss: Check each bar against $150. The first one above it is the answer.

questions.label: Short in week 4
questions.prompt: Read the table of payday bills. In week 4 the bill is $200 and you have $150. How much are you short?

figure.title: Payday bills and what you have

questions.hint: Short = due - what you have.
questions.why: Being short is the bill minus the money you have for it.
questions.miss: Take what you have off the bill due that week.

traps.why: $200 is what is due, not how much you are short.

questions.label: Total short
questions.prompt: With $150 each payday, week 2 is short by $10, week 4 by $50 and week 6 by $50. How much are you short in all?
questions.hint: Add the three shortfalls.
questions.why: The paydays that are short are weeks 2, 4 and 6. Their shortfalls add up.
questions.miss: Only the three short paydays count. Add their shortfalls.

traps.why: $50 is one short payday. Week 2 and week 6 are short too.

questions.label: Late fees
questions.prompt: In the class example a missed payment costs a $10 late fee. You miss one payment on each of the 3 short paydays. What do the late fees come to?
questions.hint: One fee for each short payday.
questions.why: One $10 fee for each of the three short paydays.
questions.miss: Multiply the fee by the number of short paydays.

questions.label: Never short
questions.prompt: Use the table of payday bills. What is the least you need each payday so you are never short?

figure.title: Payday bills and what you have

questions.hint: Look for the biggest bill.
questions.why: You are never short if your money covers the biggest bill in the table.
questions.working: The biggest bills are $200, in weeks 4 and 6, so you need $200.
questions.miss: You need enough for the biggest bill of all the paydays.

traps.why: $800 is the total of all three plans. You pay it over many paydays, not on one.

questions.label: Leo's week 4
questions.prompt: Leo has three plans of four equal payments, two weeks apart: $300 starting in week 0, $200 starting in week 2, and $120 starting in week 4. How much is due on Leo's week 4 payday?
questions.hint: Which plans have a payment in week 4?
questions.why: All three plans have a payment in week 4. Add the three payments.
questions.miss: Find one payment from each plan, then add them.

traps.why: $75 + $50 leaves out the third plan, which has its first payment in week 4.

questions.label: The real risk
questions.prompt: Which sentence names the risk of paying in four, as this level describes it?
questions.hint: Which sentence did the last card give?

options.why: In the class example there is no interest when every payment is on time.

options.text: The price is higher than the shelf price
options.why: The four payments add up to the price. The risk is stacking, not a hidden price.

options.text: A late fee is charged on every payment
options.why: A late fee comes with a missed payment, not with every payment.

options.text: It does not feel like borrowing, so plans stack up
options.why: Yes. Each plan looks small, and the bills add up when plans overlap.

levels.title: Banks without branches, and the game
learn: Say what an online-only bank is and compare two accounts over a year.
Say how sending money and autopay work in the game's Bank.

cards.text: An online-only bank has no branches. You use it through an app or a website. Because it needs no branches, it often charges lower fees. One check matters: is your money held at a CDIC member? CDIC is a deposit insurer.

Some apps that hold your money are not banks. They keep it at a partner bank. Two ideas are being built in Canada: open banking, where you choose to share your bank data with an app, and faster payments, where money moves in seconds, any time. The next unit looks at a way to move money with no bank in the middle.

Here is the trade, with made-up prices. Account A is at a bank with branches: $16.95 a month and no ATM fee. Account B is online-only: $0 a month and $3 each time you take cash from an ATM. Many banks also offer no-fee student accounts.

figure.title: Cost for a year at different numbers of ATM visits a month

cards.text: The game has a Bank too. It holds your chequing account and its statement. It can also send money to a classmate, but only after your teacher turns that on for your class. The game starts with a $50 limit for each transfer and $100 in any 24 hours, and the teacher can change both.

A game transfer goes only to someone in your own class, and the smallest is $1.00. The Bank’s screen shows how much you can still send in the last 24 hours. In this game your teacher can reverse a transfer, unless the other student has already spent the money. A real transfer usually cannot be pulled back.

Autopay moves money for you. In the Credit Bureau, card autopay can be off, pay the minimum, or pay everything owed on the card from chequing. It pays only if chequing covers the whole amount. Bills has an Autopay switch too. With autopay, the money leaves on its own.

questions.prompt: What is an online-only bank?

options.text: A bank that only lets you pay online
options.why: It is a full bank. It just has no branches, and you can do your banking in its app.

options.text: An app that holds your money at a partner bank
options.why: That describes an app that is not a bank. An online-only bank is itself a bank.

options.text: A bank with no branches that you use by app or website
options.why: Right. It has no branches, which is why it can often charge lower fees.

questions.label: App not a bank
questions.prompt: What is true of some apps that hold your money?

options.why: Some apps are not banks, so they are not always the same.

options.text: They keep it at a partner bank

options.text: They keep your money in the phone

questions.hint: The first card names the check.

questions.prompt: Account B costs $0 a month and $3 for each ATM cash withdrawal. Dev takes cash from an ATM 4 times a month. What does Account B cost him for a year? (visits x $3 x 12 months)
questions.hint: Visits a month x fee x months in a year.

questions.label: Open banking
questions.prompt: What is open banking, as this unit describes it?
questions.hint: The second card has both ideas.

options.why: Right. You choose, and Canada is building the rules for it.

options.why: Open banking has nothing to do with branches.

options.why: Yes. Sending money to a classmate is off until your teacher turns it on for your class.

options.why: The teacher turns it on for the class. Individual transfers are not approved one by one.

questions.label: Autopay all or nothing
questions.prompt: Sam's card autopay pays the full statement from chequing. This month Sam's chequing has less than the amount owed. What does autopay do?
questions.hint: The last card says what autopay needs.

options.why: It does not pay part. It pays the whole amount or nothing.

units.title: Blockchain and crypto
units.blurb: A ledger nobody owns: what a cryptocurrency is and how a blockchain keeps the list.

levels.title: What a cryptocurrency is
learn: A cryptocurrency is money that lives as entries in a shared record.
You will say how it differs from the money in a bank.

cards.text: Mr. Tang once ran a farm of machines. It had about 50 graphics cards, the same kind gamers buy, on wire shelves. Each card sat on a riser cable, and each rig had its own power supply. The cards were not playing games. They were guessing numbers, day and night.
That guessing is called mining. The cards made the room hot, and every guess used electricity. A later unit shows why mining matters. First, what is a cryptocurrency?
A cryptocurrency is digital money. There is no coin or note to hold. It is locked with math, called cryptography. No bank, no government and no one in the middle runs it. Anyone can send to anyone.

Bitcoin came first. Ethereum came next. Both run on a blockchain, which is a shared record of every payment. The table sets a dollar in a bank beside a cryptocurrency. You saw in unit 1 that a central bank manages the dollar.

figure.title: A dollar in a bank and a cryptocurrency
rows: A bank and a central bank
Notes, coins or a bank balance

cards.text: People point to three reasons to care. Payments that are online, across borders, fast and cheap. Investment. And new business ideas, such as smart contracts and digital art. Next you will see where it all began.

questions.label: Cards in the story
questions.prompt: In Mr. Tang's story, what were the graphics cards doing?
questions.hint: The card says what they were not doing, then what they were doing.

options.why: The cards are the kind gamers buy, but in this story they were not playing games.
Yes. The cards were not playing games. The guessing is called mining.
Nothing was printed. The cards were guessing numbers.
No bank was involved. The cards were guessing numbers.

questions.label: Name for the guessing
questions.prompt: What does the lesson call the guessing the cards did?
questions.hint: The second card names it.

options.why: Yes. The guessing is called mining.
Lending is when someone lets you borrow money. The guessing has another name.
Budgeting is planning how to spend. It is not the guessing.
Banking is what a bank does for you. The guessing is called mining.

questions.label: What it is
questions.prompt: Which sentence describes a cryptocurrency?
questions.hint: Read the card that says what a cryptocurrency is made of.

options.text: Paper money printed by a central bank
options.why: That describes the dollar. A cryptocurrency has no central bank.

options.text: A balance that your bank keeps for you
options.why: A bank keeps a bank balance. A cryptocurrency has no bank in the middle.

options.text: A gold coin you keep in a vault
options.why: There is no coin or note to hold.

options.text: Digital money with no coin or note to hold
options.why: Yes. It exists as entries in a shared record, with no one in the middle.

questions.label: Which came first
questions.prompt: Which cryptocurrency came first?
questions.hint: The cards put them in order.

options.why: Ethereum came next, after Bitcoin.
Yes. Bitcoin came first, and Ethereum came next.

options.text: They started on the same day

levels.title: A short history
learn: Cryptocurrency has a short history with a few turning points.
You will put six events in order and say what each one changed.

cards.text: Oct 31, 2008: banks were failing. A nine-page paper appeared, called "Bitcoin: A Peer-to-Peer Electronic Cash System". To this day nobody knows who wrote it. Its big idea was money without a middleman.
May 22, 2010: someone paid 10,000 bitcoin for two pizzas, about US$41. It was the first thing ever bought with bitcoin. It showed you could actually buy something with it.
July 30, 2015: Ethereum launched, created by a Canadian. It added smart contracts: deals that run themselves when conditions are met. People use them for automated apps, loans, games and digital art.

Oct 21, 2020: a large online payments company let its US users buy, hold and sell four cryptocurrencies, Bitcoin and Ethereum among them. When a giant company joins in, cryptocurrency is not only for technical people.
Jan 10, 2024: the US securities regulator approved the first Bitcoin ETFs. An ETF is a fund you buy like a stock. Business angle: it became Wall Street money.

Dec 5, 2024: Bitcoin first reached US$100,000. That is a price of one money in another, like an exchange rate. On that day the pizza coins were worth 10,000 x US$100,000 = US$1,000,000,000. Prices change every minute, so this lesson uses dates.

levels.title: A ledger is a list
learn: A ledger is a list of every payment, in order.
You will work out a balance from the list and see why it must be hard to edit.

cards.text: A ledger is a list of every payment, in order. Each row says who paid, who got paid and how much. A payment moves money from one person to another. The list does not store anyone's balance. Your balance is worked out from the list.
Here is a made-up club. Four friends start with $20.00 each. To find a balance: start at $20.00, take away what the person paid and add what the person got.

figure.title: The club ledger: everyone starts with $20.00

cards.text: Worked example: Ben after row 2. He starts with $20.00. In row 1 he got $5.00. In row 2 he paid $8.00. So $20.00 + $5.00 - $8.00 = $17.00. Rows that do not name Ben do not change his balance.

A good ledger refuses a payment that someone cannot cover. If Ben has $5.00, a payment of $8.00 from Ben is rejected. Spending the same money twice is called a double spend. The list stops it, because the first payment is already on the list.

Why not let anyone edit the list? Ben could rub out row 2 and write a smaller number. Balances would change, and nobody could prove what the list said before. A ledger is useful only when old entries are hard to change quietly.
The game keeps a ledger too. Every move of money in the game is an entry in a ledger that the game itself keeps. That is one keeper. The next level asks who should keep a ledger.

levels.title: Who keeps the ledger?
learn: A ledger can have one keeper or many keepers, and each has a cost.
You will match made-up situations to the side they fit.

cards.text: Someone has to keep the ledger. With one keeper, there is one book in one place. A bank keeps its ledger on its own computers, and only the bank writes in it. You have to trust the keeper.

With many keepers, many people each hold a full copy of the ledger. A new payment is accepted when a majority of the copies agree. A majority is more than half of the copies. This is the idea behind a cryptocurrency. (Real Bitcoin counts computing power, not copies.)
To find a majority, take half and go to more than that. With 15 copies, half is 7.5, so a majority is 8. With 6 copies, half is 3, and 3 is not more than half, so a majority is 4.

A cheater who changes only their own copy gets out-voted, because the other copies still agree. To win, a cheater must control a majority of the copies. Real Bitcoin goes by computing power, not by counting copies. The idea of out-voting a cheater is the same.
The table sets the two designs side by side. Each one has a price. A bank gives you someone to call. A shared ledger spreads the trust across many copies, and it has nobody to call.

levels.title: Blocks in a chain
learn: A blockchain bundles payments into linked blocks.
You will find the block that shows a change and weigh a bank against a blockchain.

cards.text: A blockchain is a ledger kept in blocks. A block is a box of payments. New payments are bundled into a block, and blocks are added one after another.
Each block has a fingerprint: a number made from everything in the block. The next block writes down the fingerprint of the block before it. That is the link, and the links make a chain.

Our toy rule: fingerprint = the fingerprint before + 2 x the first payment + the second payment. Block 1 has no block before it, so it starts from 0. Real fingerprints are far harder to fake. This is only a toy.

figure.title: A chain of four blocks (made-up payments)

cards.text: Now someone changes block 2's second payment from $4 to $14. Block 2's fingerprint changes to 59. Block 3 still holds the old one, 49. They no longer match, so block 3 shows the break.

figure.title: The same chain after block 2 is changed

cards.text: To hide the change, the cheater must redo block 3, then block 4, then every block after it, and do it on most of the copies. That is why an old entry is hard to change quietly. With a bank, the keeper decides about an old entry. A chain shows every change.

CDIC is Canada's deposit insurer. It protects eligible deposits at member banks, up to a limit. It does not cover crypto. Neither column is better. Each fits a different need. The next unit shows how new blocks are made and what can go wrong.
