units.title: Coins, engines and risk
units.blurb: How coins are made and secured, the kinds of coin, and the risks of a coin.

levels.title: The engine
learn: Say how proof of work picks who writes the next page.
Work out what a guessing machine costs to run.

cards.text: In the last unit you saw blocks in a chain. Each new page of payments (a block) has to be written by someone, and a cryptocurrency has no bank to choose who. The rule a coin uses to pick the writer is its engine. This unit starts with the engine of the first cryptocurrency.

Bitcoin uses an engine called proof of work. Computers race to guess a number. The first one to find a good guess writes the next page and earns new coins. One guess is called a hash, and G in GH/s stands for giga, a billion.
Mr. Tang ran about 50 graphics cards in a race like this one. Their job was to guess. Together they made about 3 GH/s, which is 3 x 1,000,000,000 guesses every second.
The race has a cost. Guessing uses a lot of electricity, and it costs hardware too. Mining is not free money. Before you count the coins, count what the power cost.

A page is also hard to fake because many keepers hold copies. Say a keeper named Wendell changes his copy of a line from 1 to 10. The other four copies still say 1, so Wendell is outvoted. Real coins go by computing power, not by counting copies, but the idea of outvoting a cheater is the same.

questions.label: Next page
questions.prompt: Under proof of work, who gets to write the next page?
questions.hint: Think of the word "race".

options.text: The first computer to find a good guess
options.why: Yes. The race is to guess a number, and the first computer with a good guess writes the page.

options.text: A bank that the coin picks
options.why: A cryptocurrency has no bank in charge. The race picks the writer.
Age does not matter. Whoever finds a good guess first wins the race.

options.text: The keeper with the most coins
options.why: That is a different engine, which comes next level. In proof of work the guessing race decides.

questions.label: What a hash is
questions.prompt: In mining, what is one "hash"?

terms.meaning: One guess in the proof-of-work race.

questions.hint: GH/s is a speed: how many of them per second.

options.why: Yes. A hash is one guess, so 1 GH/s is a billion guesses in a second.
Keepers are the people or machines in the race. A hash is one guess.
Coins are the prize for the winner. A hash is one guess in the race.
A page of payments is a block. A hash is a single guess.

questions.label: Reading GH/s
questions.prompt: A rig runs at 3 GH/s. How many guesses does it make in one second?

terms.meaning: Billions of guesses (hashes) every second.

questions.hint: G stands for giga, which is a billion.

options.why: Yes. G means a billion, so 3 GH/s is 3 x 1,000,000,000.
That is 3 x 1,000,000, a million. G is a billion, which has nine zeros.
That is 30 billion. The rig makes 3 billion, not 30.

questions.label: A minute of guesses
questions.prompt: A rig makes 3,000,000,000 guesses every second. How many guesses does it make in one minute?
questions.hint: How many seconds are in a minute?

options.why: That is one second of guessing. A minute has 60 seconds.
That is 3,000,000,000 x 6. A minute has 60 seconds, not 6.
That is 3,000,000,000 x 600, ten minutes of guessing.

questions.label: The winner gets
questions.prompt: What does the first computer to find a good guess get?
questions.hint: Read the second card again.

options.text: The right to write the next page, and new coins
options.why: Yes. Writing the page and earning new coins is the prize for winning the race.
CDIC protects bank deposits. It has no part in a mining race.

options.text: Nothing: the race has no prize
options.why: The prize is what makes the race worth running. The winner earns new coins.

options.text: A refund of its power bill
options.why: Nothing refunds the power. The electricity is a cost the miner carries.

questions.label: Power for a month
questions.prompt: A made-up rig uses power that costs $0.35 an hour. It runs 24 hours a day for 30 days. What does the power cost?
questions.hint: Find the hours first, then multiply by the cost of an hour.
questions.why: Power cost is the cost of one hour times the hours the rig runs.
questions.miss: Count the hours in the whole month first. Then multiply by the cost of one hour.

traps.why: That is the cost of one day, $8.40. The rig runs for 30 days.

questions.label: Coins versus power
questions.prompt: The rig's month of power cost $252.00. The coins it won that month were worth $180.00 (made up). How many dollars more did the power cost than the coins were worth?
questions.hint: Subtract the smaller amount from the larger one.
questions.why: Mining only pays when the coins are worth more than the power and the machines cost. Here they were worth less.
questions.miss: Take the value of the coins away from the power bill.

traps.why: That adds the two amounts. The question asks how much larger one is than the other, so subtract.

questions.label: Biggest power bill
questions.prompt: Tap the rig whose month of power cost the most.

figure.title: A month of power for three made-up rigs

questions.hint: Read the dollar value above each bar.
questions.why: Rig C cost $315.00, the most of the three.
questions.miss: That bar is not the tallest. The tallest bar costs the most.

questions.label: One edited copy
questions.prompt: Seven keepers each hold a copy of a line. One keeper edits their copy. How many copies still match the original line?
questions.hint: Only one copy was edited.

options.why: Only one copy changed. The other six still match.
One copy was edited, so it no longer matches. Six still do.
No copy other than the edited one changed, so more than three still match.
Yes. One copy was changed, so six of the seven still agree and the edit is outvoted.

levels.title: A second engine
learn: Say how proof of stake picks the writer and what it trades off.
Work out a keeper's chance from the coins locked.

cards.text: The second engine is proof of stake. Keepers do not race. Each locks up some of their own coins as a deposit, called a stake. The more coins a keeper locks, the better the odds of being picked to write the next page. Work is a race. Stake is a lottery.
This example has five keepers. A keeper's chance is their coins divided by all the coins locked. Farah: 50 / 100 = 50%. Hugo locked nothing, so his chance is 0%.

Each engine gives something and costs something. Proof of work uses lots of electricity but is hard to cheat. Proof of stake uses far less energy. Its catch is that the biggest holders get picked most.

figure.title: Two engines side by side
rows: Computers race to guess a number
Lots of electricity; hard to cheat
Keepers lock coins; more coins, more tickets
Far less energy; biggest holders picked most

cards.text: Under proof of stake, a keeper who cheats can lose part of their deposit. On Sept 15, 2022, Ethereum switched from proof of work to proof of stake, a change called the Merge. After it, the coin no longer ran a guessing race.

There are more engines. In delegated proof of stake, users vote for a few trusted updaters. In proof of authority, only approved parties can write pages. One coin for payments between banks uses its own system, where trusted validators agree and nobody mines.

questions.label: The race engine
questions.prompt: Computers race to guess a number, and the winner writes the next page. Which engine is this?
questions.hint: The word "race" is a clue.

options.why: In that engine only approved parties write pages. There is no race.
In that engine users vote for a few trusted updaters. There is no race.
Proof of stake picks by a lottery of locked coins, with no race.
Yes. A race to guess a number is proof of work.

questions.label: The deposit engine
questions.prompt: Keepers lock coins as a deposit, and more coins locked means better odds. Which engine is this?
questions.hint: Look back at the card that compares the two engines.

options.why: That engine lets only approved parties write. Coins are not the tickets.
Users vote in that engine. The plain version picks by coins locked.
Yes. The locked coins are the stake, and they are the tickets in the lottery.
Proof of work is a guessing race. It does not use a deposit.

questions.label: Voting engine
questions.prompt: Users vote for a few trusted updaters who write the pages. Which engine is this?
questions.hint: Look for the word "vote".

options.why: There is no race here. Users vote instead.
Plain proof of stake picks by coins locked. Here users vote for updaters.
In that engine, approved parties write. Users do not vote.
Yes. The users vote, and the updaters they pick write the pages.

questions.label: Chance of being picked
questions.prompt: Three keepers lock 25, 15 and 10 coins. What is the chance, in percent, that the keeper who locked 15 coins is picked?
questions.hint: Add up all the coins first.
questions.why: A keeper's chance is their coins divided by all the coins locked.
questions.miss: Find the total coins locked. Then divide this keeper's coins by that total.

traps.why: That is the number of coins, not a share. Divide by the 50 coins in all.

questions.label: A smaller share
questions.prompt: Three keepers lock 30, 20 and 10 coins. What is the chance, in percent, that the keeper with 10 coins is picked? Round to the nearest whole percent.
questions.hint: Add up all the coins first, then divide.
questions.why: The chance is 10 out of all the coins locked, written as a percent.
questions.miss: Find the total locked first. Then divide this keeper's 10 coins by it and round.

traps.why: That is the coins, not a share. The share is 10 out of 60.

questions.label: Twice as likely
questions.prompt: The bars show each keeper's share of all the coins locked. Tap the keeper who is picked twice as often as Ben.
questions.hint: Ben holds 20%. Find the bar with double that.
questions.why: Ben has 20% of the coins, and Ana has 40%. Twice the coins means twice the chance.
questions.miss: That bar is not double Ben's. Double 20% is a bar twice as tall as his.

questions.label: The stake catch
questions.prompt: What is the catch with proof of stake, as the class puts it?
questions.hint: Look back at the card that compares the two engines.

options.text: The biggest holders get picked most
options.why: Yes. More coins locked means more tickets, so large holders are picked most often.
The cards do not say that about either engine. That is not the catch.

options.text: You need a bank to join
options.why: No bank is needed. The catch is who gets picked.

options.text: It uses far more electricity than a race
options.why: It is the other way round. Proof of stake uses far less energy.

questions.label: The Merge
questions.prompt: What did Ethereum switch to at the Merge, on Sept 15, 2022?
questions.hint: The Merge made the coin use far less electricity.

options.text: From proof of work to proof of stake
options.why: Yes. The coin dropped the guessing race and began picking writers by locked coins.

options.text: From proof of stake to proof of work
options.why: That is backwards. The switch moved away from the race.

options.text: From proof of work to proof of authority
options.why: The new engine was proof of stake, where locked coins are the tickets.
It kept running. Only the engine changed.

questions.label: Cheating a stake
questions.prompt: Under proof of stake, what can happen to a keeper who cheats?
questions.hint: The deposit is called a stake for a reason.

options.text: They can lose part of their deposit
options.why: Yes. The deposit is at risk, which gives keepers a reason to follow the rules.
Electricity is the main cost of proof of work. A stake is a deposit of coins.
Cheating is not rewarded. The deposit is what they stand to lose.
No bank is in charge of a cryptocurrency. The system itself can take part of the deposit.

levels.title: Kinds of coin
learn: Sort coins into money and platform or service.
Match what someone needs to the kind of coin that does the job.

cards.text: Coins do different jobs, so the class sorts them into two groups. A money coin is one you send or hold. A platform or service coin is one that other things are built on, or one that feeds them data.

Money coins come in three jobs. Bitcoin is called digital gold: companies hold it as an investment, and no more than 21,000,000 will ever exist. A cousin of it is built for faster, cheaper payments. A third moves money between banks across borders in seconds, with fewer fees.

Ethereum is a platform. On it, a smart contract is a deal that runs by itself. DeFi is lending with no bank. An NFT is a one-of-a-kind digital item. Since Sept 15, 2022, Ethereum is secured by proof of stake.

A blockchain has no window. A smart contract that says "pay out if it rains on festival day" cannot see the weather. An oracle feeds real-world data, such as weather or prices, to smart contracts. The oracle coin is not its own blockchain.

figure.title: Weather to payout
rows: The smart contract on Ethereum reads it

cards.text: Here are the jobs, the groups and how each is secured. Digital gold and the faster-payments coin use proof of work. The bank-payments coin has its own system. The oracle is not its own blockchain.

questions.label: Supplier abroad
questions.prompt: Ines runs a shop and wants to pay a supplier in another country in seconds, with fewer fees. Which job fits?
questions.hint: Look back at the table of jobs.

options.why: Yes. That coin is built to move money between banks across borders quickly.
That job builds deals and digital items. It is not the cross-border payments job.

options.text: Digital gold held as an investment
options.why: Digital gold is held, not built for quick payments to suppliers.
An oracle feeds data to contracts. It does not move a payment.

questions.label: Rain cover
questions.prompt: Jory sells festival rain cover as a smart contract. It pays out if it rains. What brings the rain data to the contract?
questions.hint: A blockchain has no window.

options.why: Yes. An oracle feeds real-world data, such as weather, to smart contracts.
Digital gold is held as an investment. It does not carry data.
That coin is built for quick, cheap payments. It does not bring in weather.
Proof of work is an engine that writes pages. It does not fetch the weather.

questions.label: Digital art
questions.prompt: Mara wants to sell one-of-a-kind digital art with a smart contract. Which kind of coin is a platform for that?
questions.hint: Which job lists NFTs?

options.why: Digital gold is held as an investment. It is not a platform for art.
Yes. Ethereum is a platform for smart contracts and NFTs, which are one-of-a-kind digital items.
An oracle feeds data. The art and the contract live on a platform.

options.text: A coin for payments between banks
options.why: That coin moves money. It is not a platform for contracts and NFTs.

questions.label: Savings coin
questions.prompt: A coin can never pass 21,000,000 and is meant to be held as savings. Which job is that?
questions.hint: Which coin has the 21,000,000 cap?

options.why: That job is about paying quickly. The 21,000,000 cap belongs to digital gold.
Yes. The first cryptocurrency is capped at 21,000,000 and is held as digital gold.
An oracle feeds data. It is not a coin held for a cap.
That job is moving money between banks, not a capped coin held as savings.

questions.label: Counter payments
questions.prompt: Lena wants a coin built for fast, cheap small payments at her counter. Which job fits?
questions.hint: Look back at the table of jobs.

options.why: Yes. That coin is a cousin of digital gold, built for quick, low-cost payments.
An oracle brings in data. It does not take payments.
Digital gold is held as an investment, not built for small quick payments.
That job is a platform for building. It is not the small payments job.

questions.label: Which group
questions.prompt: An oracle feeds weather and price data to smart contracts. Which group does the class put it in?
questions.hint: Is it sent or held, or does it serve other things?

options.why: Yes. Things are built on a platform, and an oracle serves smart contracts with data.
Money coins are ones you send or hold. An oracle is not used that way.
The class sorts coins into just two groups, and an oracle is a service.
Digital gold is a money job, not a group, and an oracle is not held as an investment.

questions.label: Why an oracle
questions.prompt: Why does a rain-cover smart contract need an oracle?
questions.hint: Look at the "no window" card.

options.why: Mining is the proof-of-work race. An oracle feeds data in.

options.text: A blockchain cannot see the weather by itself
options.why: Yes. The chain has no window, so something has to bring the real-world data in.

options.text: The rain changes faster than blocks
options.why: Speed is not the issue. The contract has no way to see weather at all.

options.text: Smart contracts cannot hold any money
options.why: The problem is the data, not the money. The contract cannot see outside the chain.

questions.label: Not its own chain
questions.prompt: Which kind of coin is not its own blockchain?
questions.hint: Check the last column of the table.

options.why: The first cryptocurrency has its own blockchain.

options.text: The oracle that feeds data to contracts
options.why: Yes. It serves smart contracts on other blockchains.
Ethereum is a blockchain, and it runs on proof of stake.
It runs its own blockchain, with proof of work.

questions.label: Secured by stake
questions.prompt: Look at the table. Which job is secured by proof of stake since 2022?
questions.hint: Read down the "Secured by" column.

options.why: Yes. That row is Ethereum, which switched on Sept 15, 2022.
That job uses proof of work.
Digital gold is secured by proof of work.
Those payments use trusted validators agreeing, with no mining or stake.

levels.title: Fixed supply, growing supply
learn: Compare a coin with a cap against money that can be created.
Work out what prices do at a steady yearly rate.

cards.text: Here are two supply rules. Bitcoin has a fixed supply: there will never be more than 21,000,000. The Bank of Canada can create more Canadian dollars. Supply means how much of something exists.

Inflation is when prices rise and a dollar buys less. The class names its risk: it wrecks savings. Take a $1.00 candy bar with prices rising 10% a year. Each year, multiply the last price by 1.10, as in the Inflation unit. Round each price to the cent.

figure.title: A $1.00 candy bar at 10% a year

cards.text: Look at the steps. $1.10 x 1.10 = $1.21. Then $1.21 x 1.10 = $1.331, shown as $1.33. Then $1.331 x 1.10 = $1.4641, shown as $1.46. A 10% rise is not 10 cents more each year, because each rise is on the new price.
Deflation is the opposite: prices fall, and people wait to buy because it may be cheaper later. The class names its risk: shops empty and jobs go. Its example is the Great Depression of the 1930s.

A cap limits how many coins can exist. It does not set what one coin costs. A coin with a cap and money that can be created are two different supply rules. The next level looks at why the price of a coin can still swing.

questions.label: Which can grow
questions.prompt: Which supply can its maker make larger?
questions.hint: One of them has a cap.

options.text: Both, with no limit on either
options.why: Bitcoin has a cap. Only the dollar's supply can be made larger.
Dollars can be created by the central bank. Bitcoin cannot pass its cap.

options.text: Canadian dollars, which the Bank of Canada can create
options.why: Yes. The class points out that the Bank of Canada can create more dollars.
Bitcoin has a fixed supply. There will never be more than 21,000,000.

questions.label: Name the word
questions.prompt: Prices fall, and people wait to buy because it may be cheaper later. What is this called?
questions.hint: Which word means prices go down?

options.why: A fixed supply is a cap on how many coins exist. It is not about prices falling.
Inflation is prices rising, not falling.
Yes. Falling prices are deflation, and waiting to buy is part of the risk.
A stake is a deposit of coins in proof of stake.

questions.label: Snack in two years
questions.prompt: A snack costs $5.00 now. Prices rise 10% a year in this example. What will it cost in two years? Round to the cent.
questions.hint: Multiply by 1.10, and then multiply by 1.10 again.
questions.why: Each year's rise is on the new price, so you multiply by 1.10 twice.
questions.miss: The second rise is on the new price, not the old one. Multiply twice by 1.10.

traps.why: That adds $0.50 twice. The second rise is 10% of $5.50, which is more than $0.50.

questions.label: Item in three years
questions.prompt: An item costs $20.00 now. Prices rise 10% a year in this example. What will it cost in three years? Round to the cent.
questions.hint: Multiply by 1.10 three times.
questions.why: Three years of a 10% rise is three multiplications by 1.10.
questions.miss: Multiply by 1.10 once for each year, starting from $20.00.

traps.why: That adds $2.00 three times. Each year's rise is on a bigger price.

questions.label: Total rise
questions.prompt: The candy bar went from $1.00 to $1.46 in four years. What was the total rise, in percent?
questions.hint: Find the change in dollars, then divide by the old price.
questions.why: Percent change is the change divided by the old price.
questions.miss: Subtract the old price from the new one. Then divide by the old price.

traps.why: That adds 10% four times. Each rise is on a bigger price, so the total is more than 40%.

questions.label: Past $1.30
questions.prompt: Tap the first year when the candy bar costs more than $1.30.

figure.title: A $1.00 candy bar at 10% a year

questions.hint: Read the price on each bar from the left.
questions.why: Year 3 is $1.33, the first price above $1.30. Year 2 is $1.21.
questions.miss: That bar is not above $1.30 yet, or it is not the first. Check the price on each bar from Year 0.

questions.label: Danger of deflation
questions.prompt: What does the class warn can happen when prices keep falling?
questions.hint: Think about what a buyer does if prices fall.

options.text: Savings are wrecked because a dollar buys less
options.why: That is the risk of inflation. In deflation a dollar buys more.
The supply of coins is a different question from falling prices.
Yes. People wait to buy, so shops sell less and jobs can go.
People wait to buy, not rush. That waiting is what hurts shops.

questions.label: The same basket
questions.prompt: A basket costs $100.00 today. Prices rise 10% a year. After two years, how many more dollars do you need to buy the same basket? Round to the cent.
questions.hint: Find the price after two years, then subtract $100.00.
questions.why: The same shopping costs more, so each dollar buys less.
questions.miss: First find the basket price after two years with two multiplications. Then subtract $100.00.

traps.why: That adds 10% of $100.00 twice. The second rise is on $110.00.

questions.label: What a cap fixes
questions.prompt: A friend says: "The coin has a cap of 21,000,000, so it will always cost more next year." What does the cap fix?
questions.hint: A cap is a limit on a count.

options.text: How fast new pages are written
options.why: The cap is about the number of coins, not the speed of pages.

options.text: How many people can own a coin
options.why: Any number of people can hold coins. The cap limits the total coins.
The cap does not set a price. The price is a separate question.

options.text: How many coins can ever exist
options.why: Yes. A cap limits the number of coins. It does not set the price of one.

levels.title: Risk, swings and scams
learn: Work out the percent change on a holding that rises and falls.
Spot the warning signs of a scam and know who to ask.

cards.text: A price swing is how far a price moves up and down. Coin prices can swing a long way. The class gives one dated price: on Dec 5, 2024, the first cryptocurrency first reached $100,000. A coin that rises can fall fast. Nothing here says what any price is today.

Percent change is the change divided by the start. Priya holds $400 of a coin made up for this lesson. It rises 40% to $560, then falls 25% to $420. She is up 5% on $400. A big fall is hard to undo: after a 50% fall, a holding must rise 100% to get back.

A rise tells you nothing for sure about next month. If a friend says, "It went up all year, get in now," that is a feeling, not a reason. Hype pushes people to act fast. The class calls these emotional factors.

Two more risks. There is no CDIC, the insurer of bank deposits: crypto is not a bank deposit, so if a platform fails, nobody guarantees it. There is no undo: send to the wrong address and it is usually gone, because no one in the middle can reverse it.

One warning sign is being paid to bring in friends. The money comes from new members, so the last ones in lose. Check first with the Alberta Securities Commission. Report a scam to the Canadian Anti-Fraud Centre.
Whatever the money, three plain questions help: who keeps the record, who can make more of it, and who can undo a mistake.

questions.label: After the rise
questions.prompt: Priya holds $400 of a made-up coin. It rises 40% this month. What is her holding worth now?
questions.hint: A 40% rise means multiply by 1.40.
questions.why: A 40% rise is the start times 1.40.
questions.miss: Add 40% of $400 to $400, or multiply by 1.40.

traps.why: That is the rise alone, 40% of $400. Her holding is the start plus the rise.

questions.label: After the fall
questions.prompt: Priya's holding is worth $560.00. It then falls 25%. What is it worth now?
questions.hint: A 25% fall means multiply by 0.75.
questions.why: A 25% fall leaves 75% of the value.
questions.miss: Take 25% off $560.00. What is left is 75% of it.

traps.why: That is the size of the fall, 25% of $560. The question asks what is left.

questions.label: Since the start
questions.prompt: Priya started with $400.00 and ended with $420.00. What was her change since the start, in percent?
questions.hint: Change divided by the start.
questions.why: Percent change is the change divided by the start.
questions.miss: Use the start, $400.00, as the base. Not the $560.00.

traps.why: That subtracts 25 from 40. The fall of 25% was on $560, a bigger amount than $400.

questions.label: Getting back
questions.prompt: A $1,000.00 holding falls 50%, to $500.00. What percent rise does it need to get back to $1,000.00?
questions.hint: Divide the gain needed by what is left.
questions.why: The rise is measured on the smaller $500.00, so it must be larger than the fall.
questions.miss: The gain needed is measured against what is left, $500.00.

traps.why: A rise of 50% on $500.00 is only $250.00. It takes $500.00 to get back.

questions.label: A smaller fall
questions.prompt: A $500.00 holding falls 20%, to $400.00. What percent rise does it need to get back to $500.00?
questions.hint: Divide the gain needed by what is left.
questions.why: The rise is measured on the smaller $400.00, so it must be larger than the fall.
questions.miss: The gain needed is measured against the $400.00 that is left.

traps.why: 20% of $400.00 is only $80.00. It takes $100.00 to get back.

questions.label: After a 30% rise
questions.prompt: A coin rose 30% this month. What does that tell you about next month?
questions.hint: Look back at the card about a rise.

options.why: Yes. Past rises say nothing for sure about the next move.
Crypto is not covered by CDIC, so nobody guarantees it.
A rise does not make a coin safe. Prices can still swing.
A rise does not promise another rise. Prices can fall fast.

questions.label: The warning sign
questions.prompt: "Pay $150 to join, then get $30 for every friend you sign up." Which warning sign does this offer show?
questions.hint: Where does the money come from?

options.why: A cap is a supply rule. The offer pays for recruiting friends.
Price swings are a risk of coins. This offer is about paying people to recruit.

options.text: Being paid for bringing in friends
options.why: Yes. The money comes from new members joining, so the last ones in lose.
Engines are how pages are written. They have nothing to do with this offer.

questions.label: Wrong address
questions.prompt: You send coins to the wrong address. What usually happens?
questions.hint: Who stands in the middle of a bank transfer, and who does not here?

options.why: No bank sits in the middle of a crypto send, so no bank can undo it.

options.text: It is usually gone for good
options.why: Yes. There is no bank in the middle to undo a send.
Crypto is not covered by CDIC.

options.text: A regulator returns it within a month
options.why: The class does not describe any such refund. A mistaken send is usually gone.

questions.label: Who to ask
questions.prompt: Dee thinks an offer is a scam and wants to report it. Which agency takes the report?
questions.hint: One agency is for checking, one is for reporting.

options.why: Yes. You report to the Canadian Anti-Fraud Centre.
CDIC protects bank deposits. It does not take scam reports.

options.text: The platform that made the offer
options.why: The offer is the problem. Report it to the agency instead.
That is where you check first whether something is allowed in Alberta.

questions.label: Highest value
questions.prompt: Tap the point where Priya's holding was worth the most.
questions.hint: Read the dollar value at each point.
questions.why: After the rise it was worth $560.00, the most of the three.
questions.miss: That is not the highest point on the line. Compare the three values.

sections.title: Accounting Prep
sections.blurb: Keep the books of one small business, from its first balance sheet to its first month.

units.title: The books and the equation
units.blurb: Why a business keeps books, what it owns and owes, and its first balance sheet.

levels.title: Why businesses keep books
learn: Say why a business writes everything down.
Match each reader of a business statement to the question it answers.

cards.text: A business takes in money and pays money out all week. If nobody writes it down, nobody can say how the month went. Keeping the books means writing down every money event in an orderly way, so the facts are there when someone asks.

image.alt: A blank notebook on a workbench beside tools and gold discs

cards.text: Written books meet three needs. Is the business making money? What does it own, and what does it owe? Can the owner show the facts to someone else? Memory cannot do the third, and it is poor at the first two.

image.alt: Three blank folders on a shelf with a magnifying glass

cards.text: The books are summed up in financial statements: reports that sum up a business in numbers. Different people read them for different reasons. Here are five made-up readers, with the one question each of them asks.

figure.title: Five readers, one question each
rows: Did my shop earn more than it spent in June?
What does it own, and what does it already owe?
Does the shop own enough to cover what it owes me?
What did the business earn in June after its costs?
What is left for the owner after the debts?

cards.text: This section uses two statements. A balance sheet shows what a business owns and owes on one date, and the owner's equity. An income statement shows revenue (money earned) and expenses (costs) over a period such as a month, and ends in net income or a net loss.

image.alt: Two blank clipboards with empty sheets on a workbench

cards.text: Meet the company this section follows: Kiran's Bike Repair. Kiran repairs and tunes bikes in a small rented shop in town. Kiran is the only owner, and the shop sells repair work, not goods. The shop and its numbers are made up, and every lesson in this section uses them.

image.alt: A small bike repair shop with a blank sign and a bike on a stand

levels.title: Assets, liabilities and owner's equity
learn: Sort what a business has into assets, liabilities and owner's equity.
Use the accounting equation to find a missing figure.

cards.text: You have already sorted a person's things into what they own and what they owe. A business is sorted the same way. An asset is something of value the business owns. A liability is a debt: something the business owes to someone else.

image.alt: A toolbox on the left and a stack of gold discs on the right of a bench

cards.text: On June 1, Kiran's shop has cash, supplies, tools and equipment. It owns them, so they are assets. It owes a bank loan, and it owes a supplier for supplies already received (accounts payable). Those are liabilities.

Add the assets: $7,400. Add the liabilities: $2,400. What is left for Kiran is $5,000. That is owner's equity: the owner's share of the business, what is left of the assets after the liabilities. It is also called capital. It works like net worth.

image.alt: A level balance scale with gold discs on one tray and a toolbox on the other

cards.text: The accounting equation says Assets = Liabilities + Owner's Equity. For Kiran on June 1: $7,400 = $2,400 + $5,000. The two sides are equal. A transaction is an event that changes the business in dollars, and the equation stays true after every one.

image.alt: A level seesaw with a wheel and toolbox on one side and a pump and folder on the other

cards.text: Here are the totals after Kiran's first four June transactions. "Equity" in the table means owner's equity. Watch the two sides: assets on the left, liabilities plus equity on the right.

Rent paid: assets down, equity down, because rent is a cost of running the shop. Supplies on account: assets up, liabilities up. Repairs for cash: assets up, equity up. Repairs on account: assets up (a customer owes Kiran), equity up. Each time both sides move by the same amount.

image.alt: Gold discs moving between two piles on a bench beside a blank notepad

levels.title: The opening balance sheet
learn: Build the opening balance sheet of Kiran's Bike Repair.
Read it: the biggest asset, what is owed and the owner's share.

cards.text: A balance sheet starts with three title lines: the business name, the words Balance Sheet, and As at plus a date. Under them come three blocks in order: assets, liabilities, then owner's equity. An income statement's date line is different. It says For the Month Ended.

image.alt: A blank sheet on a corkboard with three empty strips at the top

cards.text: Build Kiran's opening sheet. First the assets: what the shop owns on June 1. List each one, then add them. The total is $7,400.

figure.title: Kiran's Bike Repair, Balance Sheet, As at June 1

cards.text: Next the liabilities: what the shop owes. Accounts payable is $400 and the bank loan is $2,000. Their total is $2,400.

figure.title: Kiran's Bike Repair, Balance Sheet, As at June 1

cards.text: Last, the owner's share: Kiran, Capital is $5,000. Add the liabilities and the capital: $7,400. The two totals agree, as they must, because Assets = Liabilities + Owner's Equity.

figure.title: Kiran's Bike Repair, Balance Sheet, As at June 1

cards.text: Read the sheet. The biggest asset is Cash, at $3,000. The shop owes $2,400 in all. The owner's share is $5,000, more than the shop owes. If the two totals ever differ, something on the sheet is wrong.

image.alt: A bench with gold discs, a toolbox, a folder and a wheel in a neat row

cards.text: "As at June 1" means these numbers are for that one day, like a photo. After rent is paid on Jun 2, cash and equity change, so Jun 2 needs a new sheet. Your own Net Worth building is a personal version: it shows what you own minus what you owe.

image.alt: A camera on a tripod facing a tidy repair bench with a blank photo print

units.title: Rules and accounts
units.blurb: Shared rules for the books, revenue and expenses, and the chart of accounts.

levels.title: Why shared rules exist
learn: Say what shared rules for the books are for.
Tell what goes wrong in the statements when a business does not follow them.

cards.text: Picture two bike shops that keep their books in their own way. One writes its tools down at what it paid. The other writes the same tools at what it hopes to sell them for. A reader cannot compare them, and cannot trust the numbers that use a hoped-for price.

image.alt: Two repair benches with the same wheel set up in two different ways

cards.text: Businesses solve this with shared rules for keeping books. They are called GAAP: generally accepted accounting principles. The rules are there for two reasons: so a statement can be trusted, and so two businesses can be compared.

image.alt: A tidy stack of identical blank ledgers with a ruler on top

cards.text: To see what the rules protect, look at Kiran's June. Revenue is money earned from the shop's work, and expenses are the costs of running it. Net income is revenue minus expenses. When expenses are larger, it is a net loss.
Now break a rule. Kiran pays a $50 grocery bill for home and lists it as a shop expense. It is not a cost of the shop. June's expenses look $50 too high, so net income looks $50 too low.

image.alt: Household items on a kitchen table beside a repair bench with a blank notebook

cards.text: Break another. Kiran's tools cost $1,800, but Kiran writes them at $2,500, a price Kiran hopes to sell them for. The balance sheet now shows assets that are too high, and an owner's share that is too high with them. A hoped-for price is a guess. The books keep the tools at what was paid.

image.alt: A wrench on a leaning tower of gold discs with a tape measure

cards.text: Two more. Two shops do the same work, but one counts a $200 bike stand as an asset and the other counts it as a cost of June. Their net incomes differ for no real reason. A shop that changes how it counts each month hides what is real.

figure.title: What can go wrong without shared rules
rows: A personal bill is counted as a shop cost
Expenses too high, net income too low
A tool is written at a hoped-for value
Assets too high, owner's equity too high
Two shops count the same thing two ways
A shop changes its way of counting
Real changes cannot be told from counting changes

questions.label: What GAAP is for
questions.prompt: What are shared rules for keeping books, called GAAP, for?

terms.meaning: Generally accepted accounting principles: the shared rules for keeping books, so that statements can be trusted and compared.

questions.hint: Think of the two reasons.

options.text: So every business shows the same net income
options.why: Businesses earn different amounts. The rules make the counting fair, not the results equal.

options.text: So statements can be trusted and compared
options.why: Yes. Those are the two reasons the second card gives.

options.text: So an owner can pick the best-looking numbers
options.why: The rules do the opposite. They stop each owner from counting in a way that flatters the business.

options.text: So a business knows what to sell
options.why: The rules are about how to keep the books, not what a business sells.

questions.label: A grocery bill
questions.prompt: Kiran lists a $50 grocery bill for home as a shop expense. What does this do to June?

terms.meaning: A cost of running the business. It lowers the owner's equity.

questions.hint: Is a home grocery bill a cost of the shop?

options.text: Expenses too low, net income too high
options.why: It is the other way. An extra expense makes net income smaller.
An expense lowers net income. It does not make assets too high.

options.text: Nothing, because it is Kiran's money
options.why: Kiran's personal money is not the shop's. Counting it as a shop cost misstates the shop.

options.text: Expenses too high, net income too low
options.why: Yes. The bill is not a cost of the shop, so counting it as one lowers net income.

questions.label: Net income shown
questions.prompt: Kiran's June revenue was $750 and expenses were $680. The $50 grocery bill is wrongly counted as a shop expense. What net income would June show?
questions.hint: Add the bill to the expenses first.
questions.why: The wrong expense makes expenses larger, so net income is smaller.

traps.why: That is the true net income, before the grocery bill is wrongly counted.
That adds the bill to net income. An extra expense takes net income down.

questions.miss: Add the bill to the expenses, then take the new expenses off the revenue.

questions.label: A big wrong bill
questions.prompt: Suppose Kiran wrongly counted a $300 personal bill as a shop expense in June. What would the statement show?

terms.meaning: Revenue minus expenses, when revenue is larger. When expenses are larger, it is a net loss.

questions.hint: Net income minus the wrong bill.

options.why: Yes. Expenses would be $980 against revenue of $750, so expenses are larger and it is a net loss.
An extra expense lowers net income. It does not raise it.
That is the true figure. The wrong expense changes it.
The bill is taken off the true net income of $70, not off zero.

questions.label: A hoped-for value
questions.prompt: Kiran writes the tools at $2,500 instead of the $1,800 paid, because that is the hoped-for selling price. What is wrong on the balance sheet?
questions.hint: Compare the written value with the real one.

options.why: Nothing owed has changed. Only the tools' value was written up.
The tools were written up, not down.
Yes. The tools are written above what is real, so assets and the owner's share are too high.

options.text: Nothing, because the tools are Kiran's
options.why: The sheet must show a value others can trust, not a hope.

questions.label: Assets shown
questions.prompt: On June 1 the assets total $7,400. If the tools were written at $2,500 instead of $1,800, what total assets would the sheet show?
questions.hint: Find how much more the tools are written at.
questions.why: Only the tools change. The other assets stay the same.

traps.why: That is the true total. The written-up tools raise it.

questions.miss: Find the difference for the tools alone, then add it to the assets.

questions.label: Same stand, two ways
questions.prompt: Two shops do the same work. Shop A counts a $200 bike stand as an asset. Shop B counts the same stand as a June expense. What is true?
questions.hint: An expense lowers net income.

options.text: Their net incomes are the same
options.why: Shop B has $200 more in expenses, so its net income is lower.

options.text: Shop A's net income is $200 lower
options.why: It is Shop B, with the extra expense, whose net income is lower.

options.text: A reader can compare them fairly
options.why: The two count in different ways, so the comparison is not fair.

options.text: Their net incomes differ by $200 for the same work
options.why: Yes. Shop B's extra expense makes its net income $200 lower, though nothing real differs.

questions.label: Changing the count
questions.prompt: A shop counts one way in May and another way in June. June looks much better. What is the problem?
questions.hint: Can a reader compare May and June?

options.why: The equation holds however things are counted. The problem is that the numbers stop being comparable.

options.text: A reader cannot tell a real change from a counting change
options.why: Yes. Shared, steady rules let a reader trust that a change is real.
Nothing says revenue falls. The problem is trust.

options.text: The statements take longer to read
options.why: Reading time is not the problem. Trust is.

questions.label: Needs a rule
questions.prompt: Which case is the kind of problem shared rules are there to fix?
questions.hint: Look for a difference in counting, not in the business.

options.text: One shop earns more revenue than another
options.why: Shops differ in what they earn. That is real, not a counting problem.

options.text: A shop pays its rent on the second of the month
options.why: Paying rent is a normal transaction.

options.text: Two shops count the same thing in two different ways
options.why: Yes. Shared rules mean the same thing is counted the same way.

options.text: A shop has a bank loan
options.why: Many shops have loans. That is a real fact the books should show.

levels.title: Revenue and expense accounts
learn: Tell revenue, expenses and drawings apart.
Work out net income for June and sort all ten June transactions.

cards.text: Revenue is money the business earns from its work. It raises the owner's equity. Kiran's revenue account is Repair Revenue. In June it is $750: $450 for repairs paid in cash and $300 for a bike club, on account. Kiran counts the $300 on Jun 8, when the work was done.

image.alt: A tuned bike on a stand with gold discs and a blank receipt pad

cards.text: An expense is a cost of running the business. It lowers the owner's equity. In June Kiran has two: rent, $600, and advertising, $80. Together they are $680.

image.alt: A cash box of gold discs and a bag of tools on a shop shelf

cards.text: Net income is revenue minus expenses: $750 - $680 = $70. It is the last line of the income statement. If expenses were larger, the last line would be a net loss.

figure.title: Kiran's Bike Repair, Income Statement, For the Month Ended June 30

cards.text: On Jun 20 Kiran took $250 in cash out for personal use. That is drawings. It lowers the owner's equity, but it is not an expense: it is the owner taking out their own share, not a cost of running the shop. It stays off the income statement.

image.alt: An empty signpost pointing from a shop bench toward a house with gold discs

cards.text: Two more that are not expenses. On Jun 25 Kiran paid $100 of the bank loan (principal only). On Jun 28 Kiran bought a $120 tool for cash. The loan payment lowers cash and the loan by the same amount. The tool lowers cash and raises tools by the same amount. Neither lowers owner's equity.

image.alt: A new tool beside a cash box and a short paper chain on a hook

cards.text: A test for any transaction. Did the shop earn money from its work? Revenue. Did it use money on a cost of running the shop? Expense. Otherwise it is neither: it moves assets and debts around, or it is drawings, or it is a customer paying what was already counted as revenue.

image.alt: Three blank baskets holding gold discs, tools and papers on a bench

levels.title: Building a chart of accounts
learn: Say what an account is and name the five kinds.
Read Kiran's chart of accounts and decide where a new account belongs.

cards.text: An account is one page of the books that tracks one thing, such as Cash or Bank Loan. A business keeps a separate account for each thing it needs to track. Kiran's shop uses 13. The numbered list of all of them is the chart of accounts.

image.alt: An open blank folder with one empty page beside an index card box

cards.text: Every account is one of five kinds: asset, liability, owner's equity, revenue or expense. In this chart each kind has its own hundred. The first digit of an account's number tells you its kind.
Here is the first part of Kiran's chart: the assets and the liabilities. Notice the gaps between the numbers.
The second part: owner's equity, revenue and expenses. Kiran, Drawings is in the 300s because it takes from the owner's equity.

The order follows the statements. Assets, liabilities and owner's equity come first, the order of the balance sheet. Revenue and expenses come after, the order of the income statement. So a number also tells you where the account is reported.

image.alt: Two blank clipboards, the first with three empty bands and the second with two

cards.text: Where does a new account go? Decide its kind first. A delivery bike Kiran buys would be an asset, so it goes in the 100s. A phone bill would be an expense, so it goes in the 500s. The kind picks the hundred, and an unused number in that hundred does the rest.

units.title: Debits and credits
units.blurb: Two sides to every entry, the opening entry, and the ledger.

levels.title: Debits and credits
learn: You will say which account is debited and which is credited.
You will see why every entry keeps the equation true.

cards.text: Every account has two sides. The left side is the debit side. The right side is the credit side. These are only names for the sides: a debit is not good, a credit is not bad, and neither word means more by itself.

Each kind of account grows on one side, its normal side. The other side makes it smaller. Assets, expenses and drawings grow on the debit side. Liabilities, capital and revenue grow on the credit side. Drawings have an account of their own.

Assets sit on the left of the equation and grow on the debit side. Liabilities and capital sit on the right and grow on the credit side. Revenue raises owner's equity, so it grows on the credit side. Expenses and drawings lower it, so they grow on the debit side.

image.alt: A bike wheel in a stand beside a level balance scale with two matching trays

cards.text: Every transaction is recorded twice. This is double entry. The debits and the credits of one transaction always have the same total, so the two sides of the accounting equation change by the same amount and the equation stays true.

image.alt: Two matching stacks of gold discs at either end of a blank sign on a counter

cards.text: Jun 2: Kiran paid the month's rent in cash. Rent Expense grows, and expenses grow on the debit side, so it is debited $600. Cash, an asset, shrinks on the credit side, so Cash is credited $600. Debits $600, credits $600.
Jun 5: Kiran repaired bikes for cash. Cash grows, so it is debited $450. Repair Revenue grows, and revenue grows on the credit side, so it is credited $450. Debits $450, credits $450.

levels.title: The opening entry
learn: You will write the first journal entry of a business.
You will check that its debits and credits match.

cards.text: The journal is the book where each transaction is first written, in date order, as debits and credits. Each journal entry has a date, the accounts debited first, then the accounts credited, the amounts and a short explanation.

image.alt: An open notebook with blank ruled columns on a bike shop counter

cards.text: In an entry, the debit line comes first. The credit line comes under it. The short explanation goes last, in words.

figure.title: A journal entry
rows: Paid the month’s rent in cash

cards.text: The opening entry is the first entry of a business. It records everything on the opening balance sheet. Here is Kiran's, as at June 1: four assets, two liabilities and the capital.
Every asset is debited, because assets grow on the debit side. Every liability and the capital are credited, because they grow on the credit side. The debits add to $7,400 and so do the credits.

Always check that the total debits equal the total credits. If they do not, an amount is on the wrong side or was copied wrongly. The opening entry also matches the balance sheet: the debits are the assets, and the credits are the liabilities and the capital.

image.alt: Two matching rows of wooden blocks on a bench with a ruler across them

levels.title: Opening the ledger
learn: You will open a ledger account for every account on the chart.
You will carry each opening amount to its own account.

cards.text: The ledger is the book of all the accounts. Each account has its own page, with a debit side, a credit side and a balance. The journal lists transactions in date order. The ledger gathers them by account.

image.alt: A shelf of identical blank-spined books with a small ladder beside it

cards.text: Open one ledger account for every line of the chart of accounts, in chart order. Kiran's chart has 13 accounts, from 101 Cash to 503 Utilities Expense. Each account opens with its number, its name and two empty sides.

image.alt: A cabinet with a row of drawers, each with a blank label holder

cards.text: Posting means copying each debit and credit from the journal into its account in the ledger. Each amount goes on the same side as in the entry. The opening entry debits Cash $3,000, so the Cash account shows $3,000 on the debit side.
The opening entry credits Bank Loan $2,000, so the Bank Loan account shows $2,000 on the credit side. Its balance is on the credit side too, because that is the side where a liability grows.

figure.title: Bank Loan (210), after the opening entry

cards.text: Some accounts start with nothing in them: Accounts Receivable, Kiran, Drawings, Repair Revenue, Rent Expense, Advertising Expense and Utilities Expense. They are opened anyway, with no debits, no credits and a balance of $0, because later transactions will use them.

image.alt: An empty tray with a clean blank card and a pencil on a bench

cards.text: Check your posting: every line of the opening entry must appear once in the ledger, on the same side as in the entry. The debit lines add to $7,400 and so do the credit lines. If they differ, an amount was posted to the wrong account or to the wrong side.

image.alt: A level balance scale with matching piles of gold discs on both pans

questions.hint: Add the debit column.
questions.why: The four assets are the debit-side balances.
questions.miss: Only the Debit column counts. Add each amount in it.

figure.title: Amounts posted from the opening entry

questions.label: Credit side total
questions.prompt: Now add the amounts posted on the credit side. What is the total?
questions.hint: Add the credit column.
questions.why: The two liabilities and the capital add to the same total as the debit side.
questions.miss: Only the Credit column counts. Add each amount in it.

figure.title: Amounts posted from the opening entry

questions.label: Posted wrongly
questions.prompt: Maya posted the Equipment amount of $2,200 to the credit side of the Equipment account. What is wrong?
questions.hint: Which side did the opening entry use for Equipment?

options.text: Nothing: assets can go on either side
options.why: Each amount keeps its entry side. For Equipment that is the debit side.
The amount is right. Only its side is wrong.

options.text: It should be posted to Cash instead
options.why: Each line goes to its own account. Equipment has its own page.

options.text: Equipment was debited, so the amount belongs on the debit side
options.why: An amount is posted on the same side as in the entry. Equipment was debited.

image.alt: An open book with a line down the middle of its blank pages on a workshop bench

units.title: Posting and comparing
units.blurb: Post a month of transactions, compare three kinds of business, and check your work.

levels.title: Posting transactions
learn: You will post a month of transactions and read the balances.
You will see that the equation still holds at the end.

cards.text: To post a transaction, first write its entry in the journal. Then copy each line to its account in the ledger. A debit goes on the debit side of its account. A credit goes on the credit side.

image.alt: Two open books with matching blank ruled grids and a pencil between them

cards.text: Here is every line posted to the Cash account in June. Cash is an asset, so its debits make it grow and its credits make it smaller. The first line is the opening entry of Jun 1.

The balance of an account is the bigger side minus the smaller side, written on the account's normal side. The debits in Cash add to $3,750 and the credits add to $1,350. The balance is $2,400 on the debit side.

image.alt: A ruler and pencil across a blank ruled page with a small weight beside it

cards.text: A balance can be zero. On Jun 8 the bike club owed Kiran $300, so Accounts Receivable was debited. On Jun 15 the club paid, so it was credited the same amount. The debits and credits are equal.
Accounts Payable is a liability, so it grows on the credit side. It opened with $400, grew by $150 on Jun 3, and shrank by $200 when Kiran paid on Jun 10. The balance is $350 on the credit side.

After all ten June transactions the books still balance. Assets are $7,070. Liabilities are $2,250. Owner's equity is $4,820: the capital, plus revenue, less expenses and drawings. $2,250 + $4,820 = $7,070.

image.alt: A level balance scale with a small bike model on one pan and blocks on the other

questions.label: What comes first
questions.prompt: For each transaction, what is done first?

terms.meaning: The book where each transaction is first written, in date order, as debits and credits.
Copying each debit and credit from the journal into its account in the ledger.

questions.hint: The journal comes before the ledger.

options.why: Posting copies lines from the journal. The entry has to be written first.

options.text: Write the entry in the journal
options.why: The journal is where a transaction is first written. Posting to the ledger comes next.

options.text: Work out the balance of each account
options.why: A balance comes from the amounts already posted, so it comes later.

questions.label: Receivable side
questions.prompt: Jun 15: The bike club paid what it owed. In the Accounts Receivable account, which side is the $300 posted to?

terms.meaning: Money customers owe the business for work already done.

questions.hint: Accounts Receivable is an asset. Did it grow or shrink?

options.text: The debit side, because cash came in
options.why: Cash came in, and Cash is debited. Accounts Receivable is the other account: it shrank, so it is credited.

options.text: The credit side, because the asset got smaller
options.why: The club paid what it owed, so the asset shrank. An asset shrinks on the credit side.

options.text: The debit side, because the club still owes it
options.why: The club paid in full on Jun 15, so the amount owed went down. It is credited.

questions.label: Jun 12 debit
questions.prompt: Jun 12: Paid for advertising in cash. Which account receives the debit of $80?
questions.hint: Which account's kind grows on the debit side?

options.why: Cash is the account credited, because it shrank.
Nothing was earned in this transaction.
Kiran paid in cash, so no new debt was created.
The cost of advertising is an expense, and expenses grow on the debit side.

questions.label: Jun 28 credit
questions.prompt: Jun 28: Bought a tool for cash. Which account receives the credit of $120?
questions.hint: Which account got smaller?

options.why: Tools grew, so Tools is debited, not credited.
Equipment is another asset. It was not touched.
Cash went out, and an asset shrinks on the credit side.
Buying a tool does not change what Kiran put in. Capital is not part of this entry.

questions.label: Cash after Jun 2
questions.prompt: Cash starts the month at $3,000. Jun 2: Paid the month’s rent in cash, $600. What is the Cash balance after Jun 2?
questions.hint: Cash is credited, so it shrinks.
questions.why: Rent paid in cash is a credit to Cash, so the balance falls.
questions.miss: Cash is credited here. A credit makes an asset smaller, so subtract.

traps.why: That adds the rent. Paying rent is a credit to Cash, which makes it smaller.

questions.label: Cash after Jun 5
questions.prompt: After Jun 2 the Cash balance is $2,400. Jun 5: Repaired bikes for cash, $450. What is the Cash balance after Jun 5?
questions.hint: Cash is debited, so it grows.
questions.why: Cash received is a debit to Cash, so the balance rises.
questions.miss: This time Cash is debited. A debit makes an asset grow, so add.

traps.why: That subtracts the repair income. Money coming in is a debit to Cash, which makes it grow.

questions.label: Supplies balance
questions.prompt: Supplies start the month at $400. Jun 3: Bought supplies on account, $150. What is the Supplies balance after Jun 3?
questions.hint: Supplies is an asset, and it is debited.
questions.why: Supplies grew, so it is debited and its balance rises by the amount bought.
questions.miss: Supplies is debited, so it grows. Add the amount bought.

questions.label: Payable balance
questions.prompt: Accounts Payable has credits of $400 and $150 and a debit of $200. What is its balance, on the credit side?
questions.hint: Bigger side minus smaller side.
questions.why: The credit side is bigger, so the balance is on the credit side.
questions.miss: Add the credits first, then take off the debit.

traps.why: That adds the debit too. A debit makes a liability smaller, so it is taken off.

questions.label: Receivable now
questions.prompt: What is the balance of Accounts Receivable after Jun 15?
questions.hint: Compare the debit and the credit.

options.why: That was the balance after Jun 8. The $300 credit on Jun 15 cancels it.

options.text: $0, because the club paid in full
options.why: The debit of $300 and the credit of $300 are equal, so nothing is left.
The credit equals the debit, so it does not leave a credit balance.
That adds the debit and the credit. The balance is the bigger side minus the smaller side.

questions.label: Assets after June
questions.prompt: After June, the liabilities total $2,250 and owner's equity is $4,820. By the accounting equation, what do the assets total?
questions.hint: Assets = Liabilities + Owner's Equity.
questions.why: The equation stays true after every transaction, so assets equal liabilities plus owner's equity.
questions.miss: Which side of the equation holds the assets? Add the other side.

traps.why: That subtracts. Assets are the sum of liabilities and owner's equity.

levels.title: Comparing statements
learn: You will tell a service, a retail and a corporation apart.
You will see what stays the same in all three.

cards.text: Kiran's Bike Repair is a service business: it sells work, here repairs, and it has no goods to resell. Its income statement shows repair revenue and expenses. Its balance sheet has assets such as cash, supplies and tools, and no stock of goods held for sale.

image.alt: A bike held in a repair stand with an open toolbox and a blank sign

cards.text: Pedal Parts is a retail business. It buys bike parts and resells them. Goods bought to be sold and not yet sold are called inventory, and inventory is an asset. When a part is sold, what it cost the business is an expense called cost of goods sold.

image.alt: Shelves of plain boxes in a parts shop with a spare wheel on the counter

cards.text: Gross profit is sales minus cost of goods sold. The other expenses come off after that. What is left is net income. Here are the figures for Pedal Parts: $1,600 of gross profit, $1,000 of other expenses, $600 of net income.

figure.title: Pedal Parts: Income Statement, one month

cards.text: The balance sheet of Pedal Parts has one new asset line, Inventory. The owner, Dana, is one person, so equity is one capital line, like Kiran's. Assets $7,000 = liabilities $2,000 + capital $5,000.

Wheelworks Inc. is a corporation: it is owned by shareholders, not by one owner. So its equity has two lines instead of one capital line. Share Capital is what the shareholders put in. Retained Earnings is the part of its earnings the business has kept. Together they are its total equity.

In all three businesses, Assets = Liabilities + Equity. Pedal Parts: $7,000 = $2,000 + $5,000. Wheelworks Inc.: $20,000 = $7,500 + $12,500. Only the lines inside the statements change from one kind of business to another.

image.alt: Three small level balance scales in a row on a shelf

questions.label: Service business
questions.prompt: Which sentence fits a service business like Kiran's?
questions.hint: Think of what Kiran sells.

options.text: It sells work and has no goods to resell
options.why: Kiran sells repairs, which is work. There is no stock of goods bought to be sold again.

options.text: It buys goods and sells them again
options.why: That describes a retail business.
Kiran is one owner. Shareholders own a corporation.

options.text: It reports inventory as an asset
options.why: Inventory is goods held for sale. Kiran has none, so there is no such line.

questions.label: What inventory is
questions.prompt: What is inventory?
questions.hint: It is a kind of asset a retail business holds.

options.why: That is accounts receivable.

options.text: The cost of the goods that were sold
options.why: That is cost of goods sold, an expense on the income statement.

options.text: Money the owner took out for personal use
options.why: That is drawings.

options.text: Goods bought to be sold and not yet sold, an asset
options.why: Inventory is the stock of goods waiting to be sold. It is an asset.

questions.label: Retail line
questions.prompt: Which line is on the income statement of a retail business but not on Kiran's?
questions.hint: Retail businesses sell goods.

options.why: That is Kiran's revenue line. A retail business's revenue comes from selling goods.
Both statements end in net income (or a net loss).
A business that resells goods records what those goods cost as cost of goods sold. Kiran has no goods to resell.
Both kinds of business can have this expense.

questions.label: Gross profit
questions.prompt: Pedal Parts has sales of $4,000 and cost of goods sold of $2,400. What is its gross profit?
questions.hint: Sales minus cost of goods sold.
questions.why: Gross profit is sales less the cost of the goods that were sold.
questions.miss: Take the cost of goods sold off the sales. The other expenses come later.

traps.why: That also takes off the other expenses. That gives net income. Gross profit comes before them.

questions.label: Net income
questions.prompt: Pedal Parts has gross profit of $1,600 and other expenses of $1,000. What is its net income?
questions.hint: The other expenses come off the gross profit.
questions.why: Net income is what is left of gross profit after the other expenses.
questions.miss: Take the other expenses off the gross profit.

traps.why: That adds the expenses. Expenses lower the result.

questions.label: Total assets
questions.prompt: Look at Pedal Parts. What are its total assets?
questions.hint: Add the three asset lines.
questions.why: Total assets add Cash, Inventory and Equipment.
questions.miss: Add all three lines, including the one that Kiran's statements do not have.

traps.why: That leaves out Inventory. Inventory is an asset too.

questions.label: Corporation equity
questions.prompt: Which lines make up the equity of Wheelworks Inc.?
questions.hint: A corporation has shareholders.

options.why: That is for a business with one owner, like Kiran's or Dana's.
A corporation shows two equity lines, one for what the shareholders put in and one for earnings it has kept.
Those are assets, not equity.
Those are liabilities, not equity.

questions.label: Total equity
questions.prompt: Wheelworks Inc. has share capital of $10,000 and retained earnings of $2,500. What is its total equity?
questions.hint: Add the two equity lines.
questions.why: A corporation's total equity is its share capital plus its retained earnings.
questions.miss: There are two lines. Add both.

traps.why: That is share capital alone. Retained earnings is part of the equity too.

questions.label: Liabilities by equation
questions.prompt: Wheelworks Inc. has assets of $20,000 and total equity of $12,500. By the accounting equation, what do its liabilities total?
questions.hint: Assets = Liabilities + Equity.
questions.why: Liabilities are what is left of the assets after the equity.
questions.miss: Liabilities and equity together equal the assets. Take the equity away from the assets.

traps.why: That adds the equity to the assets. Liabilities plus equity equal the assets.

questions.label: Same in all
questions.prompt: Which statement is true of the service business, the retail business and the corporation?
questions.hint: Look for what does not change.

options.why: The accounting equation is true for every business.

options.text: Equity is one owner's capital line
options.why: A corporation has Share Capital and Retained Earnings instead.

options.text: Each shows inventory as an asset
options.why: A service business has no goods to resell, so Kiran's has no inventory.

options.text: Each has cost of goods sold on its income statement
options.why: Only a business that resells goods has it. Kiran sells work.

levels.title: Accounting check-in
learn: You will journalize five new transactions and read the balances.
You will look back at the kinds of account and the balance sheet.

cards.text: A quick reminder of the sides. Assets, expenses and drawings grow on the debit side. Liabilities, capital and revenue grow on the credit side. The debits and the credits of every entry have the same total.

image.alt: A tidy workbench with a wrench, a notebook, a pencil and a small balance scale

cards.text: And of the equation. Revenue raises owner's equity. Expenses and drawings lower it. A balance sheet lists assets, liabilities and owner's equity on one date, and its two sides are equal. Kiran's balance sheet from June 1 is on the next card.

image.alt: A blank checklist on the wall above a small level balance scale

cards.text: This is Kiran's balance sheet at the start of June. You will use it for one of the questions.
July starts from where June ended. Here are the five July transactions. For each one, name the account debited and the account credited. Utilities Expense is the account for bills such as power.

figure.title: July transactions
rows: Paid the month’s rent in cash
Paid the power bill in cash
Repaired a school’s bikes on account

cards.text: You have opened a set of books, posted a month and kept the equation true. Each step was the same small step, repeated.

image.alt: A closed book with a ribbon bookmark and a pencil on a clean workbench

questions.label: Jul 2 entry
questions.prompt: Jul 2: Paid the month’s rent in cash. Which entry is right?
questions.hint: Rent is an expense. Cash is an asset that shrinks.

options.why: That is the wrong way round. An expense grows on the debit side, and an asset that shrinks is credited.

options.text: Debit Rent Expense, credit Repair Revenue
options.why: Kiran earned nothing here. The credit is Cash, because Cash went out.
Rent is a cost of running the business, an expense. Drawings is for money taken out for personal use.
Rent Expense grows, so it is debited. Cash shrinks, so it is credited.

questions.label: Jul 4 entry
questions.prompt: Jul 4: Repaired bikes for cash. Which entry is right?
questions.hint: Think about what each side of the entry does.

options.why: That is the wrong way round. Cash grew, so it is debited.

options.text: Debit Accounts Receivable, credit Repair Revenue
options.why: The customer paid in cash, so there is no amount owed to Kiran.
Cash grew, so it is debited. Revenue was earned, so it is credited.
Money earned from repairs is revenue. Capital is what Kiran put in.

questions.label: Jul 7 entry
questions.prompt: Jul 7: Bought supplies on account. Which entry is right?
questions.hint: No cash is paid yet. Kiran owes the supplier.

options.why: That is the wrong way round. Supplies grew, and an asset that grows is debited.
Supplies grew, so it is debited. Kiran owes the supplier, so Accounts Payable is credited.
Kiran did not pay yet. The supplies were bought on account.
Buying supplies earns no revenue.

questions.label: Jul 10 entry
questions.prompt: Jul 10: Paid the power bill in cash. Which entry is right?
questions.hint: Which expense account in the chart fits a bill like power?

options.why: The power bill is a utilities expense, so it is debited. Cash went out, so it is credited.
That is the wrong way round. An expense grows on the debit side.
This is the power bill, not rent. Its account is Utilities Expense.
Paying a bill does not earn revenue.

questions.label: Jul 15 entry
questions.prompt: Jul 15: Repaired a school’s bikes on account. Which entry is right?
questions.hint: The school has not paid yet, but the work is done.

options.text: Debit Repair Revenue, credit Accounts Receivable
options.why: That is the wrong way round. The asset grew, so it is debited.
The school has not paid, so no cash came in.

options.text: Debit Accounts Receivable, credit Accounts Payable
options.why: Accounts Payable is what Kiran owes. Here the school owes Kiran.

options.text: Debit Accounts Receivable, credit Repair Revenue
options.why: The school owes Kiran, so Accounts Receivable grew and is debited. The work earned revenue, so it is credited.

questions.label: Cash in July
questions.prompt: Cash was $2,400 at the end of June. After the Jul 2 rent, what is the Cash balance?
questions.hint: Cash is credited, so it shrinks.
questions.why: Rent paid in cash is a credit to Cash, so the balance falls.
questions.miss: Cash is credited here, which makes it smaller. Subtract the rent.

traps.why: That adds the rent. Paying rent is a credit to Cash, which makes it smaller.

questions.label: Assets in July
questions.prompt: After all five July transactions, liabilities total $2,340 and owner's equity is $4,910. What do the assets total?
questions.hint: Assets = Liabilities + Owner's Equity.
questions.why: The equation is still true after July's transactions.
questions.miss: Add the two amounts on the right side of the equation.

traps.why: That subtracts. Assets equal liabilities plus equity.

questions.label: Liability account
questions.prompt: Which of these accounts is a liability?
questions.hint: A liability is money the business owes.

options.why: That is money customers owe Kiran. It is an asset.
Supplies are something Kiran owns, an asset.
Accounts Payable is money Kiran owes to suppliers.
Revenue is what Kiran earns. It raises owner's equity.

questions.label: Effect on equity
questions.prompt: Jul 4: Repaired bikes for cash, $520. What does this transaction do to owner's equity?
questions.hint: Revenue raises owner's equity.

options.text: It lowers it, because Cash was debited
options.why: A debit to an asset makes the asset grow. The credit to revenue is what raises equity.

options.text: It raises it, because revenue was earned
options.why: Revenue raises owner's equity, so it grew by the amount earned.

options.text: It leaves it unchanged, because the sides cancel
options.why: Both sides of the equation grow: assets by the cash, equity by the revenue. The equation stays true, but equity changes.

questions.label: Total liabilities
questions.prompt: Look at Kiran's balance sheet at the start of June. What are the total liabilities?
questions.hint: Add the liability lines only.
questions.why: The liabilities are Accounts Payable and Bank Loan.
questions.miss: Use the debts only. Capital is not a debt.

traps.why: That adds the capital. Total liabilities are the debts only.
