sections.title: FinTech Marketplace
sections.blurb: Plan a small business, price its product, and read the numbers from two sales rounds.

units.title: The business idea
units.blurb: What a business is, and who will buy from yours.

levels.title: What a business is
learn: You will say what a business is and tell a product from a service.
You will test whether an idea can work.

cards.text: FIN1910 is a project course. Your group will plan a business, write its plan and pitch it. It is a plan on paper: your class does not really sell anything. The lessons here follow one example business, so you see each step done once.
Your project is not a course on its own. It draws on other CTS courses, and each one gives it a skill the project uses. This map shows where.

A business is a person or group that sells a product or a service to earn a profit. A product is a thing it makes or buys to sell. A service is work it does for a customer, such as a repair. Profit is what is left when the costs are taken away from the sales.

Kiran's Bike Repair, earlier on the road, sold a service, and Kiran owned it alone. North Star Pins sells a product: four Grade 10 students design enamel pins and sell them at their school's winter market. It is a partnership: a business owned by two or more people, called partners.
Not every idea works. Three tests help. Do people want it? Will they pay a price above what it costs? Can the group really get or make it? Here they are for North Star Pins.

figure.title: Is the idea workable?
rows: $6 a pin, and a pin costs $3
The group can get or make it
Pins the group can order and sell

cards.text: A brainstorm is a quick list of many ideas. Everyone adds ideas, and nobody says no until the list is long. Then the group tests each idea and keeps the best. Your group of three or four is your pitch group and your plan group.

questions.label: What a business is
questions.prompt: Which sentence describes a business?
questions.hint: Look for the aim of the business.

options.text: A place where people go to buy things
options.why: That is a shop or a market. A business is the person or group that sells there.

options.text: A person or group that sells a product or a service to earn a profit
options.why: Yes. A business sells to customers, and what it aims for is a profit.

options.text: A person who works for someone else
options.why: That is an employee. A business is the one that sells to customers.

options.text: A group that gives its products away free
options.why: A business earns a profit, so it needs money coming in from sales.

questions.label: Product or service
questions.prompt: Maya mows lawns for her neighbours. Does she sell a product or a service?
questions.hint: Ask what the customer gets for the money.

options.text: A product, because she uses a mower
options.why: The mower is her tool. What she sells is the work of mowing.

options.text: A service, because she does work for a customer
options.why: Yes. Mowing is work done for a customer, like a repair.

options.text: A product, because customers pay money
options.why: Customers pay money for products and for services. Ask what they get.

questions.label: Kind of owner
questions.prompt: Kiran owned the bike repair shop alone. Four students own North Star Pins together. What is North Star Pins?
questions.hint: How many people own it?

options.why: It sells a product, enamel pins, not work done for a customer.
That was Kiran's shop. North Star Pins has four owners.
A competitor is another business that sells to the same customers. This is about who owns the business.
Yes. A partnership is a business owned by two or more people, called partners.

questions.label: Course map
questions.prompt: Look at the map. Which course does the work of writing memos and letters draw on?
questions.hint: Find the row about writing.

options.why: The map puts books and statements here.
Yes. The map puts memos, e-mails, letters and speaking with Communication Strategies 1.
The map puts buying from another country here.

questions.label: Sales of ten pins
questions.prompt: North Star Pins sells 10 pins at $6 each. How much are the sales?

terms.meaning: The money a business takes in from selling.

questions.hint: Sales are the number of pins times the price of one.
questions.why: Sales are the money from selling: the number sold times the price.
questions.miss: Multiply the number of pins by the price of one pin.

traps.why: That adds the numbers. Sales come from multiplying.

questions.label: Profit on ten pins
questions.prompt: Each pin costs the group $3 to get ready to sell. The group sells 10 pins at $6 each and has no other costs. What is the profit?

terms.meaning: What is left when the costs are taken away from the sales. In the books it is called net income.

questions.hint: Work out the sales, then the costs, then take one from the other.
questions.why: Profit is what is left when the costs are taken away from the sales.
questions.miss: Find the sales and the costs of the 10 pins first. Profit is the difference.

traps.why: That is the sales, $60. The costs must come off to find the profit.

questions.label: A test that fails
questions.prompt: A group plans to sell pins for $2 each. Each pin costs the group $3 to get ready to sell. Which test does the idea fail?

figure.title: Is the idea workable?
rows: $6 a pin, and a pin costs $3
The group can get or make it
Pins the group can order and sell

questions.hint: Compare the price with the cost of one pin.

options.why: The case says nothing about whether people want pins.
Yes. At $2 the group takes in less than each pin costs.

options.text: The group can get or make it
options.why: The group can get the pins. The trouble is the price.

questions.label: Plan or sale
questions.prompt: What will your class do with its business idea in this project?
questions.hint: Think about the first card of this level.

options.text: Plan it on paper and pitch it
options.why: Yes. It is a plan on paper. The class does not really sell anything.
The class does not really sell. The project is a plan.

options.text: Borrow real money to start it
options.why: The money in the project is part of the plan, on paper.

options.text: Hand it to a real business to run
options.why: The group plans and pitches its own idea.

questions.label: Brainstorm rule
questions.prompt: A group is brainstorming. What should it do first?
questions.hint: The idea comes before the judging.

options.text: Choose the best idea at once
options.why: Choosing comes after the list is long.

options.text: Test each idea against the price
options.why: Testing comes after the list is made.
The plan comes after the group has chosen an idea.

options.text: Add many ideas without saying no to any
options.why: Yes. Say no later, when the group tests the ideas.

levels.title: Who will buy
learn: You will name a target market and read a competitor table.
You will read a quick survey to compare prices.

cards.text: A target market is the group of people a business most wants to sell to. "Everyone" is too wide to plan for. North Star Pins picks the students at its school's winter market. It then asks what those students want and what they will pay.
A competitor is another business that sells to the same customers. A competitor table lists them side by side. Here are three at North Star Pins' market, with what each sells and what it charges.
A competitive matrix goes one step further: it gives each competitor a strength and a weakness. A weakness is a gap your business may fill. A strength is a reason customers may go there instead.

figure.title: Strengths and weaknesses
rows: costs more and takes two weeks to arrive

cards.text: A survey is a short set of questions asked to many people, to learn what they want. North Star Pins asked 40 students: "What is the most you would pay for a pin?" Each student gave the highest price they would accept.

figure.title: Survey: the most each student would pay

cards.text: A student who would pay up to $8 would also pay $6 or $4. So the buyers at one price are everyone whose highest price is that price or more. Each price brings in the buyers times the price, if each buyer takes one pin.

figure.title: If each buyer takes one pin

cards.text: A survey only tells you what these 40 students said. It does not say how many pins will sell. Use it to compare prices and to spot a price that few would pay. Your group will do the same for its own business.

questions.label: Target market
questions.prompt: Which is the best description of a target market for North Star Pins?
questions.hint: It is the group the business most wants to sell to.

options.why: That is too wide to plan for. A target market is a chosen group.

options.text: The four partners of the business
options.why: The partners own the business. The target market is who they want to sell to.

options.text: The students at the school winter market
options.why: Yes. It is the group the business most wants to sell to, and it is specific.

options.text: The other businesses at the market
options.why: Those are competitors, not customers.

questions.label: Spot the competitor
questions.prompt: Which one is a competitor of North Star Pins at the market?
questions.hint: A competitor is another business.

options.text: A student who buys a pin

cards.text: A business makes four main choices about how it sells. Together they are the marketing mix: product, price, place and promotion. People call them the 4 Ps. A good mix suits the target market.

Place is where customers can buy. For North Star Pins it is a table at the school winter market. Promotion is how a business tells its target market about the product. Here it is posters and announcements. The posters cost $30.
Compare two mixes. The online pin shop sells the same kind of product, but its place and price are different. Each business fits its mix to its own customers.

levels.title: Price and product mix
learn: You will find a markup and price a product from its cost.
You will check a price against competitors and a survey.

cards.text: Cost per unit is what one item costs the business to get ready to sell. For North Star Pins it is $3 a pin. A later unit shows where the $3 comes from. A price below the cost per unit loses money on every pin.

Markup is the amount added to the cost per unit to make the price. Pricing from cost means picking a markup and adding it. As a percent of cost, the markup is markup divided by cost, times 100. Here it is $3 on a $3 cost, so it is 100%.

figure.title: North Star Pins: cost to price

cards.text: Pricing against competitors means looking at what they charge. A price far above theirs needs a reason, such as more designs or an easier place to buy. A price below the cost per unit loses money on each item. A price equal to it earns nothing on each item.

Now check the price against the survey. Sales minus the cost of the goods sold is gross profit. At each price, gross profit is the buyers times the price minus the cost per unit, if each buyer takes one pin.

A product mix is the set of different products a business sells. North Star Pins sells two designs, Aurora and Bison. Both cost the same to get ready to sell and sell at the same price. A mix gives buyers a choice.
Your group will do the same for its own business: find the cost per unit, choose a price, and check it against the competitors and a survey.

levels.title: The pitch
learn: You will name the parts of a pitch.
You will speak and introduce your team well.

cards.text: A pitch is a short talk that asks someone to back a business idea. Backing it means saying yes to going ahead. A pitch must be clear, quick and complete, because the listeners decide from what they hear.
A pitch has parts, and each part answers one question the listeners will have. Here are the parts, in the order a pitch can use.

figure.title: The parts of a pitch
rows: What do you sell, and why will it work?
How much does it take to start?

cards.text: One question is how much money it takes. Start-up money is the money a business needs before it can make its first sale. North Star Pins needs $750: $600 for the pins and $150 for the market costs.
An org chart shows who does which job in a business. Each North Star Pins partner has one role. A pitch names the team and their roles, so the listeners know who is responsible for what.

Speaking is oral communication. Your face, posture and hands are nonverbal language. Both tell the listeners how sure you are, so they should match your words. Here is what each skill looks like in a pitch.

figure.title: Speaking well in a pitch
rows: Steady pace, loud enough for the back
Look at the listeners, not only your notes
Stand upright and face the audience
Say your name and your role

cards.text: Start by saying who you are: your name, then your role. Introduce each teammate the same way. For example: "Hello, I'm Amara, the team lead of North Star Pins. This is Devon, our finance lead."

units.title: The plan on paper
units.blurb: The six sections of a business plan, and the memo, e-mail and letter a business writes.

levels.title: Section 1 and who does what
learn: Name the six sections of a business plan and say what section 1 holds.

cards.text: A business plan is a written plan that says what the business will sell, to whom, how, and with what money. North Star Pins uses six sections, always in this order. Your group will write the same six sections for its own business.

figure.title: The six sections of the plan

cards.text: Section 1 begins with the business description: what the business is. A partnership is a business owned by two or more people, called partners. North Star Pins is a partnership of four students.

Section 1 also holds the mission: one sentence that says what the business is for. It is not a sales goal and has no numbers. A mission for North Star Pins: "We design enamel pins that students are proud to wear."
An org chart is a list or drawing that shows who does which job. Each partner of North Star Pins has one role. A reader of the plan can see who to ask about the money, the pins or the sales.
A memo is a short written message to people inside a business. Choose the format before you write. Put the point first, then say what you want done and by whom.

figure.title: A memo from Amara
rows: Mei orders 200 pins. Devon checks the money first.

cards.text: An e-mail is a message sent on a screen. It may go to people inside or outside the business. Write a subject line that says what the message is about, then a greeting, the message and your name.

cards.text: Section 2 is the marketing plan. It writes down who the business sells to, and how. It starts with the target market. A target market is the group of people a business most wants to sell to. For North Star Pins, that is students who visit the school winter market.
Then the plan lists the marketing mix, or the 4 Ps: product, price, place and promotion. This table writes the 4 Ps for North Star Pins as a plan.

figure.title: The 4 Ps for North Star Pins
rows: Enamel pins in two designs: Aurora and Bison

cards.text: A plan also shows why the price fits. Here is the pin beside three competitors, which are other businesses that sell to the same customers. The pin costs more than the stickers and buttons, and less than the online shop.

A business letter is a formal letter from a business to someone outside it. A memo stays inside the business. A personal business letter is one you write for yourself, such as a job application. A business letter is written for the business. Pick the letter format before you write.

A business letter has a job. It can sell products or services, request information, answer inquiries or complaints, build goodwill, or keep a record. Before you write, name the purpose and the reader, list the details you need and put the points in order.
North Star Pins writes to its supplier to ask for the price of a pin, the smallest order and the delivery time. Each part of the letter has its own place.

cards.text: Section 3 is production and operations: how the product is made or bought, and who does what. North Star Pins imports its pins. To import is to buy goods from another country and bring them in. The supplier is in another country and sets its prices in US dollars.
The supplier charges US$1.50 a pin. An order of 200 pins is US$300.00. In class, US$1 = C$1.40, a made-up rate, only an example. Multiply by the rate: US$300.00 x 1.40 = C$420.00.

A tariff is a tax on goods that come in from another country. In this example the tariff is 10% of C$420.00, which is $42.00. It is only an example, not a real rate. Add shipping of $38.00. The landed cost is the full cost of imported goods once they arrive: the goods, the tariff and the shipping.

cards.text: Divide the landed cost by the pins: $500.00 / 200 = $2.50 a pin. Add the backing card and bag, $0.50 for each pin. That makes $3.00, the cost per unit: what one item costs the business to get ready to sell. The bars show where it goes.

levels.title: Section 4: the money to start, and break-even

cards.text: Section 4 is the financial plan. Start-up money is the money a business needs before it can make its first sale. For North Star Pins it is the stock plus the planned fixed costs. The stock is inventory: goods bought to be sold and not yet sold.

Each of the four partners puts in $150.00, which is $600.00. A loan of $150.00 is paid back after the market. A liability is a debt, so the loan is one. The partners' share is their equity: Partners' Capital.

figure.title: Where the start-up money comes from

cards.text: A fixed cost is a cost that stays the same however many items are sold. A variable cost is a cost that grows with each item sold. For North Star Pins, the variable cost is the cost per unit, $3.00 a pin.

The break-even point is the number of items a business must sell for its sales to cover all of its costs. Each pin sells for $6.00 and costs $3.00, so each pin leaves $3.00 toward the fixed costs. Step 1: $6.00 - $3.00 = $3.00. Step 2: $150.00 / $3.00 = 50 pins.
Check it. At 50 pins, sales equal all costs, so the business neither makes a profit nor falls short. Fewer pins leave it short. More pins make a profit.

When the money is collected, the balance sheet shows $750.00 in cash. The loan is a liability. Partners' Capital is the equity. Assets = liabilities + equity, as in Accounting Prep: $750.00 = $150.00 + $600.00.

levels.title: Reading a sales day
learn: You will read the results of a market day: pins sold, sales and cost of goods sold.
You will check the day against the forecast and the break-even point.

cards.text: The first market day is over, and the partners of North Star Pins read the results. Start with the count: how many pins of each design sold. Sales are the pins sold times the price, $6 a pin. Your class will read its own business's numbers the same way.

Before the day the partners made a forecast of 60 pins. A forecast is a careful estimate of future sales and costs, made before they happen. They sold 70 pins, which is 10 more. Comparing the two shows how good the estimate was.

Each pin cost the business $3 to get ready to sell: that is the cost per unit. Cost of goods sold is what the goods that were sold cost the business. It is the cost per unit times the pins sold, not the price: 70 x $3 = $210.

The partners ordered 200 pins and sold 70, so 130 are left. Goods bought to be sold and not yet sold are inventory. Inventory is counted at cost: 130 x $3 = $390. Added to the $210 sold, that is the $600 the 200 pins cost.

figure.title: Where the cost of the pins went

cards.text: The break-even point is the number of items a business must sell for its sales to cover all of its costs. At $6, each pin leaves $3 after its cost. The fixed costs are $150, so the break-even point for the whole plan is 50 pins. The first day alone sold 20 more than that.

levels.title: The income statement from sales
learn: You will build an income statement from a day of sales.
You will make the same statement before the day, as a forecast.

cards.text: An income statement shows what a business earned over a period. For North Star Pins the period is the first market day. It starts with sales, takes off cost of goods sold to reach gross profit, takes off the other expenses, and ends with net income.

Gross profit is sales minus cost of goods sold. The other expenses are the costs of running the day that are not the pins themselves. On the first market day there were four. Together they came to $120.

Here is the whole statement. Sales $420 less cost of goods sold $210 is gross profit $210. Gross profit less the other expenses $120 is net income $90. Net income is what is left once all the costs are taken away.

figure.title: Income Statement / For the first market day

cards.text: Section 5 of the plan is the Forecast. It is the same income statement, made before the day. The partners forecast 60 pins: sales 60 x $6 = $360, cost of goods sold 60 x $3 = $180, and the same $120 of other expenses. Your group will do the same for its own business.

figure.title: Income Statement / Forecast for the first market day

cards.text: Now put the forecast beside what happened. The day sold 10 more pins than the forecast. That made sales $60 higher and cost of goods sold $30 higher. The other expenses did not change, so net income was $30 higher.

A forecast is a careful estimate, so the result is rarely equal to it. What matters is the gap and why it happened. Here, ten more pins sold and nothing else moved. The partners can use that to make a better estimate next time.

units.title: Round two and the wrap

levels.title: Changes for the second day
learn: You will read what the partners changed for the second market day.
You will see what the changes did to pins, sales and gross profit.

cards.text: After the first market day the partners made two changes for the second. They lowered the price from $6 to $5, and they bought $20 more posters. Both aim at selling more pins. Your class will read its own second day the same way.

The cost per unit is still $3. What a pin leaves after its cost is the price minus the cost per unit. At $6 a pin leaves $3. At $5 it leaves $2. That is $1 less on every pin, so more pins are needed to cover the same costs.

The extra posters are a fixed cost, so the fixed costs rise from $150 to $170. Each pin now leaves $2, so the new break-even point is $170 / $2 = 85 pins, if every pin sold at $5. That is 35 more than before.

Now read the second market day. The partners sold 60 Aurora pins and 50 Bison pins at $5 each. That is 110 pins and $550 of sales. The whole plan needed 85 pins at $5 to cover all its costs, and this one day sold 25 more than that.

Set the two days side by side. The second day sold 40 more pins and had $130 more sales. Cost of goods sold rose by $120, so gross profit rose by only $10. More pins and more sales, but less gross profit on each pin.

levels.title: The balance sheet, and the two days side by side
learn: You will read the balance sheet after each market day.
You will compare the two days and explain why net income rose more than gross profit.

cards.text: A balance sheet shows what a business owns and owes on one date, and the partners' share. The partners put in $600 and took a $150 loan, repaid after the market. Assets = liabilities + equity: $750 = $150 + $600. The partners' share is one line, Partners' Capital.

figure.title: Balance Sheet / The day the money is collected

cards.text: After the first market day the business has less cash and some inventory. The partners paid $600 for the pins and $120 of expenses, and took in $420 of sales, so cash is $450. The 130 pins left are inventory at cost, $390.

figure.title: Balance Sheet / After the first market day

cards.text: Partners' Capital grew from $600 to $690. That is the first day's net income, $90. Net income links the two statements: what the business earned is added to what the partners own. Assets $840 = liabilities $150 + equity $690.
After the second market day cash is $950: the day took in $550 and paid $50 of expenses. Only 20 pins are left, worth $60 at cost. Partners' Capital is $690 + $170 = $860.

figure.title: Balance Sheet / After the second market day

cards.text: Here are the two days side by side, and both together. Read across: $90 + $170 = $260 of net income, and the 180 pins are the 70 and the 110.

Net income rose by $80, but gross profit rose by only $10. The other expenses explain it. The first day paid $120 of them and the second only $50, because the first day carried most of the fixed costs. Your group will compare its own two days the same way.

levels.title: Section 6: risks and conclusions
learn: You will name the risks in a plan and say what the partners could do about each.
You will write conclusions that point to numbers.

cards.text: Section 6 of the plan is Risks and conclusions. A risk is something that could go wrong and cost the business money. The section names the risks and what the partners could do about each. Then it says what the plan aimed for, what happened, and what they would change.

figure.title: The six sections of the plan

cards.text: Three risks come from buying the pins abroad. The supplier could be late and the pins could miss the market day. The exchange rate could move, so the same US dollars cost more. The tariff could change. Each one has something the partners can do.

figure.title: Risks of importing
rows: Order early; ask for a date

cards.text: Two risks come from selling. Pins can be left unsold: after both days 20 pins, $60 at cost, are left. And pin backs are sharp, so the table needs a safety rule, such as keeping the backs covered.
The conclusions compare the plan with what happened. The plan forecast 60 pins on the first day and 70 sold. It forecast $60 of net income and the day made $90. Of the 200 pins ordered, 180 sold.

Then the partners say what they would change next time, and they point to a number. For example, the second day sold 40 more pins, but each pin left $1 less, so gross profit rose by only $10. And 20 pins were left over. A good conclusion points to a number like these.

At the end the $150 loan is repaid, and the profit is shared equally. The two days made $260 of net income, so each of the 4 partners gets $65. That is one business, followed from its first idea to its last number.
